flashcards.back: Having upstream agents return key facts, citations and relevance scores instead of long prose and reasoning chains, when the downstream agent has a limited context budget.
flashcards.detail: Change the producer, not the consumer: verbose upstream output wastes the downstream window.

flashcards.back: Dates, source locations and methodological context carried alongside findings in a subagent's structured output, so downstream synthesis can interpret and reconcile them correctly.
flashcards.detail: Without it, numbers from different sources or periods cannot be compared fairly.

flashcards.back: For long documents, asking the model to extract word-for-word quotes first and base its analysis on them, which focuses it on the relevant text and reduces unsupported claims.
flashcards.detail: Docs recommend it for inputs over about twenty thousand tokens.

flashcards.back: The situations that justify handing a case to a human: an explicit request for one, a policy exception or gap the agent cannot decide, and an inability to make meaningful progress. Mere complexity is not on the list.
flashcards.detail: Make them explicit in the system prompt, with examples of escalating and of resolving.

flashcards.back: Transferring right away when a customer explicitly asks for a person, without first trying to investigate or resolve the issue.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with mere frustration, where offering a fix first is appropriate.

flashcards.back: When a customer is upset but has not asked for a person and the issue is within the agent's ability, acknowledging the frustration and offering a resolution, escalating only if they repeat the wish for a human.
flashcards.detail: It honors the customer without handing off cases the agent can fix.

flashcards.back: Escalating when the written policy is ambiguous or silent about the specific request, for example a competitor price match when the policy covers only adjustments to the company's own prices.
flashcards.detail: The agent should not improvise policy. A gap, not mere difficulty, is the trigger.

flashcards.back: Triggering a handoff from detected customer emotion. Sentiment does not track how complex or risky a case is, so it sends easy cases to humans and keeps hard ones with the agent.
flashcards.detail: An unreliable proxy for the thing that matters, which is whether the agent can resolve the case.

flashcards.back: A number the model gives for how sure it is of its own answer. It is poorly calibrated, since the model is often confident on exactly the hard cases it gets wrong, so it is a weak basis for escalation.
flashcards.detail: Confidence becomes usable only after calibration against labeled outcomes.

flashcards.back: When a lookup returns several candidates, such as multiple customers with the same name, asking the user for an additional identifier instead of choosing by a heuristic like recency.
flashcards.detail: Guessing the wrong account is worse than one more question.

flashcards.back: Explicit rules in the system prompt for when to escalate and when to resolve, backed by worked examples of both, which fix unclear decision boundaries before heavier infrastructure is considered.
flashcards.detail: The proportionate first fix when an agent escalates the wrong cases.

flashcards.back: An error report that gives the failure type, the query or action attempted, any partial results and possible alternatives, so a coordinator can pick an informed recovery.
flashcards.detail: It is what lets the coordinator choose between retrying, trying another source and continuing with what it has.

flashcards.back: Returning an empty or default result as if the step succeeded when it actually failed, so nothing downstream knows anything went wrong.
flashcards.detail: Worse than a visible failure: the coordinator reports a gap as if the topic had no findings.

flashcards.back: Terminating an entire multi-step workflow because one step failed, discarding the work already done when recovery or partial results were possible.
flashcards.detail: The opposite error to suppression. Both hide the useful middle path.

flashcards.back: Notes in a synthesized report marking which findings are well supported and which topic areas have gaps because sources were unavailable.
flashcards.detail: It lets readers trust the strong sections and see the weak ones.

flashcards.back: Returning whatever a failed or interrupted subagent had gathered before it stopped, together with the error, so the coordinator can use it rather than starting over.
flashcards.detail: Pair it with a note of what was attempted and what is missing.

flashcards.back: The drift in a long exploratory session where answers become inconsistent and the model cites "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it discovered earlier.
flashcards.detail: Counter it with scratchpad notes, subagent delegation, summaries between phases and compaction.

flashcards.back: A notes file in which an agent records key findings as it works and rereads for later questions, so facts survive context boundaries and compaction.
flashcards.detail: Docs use the same idea for long tasks: structured state in JSON, free-form progress notes, and git history.

flashcards.back: Handing specific questions, such as locating all test files or tracing a flow's dependencies, to subagents whose verbose output stays in their own context, while the main agent keeps the high-level picture.
flashcards.detail: The main agent coordinates and receives summaries instead of raw search output.

flashcards.back: Summarizing the findings of one exploration phase and placing that summary in the starting context of the agents that handle the next phase.
flashcards.detail: It avoids both rediscovery and carrying the whole earlier transcript forward.

flashcards.back: A file in a known location that records each agent's exported state, which the coordinator loads when resuming after a failure and injects into the agents' prompts.
flashcards.detail: Without it, a crash in a long multi-agent run means starting over.

flashcards.back: The Claude Code command that summarizes the conversation so far to free context while continuing the same session. Optional focus instructions steer what the summary keeps.
flashcards.detail: Use it when discovery output has filled the window; it differs from clearing, which discards the conversation.

flashcards.back: Claude Code's behavior of summarizing older conversation when the window nears its limit. The project-root instruction file is re-read from disk afterward, while instructions given only in chat can be lost.
flashcards.detail: Put anything that must persist in the instruction file, not in a one-off message.

flashcards.back: The Claude Code command that starts a fresh conversation with empty context, used between unrelated tasks or after repeated failed corrections.
flashcards.detail: It resets rather than summarizes, so carry over anything you still need.

flashcards.back: An API feature in which Claude summarizes earlier turns on the server so a long conversation can continue past the context limit without custom summarization code.
flashcards.detail: Currently in beta, available in on-demand and token-threshold forms.

flashcards.back: A context-editing strategy that removes the oldest tool results once the conversation passes a threshold, leaving placeholders, so agentic workflows do not drown in stale output.
flashcards.detail: Works by rule rather than by summarizing. Clearing invalidates cached prefixes, so clear enough to be worth it.

flashcards.back: A client-side tool through which Claude reads and writes files in a /memories directory that the application implements, giving agents persistence across context windows and sessions.
flashcards.detail: Claude requests the file operations and your code executes them against storage you control.

flashcards.back: The way an overall accuracy figure, such as 97 percent, can hide poor results on particular document types or fields.
flashcards.detail: Always break accuracy down by segment before reducing human review.

flashcards.back: Drawing random samples separately from each segment, such as document type or confidence band, to measure error rates and spot new failure patterns, including among high-confidence extractions.
flashcards.detail: It keeps checking the outputs that automation would otherwise stop checking.

flashcards.back: A per-field value the model reports for each extracted item, used to decide which fields need human review once the thresholds have been calibrated.
flashcards.detail: Finer-grained than a score per document, so reviewers see only the doubtful fields.

flashcards.back: Checking model-reported confidence against a labeled validation set and setting review thresholds from the accuracy actually observed at each confidence level.
flashcards.detail: Uncalibrated scores mislead. A 0.9 should mean roughly nine in ten are right.

flashcards.back: Measuring accuracy separately by document type and by field before reducing human review, to confirm that performance is consistent in every segment.
flashcards.detail: Automate a segment only after it passes on its own.

flashcards.back: Sending extractions with low confidence, or with ambiguous or contradictory sources, to human reviewers first, so limited review capacity goes where errors are likeliest.
flashcards.detail: Combine it with random sampling of the confident ones.

flashcards.back: A structured record linking each claim to its source URL or document name and a supporting excerpt, preserved and merged as findings pass through summarization and synthesis.
flashcards.detail: It is what makes a synthesized report auditable.

flashcards.back: The disappearance of where a claim came from when findings are compressed into summaries without carrying their source mappings along.
flashcards.detail: Prose summaries are where citations quietly vanish.

flashcards.back: Keeping both values when credible sources disagree and labeling each with its source, rather than silently choosing one.
flashcards.detail: Let the reader or coordinator reconcile with the evidence in view.

flashcards.back: Requiring publication or data-collection dates in structured outputs so that numbers from different times are not mistaken for contradictions.
flashcards.detail: A statistic that changed between 2021 and 2025 may be a trend, not a conflict.

flashcards.back: A report layout that separates well-established findings from disputed ones while keeping the original sources' characterizations and methods.
flashcards.detail: Readers can see at a glance where confidence is high.

flashcards.back: Presenting synthesized material in the form that suits it, such as financial data in tables, news as prose and technical findings as structured lists, instead of one uniform format.
flashcards.detail: Forcing everything into bullets destroys information.

flashcards.back: A design in which a document-analysis agent returns conflicting values explicitly annotated and the coordinator decides how to reconcile them before synthesis.
flashcards.detail: The analysis agent reports; the coordinator, which sees the whole task, decides.

questions.question: Maya's support agent runs on the Messages API. Her loop exits as soon as a response contains any text block. During testing the model often writes a short line such as "Checking the order now" in the same response as a tool request, so tasks silently stop half-way. What is the best fix?
options: Keep looping while the stop reason is tool_use, and finish only when it is end_turn
Scan each text block for completion phrases such as "done" before deciding whether to stop
Raise the maximum number of loop iterations so the model has more chances to finish
Tell the model in the system prompt never to write any text before it calls a tool
questions.explanation: The stop reason is the structured signal that the model wants tools run (tool_use) or has finished (end_turn). Text can accompany a tool request, so its presence says nothing about completion. Phrase scanning is brittle, a higher cap does not address the early exit, and forbidding text is a probabilistic prompt fix for a control-flow bug.

questions.question: A response arrives with stop_reason "tool_use" and three tool_use blocks. After your code has run all three tools, which next request lets the model continue correctly?
options: A fresh user message that summarizes the three tool outputs in plain prose and drops the earlier assistant turn
The three outputs inserted into the system prompt, with the assistant response removed
The assistant response, then one user message with a matching tool_result for each request
The assistant response, then a user message that opens with an explanatory text note before the results
questions.explanation: Each tool request must be answered by a tool_result block carrying the matching id, in the user message that directly follows the assistant message that made the requests, with the result blocks ahead of any text. A prose summary loses the pairing, and neither system-prompt placement nor a leading text note respects the required format.

questions.question: A helpdesk agent diagnoses employee laptop problems. Depending on the symptoms, the useful next step might be checking VPN logs, the device-management console or a licensing service, and each result changes what to check next. Which design best uses model-driven decision-making?
options: A coded decision tree that picks the diagnostic tools in a fixed order determined by the ticket category
A loop that offers all diagnostic tools and lets the model choose each next call from the results gathered so far
A keyword router that maps words found in the ticket text to a fixed list of tool calls to run in order
A classifier that selects a single tool up front and never allows a second request
questions.explanation: When the next step depends on what earlier results reveal, the model should decide, with each result appended to the history before the next iteration. Decision trees, keyword routers and one-shot classifiers are pre-configured paths: predictable, but unable to adapt to intermediate findings.

questions.question: A response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens", and its final block is a tool_use whose JSON input stops in the middle of a field. What should the loop do?
options: Run the tool with the partial input it received, filling any missing fields with sensible defaults
Treat the response as final and show whatever text it contains to the user
Append a user message saying "please continue" and send the history again
Retry the request with a higher max_tokens so the tool request can be completed
questions.explanation: A cut-off tool request has incomplete input and must never be executed. The output limit caused it, so the request is repeated with more room. Showing it to the user as if the reply were complete ignores the pending tool use, and a "continue" nudge would build on a broken block.

questions.question: An agent needs about 3 tool calls for simple requests and up to 14 for complex ones. To "be safe", an engineer makes a hard 8-iteration limit the only thing that ends the loop. What is the main problem?
options: Complex tasks are cut off mid-way, whereas the model's own end signal should decide normal completion
Eight is too generous; lowering it to match the typical three calls would cut cost without harming results
The model should count its own iterations, so the limit belongs in the system prompt instead of in code
The cap is a sound primary stop condition once it is logged, so the only gap is missing logging
questions.explanation: A fixed counter truncates legitimate long runs and says nothing about whether the work is done. The loop should end when the model signals it has finished (end_turn). A limit is still useful as a guardrail, but hitting it ends the run with an error result rather than a finished answer. Lowering it makes truncation worse, and prompt-side counting is unreliable.

questions.question: An Agent SDK run ends and your code finds no result text on the final message. Its subtype is error_max_turns. What does this indicate, and what is a sensible response?
options: The model answered with an empty string, so the identical prompt should simply be sent again
A tool crashed and the SDK discarded the answer, so the offending tool should be removed before rerunning
The run hit its turn limit before finishing; resume the session with a higher limit or split the task
The run succeeded but streamed its answer separately, so reassemble it from earlier assistant messages
questions.explanation: Only the success subtype carries a final result. error_max_turns means the cap on tool-use turns was reached with work unfinished. Every result message carries the session id, so the run can be resumed with a larger limit or divided into smaller tasks. It is not an empty answer, a crash, or a hidden success.

questions.question: One model response requests get_order_status and get_shipping_quote, two independent read-only lookups. How should the application respond?
options: Run only the first request now and expect the model to repeat the second on its next turn
Run both, then return both tool_result blocks together in the next user message
Send a separate user message as each tool finishes, so the model sees results as they arrive
Merge the two outputs into one tool_result and drop the second request id
questions.explanation: Every tool request needs its own result, matched by id, and all of them go back together in a single user message. Independent read-only calls can run concurrently. Splitting results over several messages breaks the required structure, dropping an id leaves a request unanswered, and skipping a call only adds a round trip.

questions.question: A developer finds that her agent seems to forget earlier tool output at every iteration. Her code builds each request from the original user message plus only the newest tool result. What explains the behavior?
options: The model needs a memory feature switched on before it can recall anything from earlier iterations
The max_tokens value is too small, so earlier tool results are cut off from the reply
tool_choice is set to auto, which resets the conversation state between consecutive tool calls
The API is stateless, so every request must resend the full history, tool calls included
questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless. New tool results only influence the next decision because the application appends them to the history and sends the whole list again, including the assistant's earlier tool requests. Sending just the latest result removes the context the model needs. The other options describe settings that do not wipe history.

questions.question: When you drive an agent with the Agent SDK's query function, which check best tells your code that the run finished its task successfully?
options: The final result message has the subtype success
The stream's last assistant message includes the word "complete"
The message stream ended without any further messages
At least one turn finished before the budget ran out
questions.explanation: The final result message reports how the loop ended: success for a normal finish, with separate subtypes for turn limits, budget limits and errors. Wording in prose is not a signal, a stream also ends after failures, and finishing a turn proves nothing about the outcome.

questions.question: In a due-diligence platform, the search agent passes its raw findings straight to the analysis agent to save a hop. After a search timeout, analysis quietly continues with half the data and nobody notices. Which redesign best fits the coordinator-subagent pattern?
options: Add retry logic inside the analysis agent so that it can re-request any missing data from the search agent
Give the analysis agent the search tools so that it no longer depends on the search agent at all
Route every hand-off through the coordinator, which sees each result and failure and decides what happens next
Introduce a shared scratchpad that both agents read and write in order to keep their data in sync
questions.explanation: A hub-and-spoke design keeps communication, error handling and information flow in one place, so the timeout becomes visible and a deliberate decision (retry, alternative source, or proceed with a caveat) can be made. Direct links hide failures. Extra retries or tools inside analysis blur roles, and a shared scratchpad is shared mutable state that makes results order-dependent.

questions.question: A compliance assistant is asked about "data-privacy obligations for small online retailers". The coordinator creates three subtasks, all about one European regulation, so the report ignores US state laws and card-payment rules even though every subagent did its job well. Which change most directly improves coverage?
options: Increase the number of search results each subagent retrieves per query so that every slice is covered more deeply
Have the coordinator list the topic's major dimensions, assign distinct partitions, and check the output for gaps
Add a second synthesis pass that rewrites the report so that it reads as more comprehensive and balanced
Move the synthesis step to a larger model so that it can infer the regulations that are missing from the findings
questions.explanation: The fault sits upstream of the subagents: the decomposition was too narrow, so nobody was assigned the other areas. Improving how the coordinator partitions the topic, and reviewing coverage afterwards, fixes the cause. More results per query only deepens the same slice, and a rewrite or bigger synthesis model cannot recover material that was never gathered.

questions.question: A research tool receives both broad requests ("compare five payroll vendors") and quick lookups ("what year was this firm founded?"). The coordinator always runs search, analysis, synthesis and report agents, so quick lookups take minutes and cost far more than needed. What is the best improvement?
options: Remove the report agent from every request, since most users only read the summary anyway
Run all four agents in parallel for every request so that the total time drops to a single step
Cache the answers to earlier lookups and otherwise keep the pipeline exactly as it is today
Let the coordinator judge each query's complexity and invoke only the specialists it needs
questions.explanation: Selecting subagents dynamically matches effort to the question: a simple lookup may need one search call, a broad comparison the full pipeline. Dropping the report agent breaks broad requests, the stages depend on one another so they cannot all run at once, and caching helps only repeated questions, not new quick ones.

questions.question: The first synthesis draft on "urban flood resilience" has strong engineering content but nothing about funding or insurance. What should the coordinator do next?
options: Spot the gaps, send targeted queries to search and analysis, then re-run synthesis with those new findings
Ask the synthesis agent to cover funding and insurance from its general background knowledge
Publish the draft as it stands, adding a note that funding and insurance were out of scope for this report
Restart the entire pipeline from the beginning, reusing the same decomposition as in the first attempt
questions.explanation: An iterative refinement loop lets the coordinator evaluate the output for gaps, re-delegate narrowly, and re-invoke synthesis until coverage is adequate. Asking synthesis to improvise sacrifices sourcing, a disclaimer leaves the gap, and a blind restart with the same decomposition would reproduce it.

questions.question: Three parallel search subagents each receive the same instruction, "research the electric-vehicle battery market", and return heavily overlapping sources. What is the best way to reduce the duplication?
options: Add a deduplication step in synthesis that removes repeated sources from the combined results
Run the subagents one after another so that later ones can see what earlier ones found
Assign each subagent a distinct slice, such as chemistry type, region or source type
Raise the sampling temperature of the subagents so that their queries differ more
questions.explanation: The overlap comes from identical assignments. Partitioning the scope up front means each agent explores something different and the union covers more. Deduplicating afterwards still wastes the work, sequential runs give up parallelism, and random variation does not guarantee coverage.

questions.question: A coordinator gives each web-research subagent a rigid twelve-step procedure. When a site blocks access at step four, subagents stall or return nothing. Which change to the coordinator's prompts is best?
options: Add a thirteenth step that tells the subagent exactly what to do whenever step four fails
State the goal and the quality criteria, and let each subagent choose how to meet them
Lower the temperature of the subagents so that they follow the procedure more precisely
Repeat the full procedure at both the start and the end of each prompt to increase compliance
questions.explanation: Goal-and-criteria prompts leave subagents room to adapt when a source is unavailable, which a step-by-step script cannot. Adding one more step only patches a single failure, and more precision or repetition makes the rigid script even more brittle.

questions.question: In a multi-agent research system, which task belongs to the coordinator rather than to a specialist subagent?
options: Running the web searches for one of the assigned subtopics and returning the sources it finds
Extracting figures and tables from a supplied report and returning them in a structured form
Writing the formatted sections of the final document from the findings it has been given
Judging whether the combined findings cover the question and deciding what to delegate next
questions.explanation: The coordinator owns decomposition, delegation, aggregation and the coverage decision. Searching, extracting and writing are specialist work that it hands out, and none of the specialists can see the whole picture needed to judge coverage.

questions.question: A user requests a market summary and attaches no documents. The pipeline still launches the document-analysis agent, which returns nothing after twenty seconds. What is the best design change?
options: Have the coordinator decide per query which specialists are relevant and skip those with no input
Let the document-analysis agent run in the background and ignore its result when it arrives
Instruct the document-analysis agent to browse the web for material whenever it has no documents to analyze
Shorten the timeout of every agent in the pipeline to five seconds so that failures surface quickly
questions.explanation: A coordinator that analyzes the request and invokes only the useful subagents avoids pointless work. Ignoring a running agent still spends the resources, telling an analysis agent to browse invites out-of-role tool use, and a tight global timeout would break legitimate slow tasks.

questions.question: A coordinator keeps re-delegating to close coverage gaps in a report. Which stopping rule is best?
options: Stop after exactly three rounds of re-delegation, whatever the synthesis contains at that point
Stop as soon as the draft reaches the target word count agreed with the client
Stop when the coverage check finds no material gaps, keeping a round limit only as a final backstop
Stop as soon as every subagent has returned at least one result to the coordinator
questions.explanation: The refinement loop should end on a coverage criterion, the same principle as ending an agent loop on the model's own signal rather than on a counter. A round limit is acceptable only as a backstop. Word count and "everyone replied once" say nothing about whether the topic is covered.

questions.question: An engineer defines three specialized subagents for a research coordinator, but at runtime the coordinator always answers on its own and never delegates. Its allowed-tools list contains only Read and Grep. What is the most likely fix?
options: Copy every subagent's tools into the coordinator's list so that the coordinator can do the work itself
Add the subagent-launching tool (Task in the guide, Agent in current SDKs) to its allowed tools
Rewrite each subagent's system prompt to state clearly that it may be invoked by the coordinator
Set the subagents' model to the coordinator's model so that they become eligible for delegation
questions.explanation: Delegation happens through a tool call. If the coordinator cannot use the tool that spawns subagents, it cannot delegate, however good the definitions are. Copying tools defeats specialization, a subagent's own prompt does not decide whether it can be launched, and the model choice has no bearing on eligibility.

questions.question: A coordinator passes web-search findings to a synthesis subagent as one long prose paragraph. The final report states facts but cannot say where any of them came from. Which change best preserves attribution?
options: Ask the synthesis agent to re-run searches afterwards to find a source for every statement it makes
Ask the search agent to write shorter summaries so that less detail is lost along the way
Add an instruction to the synthesis prompt telling it to cite sources wherever it possibly can
Pass findings as structured records that keep each claim apart from its source, page and date
questions.explanation: Structured records separate content from metadata, so attribution travels with each claim through the hand-off. Prose summaries are where citations disappear. Re-searching duplicates work, shorter summaries lose more, and a "cite where possible" instruction cannot cite what the agent was never given.

questions.question: A subagent named billing-analysis is repeatedly invoked for refund-policy questions it was never meant to handle. Which change to its definition most directly fixes the routing?
options: Rewrite its description to say what it is for and which requests it should not receive
Give it more tools so that it can answer refund questions correctly when they arrive
Move its instructions out of the definition and into the coordinator's own system prompt
Shorten its system prompt so that it appears to match fewer of the incoming requests
questions.explanation: The coordinator chooses a subagent by reading its description, so a precise description with explicit boundaries is the direct fix. More tools would reward the misrouting, moving instructions removes the specialization, and the subagent's internal prompt is not what the coordinator uses to route.

questions.question: After two hours of analyzing a payments module, an engineer wants to compare two refactoring strategies from the same understanding, without repeating the analysis and without the experiments affecting each other. What is the best approach?
options: Try the first strategy in the session, then ask the agent to undo it and try the second
Start two brand-new sessions and let each one re-analyze the module from scratch
Fork the analyzed session into two branches and continue each with a different strategy
Spawn two subagents that share one scratchpad file so they can compare notes as they work
questions.explanation: Forking copies the session's history into independent sessions, so the costly analysis is reused and the branches diverge cleanly. Undoing inside one session mixes the histories, re-analyzing wastes the earlier work, and a shared scratchpad brings back shared mutable state. Because forks branch the conversation but not the files, give edit-heavy experiments separate copies or worktrees of the code.

questions.question: A subagent meant only to review code sometimes edits files, even though its prompt already says "never modify files". What is the most reliable way to stop this?
options: Strengthen the wording in its prompt with capital letters and repeated warnings about editing
Restrict its tool list in its definition to read-only tools such as Read, Grep and Glob
Add few-shot examples showing the subagent politely refusing requests to edit files
Have the coordinator re-read every file the subagent touched after each run and revert changes
questions.explanation: A tool the subagent does not have cannot be misused, so restricting its tool list is a deterministic control. Emphatic wording and examples are still probabilistic, and auditing afterwards detects a violation instead of preventing it.

questions.question: The coordinator invokes a documentation subagent twice. The second prompt says, "Continue where you left off and add the security section." The subagent produces a document that ignores everything from the first run. What change fixes this?
options: Increase the subagent's maximum turns so that it can recall more of the earlier run
Tell the subagent in its system prompt to remember what happened in previous invocations
Switch the subagent to a model with a larger context window so more of the history fits
Put the first run's output into the new delegation prompt rather than relying on any memory
questions.explanation: Each invocation starts with a fresh context and no shared memory, so anything it needs from earlier work must be placed in the prompt (or the earlier subagent must be explicitly resumed). A turn limit, a "remember" instruction or a larger window cannot retrieve content that the new instance never received.

questions.question: The coordinator must brief a document-analysis subagent about five uploaded contracts. Which delegation prompt is best?
options: The goal, the contract text or paths, the fields to return with source page and date, and how to handle missing fields
A brief request to "analyze the contracts we discussed earlier", relying on the subagent's own judgment to fill in the rest
A numbered click-by-click procedure for opening each file and scrolling to each clause, with no goal or output format stated
A pointer telling the subagent to read the coordinator's conversation history for the details of the five contracts
questions.explanation: A good delegation prompt is self-contained: objective, the actual material, the output structure including metadata, and handling for missing data. Subagents cannot see the coordinator's history, so references to earlier discussion fail, and a procedure without a goal leaves the subagent unable to adapt.

questions.question: Five parallel subagents return findings as free-form text in five different styles, and the coordinator struggles to merge them and keep track of sources. What is the best fix?
options: Ask the synthesis agent to normalize all five styles on its own, whatever form the findings arrive in
Limit each subagent's response to one hundred words so that the styles become more similar
Define one structured output format (claim, evidence, source, date) that every subagent must use
Run the subagents one after another so that each one can imitate the style of the previous one
questions.explanation: A shared structured format makes merging mechanical and keeps metadata attached to each claim. Pushing normalization to synthesis hides the problem, a word limit discards information, and sequential imitation sacrifices parallelism without guaranteeing consistency.

questions.question: A coordinator needs the same kind of lookup for four independent regions. It currently launches one subagent per turn, so latency is about four times a single lookup. What change produces genuine parallelism?
options: Raise the coordinator's maximum number of turns so that it can get through the regions faster
Have the coordinator emit all four subagent calls in a single response
Switch the subagents to a smaller model so that every turn finishes sooner
Chain the subagents so that each passes its context on to the next one
questions.explanation: Parallel subagents come from multiple subagent-launching calls in one coordinator response, so the four tasks run at once and the total time approaches the slowest of them. A turn limit does not change the schedule, a smaller model only shortens each serial step, and chaining forces the tasks to run in order.

questions.question: A prescription-refill assistant has the tools verify_patient, check_insurance and submit_refill. Audit logs show that in about 4% of sessions submit_refill is called before verify_patient has returned a match, and one refill went to the wrong account. Which change most effectively prevents this?
options: Add a bold warning to the system prompt that verification must always come first, before any other tool
Add five few-shot examples in which verify_patient is always called before anything else
Reject submit_refill in the execution layer until verify_patient has returned a verified id
Lower the temperature so that the assistant follows the prescribed order more consistently
questions.explanation: The rule is a strict ordering requirement with serious consequences, so it needs a deterministic gate in code. Prompt warnings, examples and lower temperature all reduce the failure rate but leave a non-zero chance that a refill is submitted unverified.

questions.question: An expense agent has an approve_payment tool. Policy says any payment above $2,000 needs a finance manager. The prompt already states the rule, but a few larger payments were approved anyway. What should the team add?
options: A pre-execution hook that denies approve_payment above the limit and routes the case to a finance manager
A post-execution hook that reads each approval result and warns the finance team once the payment has gone out
A second paragraph in the system prompt that restates the threshold in capital letters, with an example
A weekly report of every approval above the threshold, for the finance team to review manually
questions.explanation: A pre-execution hook sits in front of the action, blocks it deterministically, and its reason can steer the agent to the human workflow. A post-hoc warning or weekly report detects the violation after money has moved, and restating the rule is still prompt-based.

questions.question: When a support agent escalates a billing dispute, the human agent works in a different system without access to the AI transcript and receives only a case id and the note "customer unhappy". Humans spend minutes re-asking questions. What is the best improvement?
options: Add a longer free-text note that describes the whole conversation in chronological order, turn by turn
Ask the model to rate the customer's mood from one to ten and include the score in the note
Give the human agents read access to the model's raw tool logs for every case they receive
Have the agent compile a structured summary: customer, root cause, amounts, actions, next step
questions.explanation: Humans without the transcript need a compact, structured handoff containing exactly what they must act on. A long chronological note buries the facts, a mood score does not help resolve the dispute, and raw logs shift the analysis work onto the human.

questions.question: A customer writes one message with three issues: a double-charged invoice, a delayed shipment, and a request to change the delivery address on a pending order. Which approach gives the best result?
options: Resolve the first issue completely, then ask the customer to send the others as separate messages
Split the message into three items, investigate them in parallel with shared context, and reply once
Pick the most urgent issue and escalate the other two to human agents without investigating them
Work through the three issues one after another in the order mentioned, replying separately after each one
questions.explanation: Decomposing a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigating them concurrently with shared context, and synthesizing a unified answer is both faster and a better customer experience. Pushing work back to the customer, over-escalating, or replying piecemeal wastes time.

questions.question: A fintech team notes that its prompt clearly says wire transfers require a second confirmation, and testing shows 99.5% compliance. Why is that still not enough for the transfer tool?
options: Prompts cannot refer to tool names, so the rule was probably never seen by the model at all
A rate of 99.5% is acceptable, so the team only needs to log the remaining cases for later review
Prompt compliance is probabilistic, so irreversible financial actions need a gate enforced in code
Models ignore the system prompt after the first five turns, so the rule must be repeated
questions.explanation: Instruction-following is probabilistic, and for irreversible financial actions the remaining failures are unacceptable. A code-enforced prerequisite gives a guarantee that prompt wording cannot. Prompts can name tools, and logging the violations is detection, not prevention.

questions.question: A gate blocks process_refund until get_customer has succeeded. In testing, when the gate fires, the agent retries the same refund call five times and then apologizes to the customer. How should the gate respond to a blocked call?
options: Return an error saying verification must come first, so the agent can verify and retry
Silently drop the call and return an empty success so that the agent simply moves on to the next step
End the whole support session immediately to avoid any chance of an endless retry loop
Allow the call through, but write a warning to the log so that the team can review it later
questions.explanation: A gate should block deterministically and also tell the agent why and what to do next, which turns the denial into a recovery path. Silent success hides the problem, ending the session is heavy-handed, and letting the call through defeats the gate.

questions.question: An escalate_to_human tool accepts a single free-text "reason" parameter. Human agents complain that escalated cases often lack key facts. What is the best redesign?
options: Add a line to the prompt telling the model to write longer and more detailed reasons for every escalation
Let human agents ask the model follow-up questions after the escalation has been sent
Switch to a more capable model so that its free-text reasons become more complete and consistent
Make customer id, root cause, amount, actions taken and next step required fields in the schema
questions.explanation: Making the handoff fields required in the schema means an incomplete handoff cannot be produced, so quality does not depend on the model remembering to include everything. Longer free text, a better model and later follow-up questions are all indirect fixes for a structural gap.

questions.question: Which requirement for a customer-service agent is the best candidate for programmatic enforcement rather than prompt guidance?
options: Replies should use a friendly and concise tone that matches the brand voice
Refunds must never be issued for an account that has not been verified
Summaries should mention the order number whenever one is available in the case
The agent should apologize to the customer whenever a delivery is running late
questions.explanation: Rules with financial or security consequences need deterministic enforcement. Tone, helpful details and courtesy are quality preferences where occasional lapses are tolerable, so prompt guidance is the proportionate tool.

questions.question: A customer message contains three separate issues, and each will be investigated by its own parallel subagent. How should the customer identity step be handled?
options: Each subagent verifies the customer on its own, to keep the three investigations independent
Only the first subagent verifies the customer, and the others proceed without checking
Verify the customer once and share the verified record with every investigation
Let the subagents take turns writing to one shared customer record so they stay in sync
questions.explanation: Verifying once and passing the verified record to each investigation avoids duplicate lookups and keeps every branch working from the same facts. Repeating the check wastes calls, skipping it in some branches breaks the prerequisite, and a shared writable record introduces order-dependent state.

questions.question: An agent combines three third-party MCP tools that you do not control. They return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings and "MM/DD/YY" text, and the agent sometimes compares them incorrectly when computing a deadline. What is the most robust fix?
options: Add a table of the three date formats to the system prompt and ask the agent to convert each value carefully
Register a post-execution hook that converts the dates in tool results to one format before the model reads them
Give the agent a calculator tool and ask it to convert dates whenever it happens to notice a mismatch
Ask the owners of the three third-party tools to change their output formats to match each other
questions.explanation: A post-execution hook transforms results deterministically, before the model reasons over them, and works even for tools you cannot change. Prompt tables and on-demand conversion rely on the model noticing every case, and waiting for third parties to change their formats is not a solution you control.

questions.question: A procurement agent can call create_purchase_order. Company policy forbids orders above $10,000 without human approval. Which implementation best matches the recommended pattern?
options: A prompt rule plus a few-shot example showing the agent refusing to create a very large order
A post-execution hook that cancels any over-limit order shortly after it has been created
A scheduled job that scans all purchase orders each night and flags the large ones for review
A pre-execution hook that blocks over-limit calls and points the agent to human approval
questions.explanation: Intercepting the outgoing call prevents the violation and redirects the agent to an alternative workflow. Prompt guidance is probabilistic, and cancelling or flagging afterwards means an unauthorized order already existed, however briefly.

questions.question: A legal-research agent must never send documents tagged "privileged" to an external summarization tool. The tag is part of each document's metadata passed in the tool call. Which hook design is correct?
options: Register a pre-execution hook for that tool and inspect the document tags in its input inside the callback
Register a hook whose matcher is the word "privileged", so that it fires only for those documents
Add a few-shot example that shows a privileged document being withheld from the external tool
Register a post-execution hook that deletes any summary created from a privileged document
questions.explanation: Hook matchers select by tool name, not by argument content, so the content check belongs inside the callback, which can then deny the call before the document leaves. A matcher on the tag cannot work, examples are probabilistic, and deleting the summary after the fact does not undo the disclosure.

questions.question: Two pre-execution hooks apply to the same Bash call. One returns allow, the other returns deny with a reason. What happens?
options: The call runs, because the first registered hook decides the outcome
The user is always asked to decide, because the hooks disagree
The call is blocked, because a deny outranks the other answers
The outcome is random, because hooks for one event run in parallel
questions.explanation: When decisions conflict the most restrictive one wins: deny beats defer, ask and allow, so any single deny blocks the call. Hooks do run in parallel, but the combination rule is deterministic, which is why independent safety hooks can be stacked without ordering concerns.

questions.question: A team wants to stop a delete_records tool from touching production tables. A colleague proposes a post-execution hook that restores the rows if a production table was affected. What is the main weakness?
options: Post-execution hooks cannot see the arguments that the tool was called with
Post-execution hooks run after the side effect, so they cannot prevent it
Post-execution hooks consume a large amount of context in every single request
Post-execution hooks cannot be attached to tools that come from MCP servers
questions.explanation: Prevention requires intercepting the call before it executes. A post-execution hook receives the tool input and can be attached to MCP tools, and hooks run in the application process without using context. Its limitation is timing, not visibility.

questions.question: A pre-execution hook denies refunds above a limit. After the denial the agent simply tells the customer it cannot help. What change would improve the outcome most?
options: Switch the denial to an allow decision and attach a warning for the finance team
Remove the hook and rely on the prompt to describe the limit and what to do next
Make the hook retry the blocked call three times before it finally denies it
Put the next step in the denial reason, e.g. "over limit; escalate to a human agent"
questions.explanation: A denial reason is read by the model, so it can carry the redirect that turns a dead end into an escalation. Allowing the call defeats the control, dropping the hook loses the guarantee, and retrying a policy denial cannot change the outcome.

questions.question: You want a hook to audit calls to every tool from your "crm" MCP server without firing for built-in tools. Which matcher is the best fit?
options: A pattern that matches tool names beginning with mcp__crm__
The exact tool name "crm", written as a plain string without a pattern
A pattern that tests the tool arguments for the string "crm"
The pattern "Bash|Edit|Write", which selects the built-in file and shell tools
questions.explanation: MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, so a pattern on that prefix selects exactly one server's tools. There is no tool named just "crm", matchers do not inspect arguments, and the pattern naming Bash, Edit and Write selects built-in tools.

questions.question: A support agent needs two controls: (a) refunds above a limit must be blocked, and (b) timestamps in order-lookup results must be converted to one format. How should the hooks be placed?
options: Both as pre-execution hooks, since those run first and can see everything
Both as post-execution hooks, since those can see the complete results
Block in a post-execution hook, and convert in a pre-execution hook
Block in a pre-execution hook, and convert in a post-execution hook
questions.explanation: Blocking has to happen before the action runs, so it belongs in a pre-execution hook. Normalizing data happens after a tool returns and before the model reads the result, which is a post-execution hook. The other combinations put each control at a point where it cannot do its job.

questions.question: A deployment-configuration change touches 22 YAML files. A single-pass automated review gives rich feedback on the first few files, one-line remarks on the rest, and calls a naming pattern wrong in one file while approving the same pattern in another. Which restructuring addresses the cause?
options: Review each file in its own pass, then add an integration pass over the cross-file relationships
Add "give every file equal attention and do not skim" to the review prompt, with an example
Raise the output token limit so that the reviewer can write more comments for each file
Sort the files alphabetically so that the order in which they receive attention is predictable
questions.explanation: Uneven depth and contradictory verdicts are signs of attention dilution from reviewing too much at once. Focused per-file passes give consistent depth, and a dedicated integration pass handles cross-file concerns. A prompt reminder, a longer output and a sorted order do not change how thinly attention is spread.

questions.question: For which job is a fixed prompt chain the best fit?
options: Investigating an unfamiliar production outage where each finding decides the next step
Exploring a legacy codebase to decide where new tests would help the most
Debugging a failing build whose cause is not yet known and may lie anywhere
A weekly report that always extracts, validates, summarizes and formats in a fixed set order
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining suits predictable, repeatable steps whose order never changes. The other three are open-ended investigations where the next subtask depends on what was just found, which calls for dynamic, adaptive decomposition.

questions.question: A team must add test coverage to a ten-year-old billing codebase that nobody fully understands. Which plan is best?
options: Generate tests for each file in alphabetical order until the coverage target is reached
Map the structure, find high-impact areas, build a prioritized plan, and revise it as you learn
Ask the model to write a complete test plan for the entire repository up front and follow it unchanged
Start with the largest file and keep writing tests there until the context window is full
questions.explanation: Open-ended work needs an adaptive plan: understand the structure first, put effort where it matters, and update the plan as discoveries change it. Alphabetical order, a rigid up-front plan and size-based ordering ignore what the code actually contains.

questions.question: Why does splitting a large review into per-file passes followed by an integration pass tend to improve results?
options: It lets the review run on a model with a much larger context window than before
It lets the reviewer skip any files that look unimportant to the integration pass
It narrows each pass, so attention is not spread thin and cross-file issues get a dedicated look
It guarantees that the per-file pass and the integration pass can never disagree with each other
questions.explanation: Focused passes counter attention dilution, and the separate integration pass makes sure interactions between files are examined deliberately. It does not change the context window, it is not about skipping files, and it cannot guarantee agreement.

questions.question: During a dependency-upgrade investigation, the agent discovers that three services share a deprecated client library that was not in the original plan. What should happen to the plan?
options: Add subtasks for those services, re-prioritize the plan, and continue with the updated plan
Keep to the original plan and mention the three services only in the final report
Stop and ask the user to write a completely new plan before any further work is done
Ignore the finding because it was outside the scope of the original upgrade plan
questions.explanation: Adaptive investigation plans are meant to grow subtasks from what each step discovers. Ignoring or deferring a material finding wastes the discovery, and stopping to request a full rewrite is unnecessary friction.

questions.question: Which result of a single-pass review of many files most clearly points to attention dilution?
options: Uneven depth, missed obvious bugs and contradictory verdicts on identical code patterns
The reviewer repeats the same generic comment on every single file in the change
Comments are accurate but arrive in a different order from the files in the diff
The reviewer refuses to comment on any file that is larger than a few hundred lines
questions.explanation: Attention dilution shows up as inconsistent quality: some files get depth, others a glance, and the same pattern is judged differently in different places. Boilerplate repeated on every file, an odd ordering of comments, or refusals on long files are different failure modes.

questions.question: After per-file review of a 12-file change, every file looks fine on its own, yet a changed return type in one module breaks callers in two others. Which part of the design should catch this?
options: A stricter prompt for the per-file passes that tells them to look harder for cross-file effects
A dedicated integration pass that gets the per-file findings and the changed interfaces
Running each per-file pass a second time with a different random seed and merging the results
A lower sampling temperature on the per-file passes so that their output is more consistent
questions.explanation: Problems that live between files are invisible to passes that see one file. The integration pass exists to examine data flow and contracts across them. Repeating or tightening the per-file passes cannot reveal what they never look at.

questions.question: An engineer investigates a flaky test over several days, closing her terminal each evening, and also runs other Claude Code sessions in the same directory. Which workflow keeps the investigation continuous?
options: Paste a fresh summary of yesterday's findings into a brand-new session every morning
Use the continue option each morning, which reopens whichever session was most recent
Name the session at the start and reopen it later with claude --resume and that exact name
Keep a single terminal open for the whole week and never close the laptop lid
questions.explanation: A named session can be resumed directly with its context intact, even when other sessions have been active in between. The continue option picks the most recent session, which may belong to different work, and re-pasting summaries throws away the actual history.

questions.question: Yesterday an agent analyzed a service's module structure. Overnight a teammate refactored four of its files. The engineer resumes the session to get a test plan. What is the best way to proceed?
options: Resume it and tell the agent which four files changed so that it re-reads those before planning
Resume it and proceed, because the stored analysis stays valid until the session is deleted
Delete the session and require the agent to re-read the entire repository
Ask the agent whether it believes any file has changed since it last looked
questions.explanation: Most of the analysis is still valid, so a targeted update is efficient: name the changed files and let the agent refresh just those. Trusting stale results risks wrong conclusions, a full restart is wasteful, and the agent has no way to notice changes it has not looked at.

questions.question: A long session explored a large codebase. Since then, sixty commits have been merged that touch most of the modules it analyzed. What is the most reliable way to continue the work?
options: Resume the old session and trust its earlier findings, since they were verified at the time
Fork the old session and trust the findings in the fork, because a fork starts clean
Resume the old session and ask the agent to double-check everything it remembers
Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of findings that still hold
questions.explanation: When most prior tool results are stale, a fresh session with a distilled summary is more reliable than carrying a history full of outdated file contents. Resuming or forking inherits the staleness, and asking the agent to self-verify memories it cannot re-observe does not fix it.

questions.question: An engineer forks a session to try an experimental refactoring. What is true of the original session?
options: It receives the fork's new messages, so that both sessions stay in sync with each other
It stays unchanged, and the fork gets a new session id of its own
It is deleted as soon as the fork has been created, to avoid duplicate histories
It automatically reverts any file edits that were made inside the fork
questions.explanation: A fork copies the history into a new, independent session; the original is untouched and can be resumed on its own. Forking does not sync the two, delete the original, or roll back files, because sessions store conversations rather than file state.

questions.question: Two engineers want to continue from the same completed codebase analysis, each exploring a different design. Both resume the original session, one in each terminal. What goes wrong?
options: Both sets of messages land in one shared transcript and interleave; forking was needed
The second resume fails with an error, because a session can only be resumed one time
Each engineer silently receives a private copy of the session, so nothing goes wrong at all
The session is converted into a subagent that both engineers now share and can message
questions.explanation: Resuming the same session in two places without forking mixes both conversations into a single history. Fork gives each person an independent branch from the shared baseline.

questions.question: A service runs one agent conversation per customer and must reopen a particular customer's earlier conversation days later. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Store the session id for each customer and resume that specific session
Use the continue option so the latest session in the directory is reopened
Fork the newest session each time and rename it after the customer
Always start fresh and hope the model remembers prior customers
questions.explanation: Resume with a specific id is for exactly this case: several sessions exist and you need a particular one. Continue would reopen the most recent session, which may belong to another customer, and the model has no memory outside the history it is given.

questions.question: An agent in a forked session edited several files to test approach B. The engineer now returns to the original session to try approach A in the same working directory. What must she keep in mind?
options: Forking rolled the files back when she switched sessions, so she can start on approach A right away
The original session restores its own file versions whenever it is resumed, so nothing is lost
The fork's edits are quarantined to the fork and are invisible to every other session
Sessions store the conversation, not the files, so approach B's edits stay on disk unless they are reverted
questions.explanation: Session history and the filesystem are separate. Edits made by any branch are real files that every other branch will see, so experiments that write code need separate copies or worktrees, or the changes must be reverted first.

questions.question: A support agent has two tools, search_tickets and search_knowledge_base. Which description of search_tickets gives the model the best basis for choosing it correctly?
options: Searches the support platform quickly and reliably, returning the most relevant information for whatever the user is looking for, whether that is a case, an article, an account or a policy document, ranked by relevance.

Searches support tickets (open and closed) by keyword or ticket number such as TCK-1042 and returns id, status and last update for up to 20 matches. Use it for a specific case or customer history; for how-to questions use search_knowledge_base.

Looks up tickets in the support system. Takes a query string as input and returns the tickets that match it. Use this tool whenever a user request has anything at all to do with support, customers, orders or accounts.

Searches both support tickets and knowledge-base articles in one call, so case lookups and how-to questions can all be sent to this tool, and it will return whichever kind of record matches the query best.
questions.explanation: A good description says what the tool does, what inputs it accepts (with an example format), what it returns, and when to use it versus its neighbor. The vague, over-broad and overlapping alternatives all leave the model guessing, and the last one actively erases the boundary between the two tools.

questions.question: An agent has find_documents and search_documents, both described as "Searches the document store". It picks between them almost at random. Which change best removes the problem?
options: Add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to alternate between the two tools on successive requests
Merge both into a single tool that guesses internally which kind of search it should run for each query
Add six few-shot examples of correct tool choices to the prompt without changing the tool definitions
Rename and rewrite them so each has its own purpose and boundary, e.g. exact lookup by id versus topic search
questions.explanation: The root cause is overlapping, near-identical descriptions. Giving each tool a distinct name, contract and "use this instead of that" boundary fixes the cause. Alternating is meaningless, merging hides the ambiguity inside the tool, and examples add tokens without correcting the definitions the model reads.

questions.question: After a prompt edit that added "Always check the customer's history before answering billing questions", the agent calls get_history even for "how do I update my card?". Both tool descriptions are unchanged and clear. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The new line tied "billing" to get_history; reword it to say exactly when that history is needed
The get_history description is too long, so it should be cut down to a single short sentence
The sampling temperature is too high, so lower it step by step until the behavior disappears
Strict tool use is switched off, so enable it in order to restrict which tool gets called
questions.explanation: Keyword-sensitive wording in the system prompt can override good tool descriptions by tying a topic to a tool. The fix is to state the condition exactly, for example only for disputes about past charges. Shortening a clear description, changing temperature or strict mode do not address the association, and strict mode only constrains argument shapes.

questions.question: A tool called process_document takes a "mode" string. Depending on the mode it extracts fields, writes a summary, or checks a claim against a source, and each mode returns a different shape. The agent often picks the wrong mode. What best fits the recommended design?
options: Add a longer system-prompt paragraph that explains each mode and its output shape in detail
Rename the tool process_anything so that its breadth is obvious to the model
Split it into purpose-specific tools, each with its own input and output contract
Use forced tool selection so that the model must name the correct mode before every call
questions.explanation: One tool serving several purposes with different output contracts is overloaded. Splitting it into focused tools such as extract, summarize and verify gives the model clear choices and callers predictable outputs. More prompt text, a vaguer name or forced selection leave the overload in place.

questions.question: A tool lookup_shipment accepts either a tracking number or an order number, but its description just says "Look up a shipment". Users often supply the wrong kind of identifier and receive empty results. Which description change helps most?
options: Add a sentence saying that the tool is very reliable and should be used as often as possible
Give accepted formats with examples (tracking number versus ORD-12345), the output, and a boundary
Remove the description entirely so that the schema alone defines how the tool is used
Make the description as long as possible by adding the full history of the shipping system
questions.explanation: Input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries are exactly what a model needs to call a tool correctly. Praise adds nothing, removing the description removes the main selection signal, and sheer length without relevant detail does not help.

questions.question: A team exposes 40 tools from five systems. Many have generic names such as search, get and list, and selection errors are climbing. Which change helps most?
options: Shorten the names further so that they use fewer tokens and are quicker for the model to scan
Sort the tool list alphabetically before sending it, so that related tools sit next to each other
Add a one-line usage example for each tool to the matching section of the system prompt text
Prefix each name with its service and resource, such as jira_search_issues, with distinct descriptions
questions.explanation: Namespacing by service and resource removes ambiguity as the toolset grows, and distinct descriptions finish the job. Shorter names remove information, ordering does not change what the names mean, and generic examples do not separate similar tools.

questions.question: Customers often say "receipt" when they mean an invoice, and the agent calls search_orders instead of lookup_invoice. Neither description mentions receipts. What is the best fix?
options: Add example phrasing, including "receipt", and a clear boundary to the description of lookup_invoice
Ask customers to use the word "invoice" instead of "receipt" in the chat widget instructions
Delete search_orders so that the agent has no other tool to choose for these requests
Add a system-prompt rule that any message containing the word "receipt" must call lookup_invoice
questions.explanation: Putting realistic user phrasing and a clear boundary in the tool description teaches the model when the tool applies. Asking customers to change their vocabulary is unreliable, deleting a needed tool breaks other requests, and a keyword rule in the prompt is the kind of brittle, keyword-sensitive instruction that creates new misroutes.

questions.question: Tool selection errors began right after a system-prompt edit, and the tool definitions have not changed. What is the best investigation step?
options: Increase max_tokens so that the model has more room to reason about which tool it should use
Diff the old and new prompt, looking for instructions that tie request types to specific tools
Set tool_choice to any for every request so that the model is always forced to pick some tool
Rewrite every tool schema from scratch, in case one of the old schemas was the real problem
questions.explanation: When behavior shifts after a prompt change and definitions are the same, the prompt wording is the prime suspect, especially phrases that associate topics with tools. Output length, forcing a tool call and rewriting unchanged schemas are not targeted at the change that introduced the problem.

questions.question: A custom MCP tool wraps a payments API. When the API answers "card declined", the tool returns the text "Error: card declined" as ordinary content with no failure flag. The agent sometimes treats this as success and tells the customer the payment went through. What is the best fix?
options: Add a system-prompt line telling the agent to read all tool output very carefully before replying
Have the server crash with an unhandled exception whenever the payments API declines a card
Return the message in the result with the error flag set, so the failure is explicit
Return an empty result when the card is declined and let the agent infer that it failed
questions.explanation: The MCP error flag marks a tool result as a failure so the model treats it as one. Unflagged text looks like valid data. A crash is a protocol-level failure the model is less able to act on, and an empty result is ambiguous with "nothing found".

questions.question: A tool can fail in three ways: (1) a timeout from a flaky upstream service, (2) "amount exceeds the refund window", (3) "caller lacks access to this account". Which handling matches the three, in order?
options: Retry with backoff; explain the policy and do not retry; do not retry, but escalate or ask for access
Retry all three with backoff, since retries cannot hurt and one of them is bound to succeed eventually
Escalate to a human immediately in all three cases, without attempting any recovery of their own first
Explain the timeout to the customer; retry the policy failure; retry the permission failure as well
questions.explanation: Transient errors are worth retrying; business-rule errors are final and need a customer-appropriate explanation; permission errors need different access or a human. Treating all failures alike either wastes retries or escalates trivial blips, and retrying a policy or permission failure can never succeed.

questions.question: Which tool error response gives the agent the most useful basis for choosing a recovery?
options: {"error": "Operation failed", "details": "An unexpected error occurred while processing the request"}
A plain sentence: "Something went wrong while processing your request, please try again later."
A raw server stack trace with file names, line numbers and the names of internal functions
{"errorCategory": "transient", "isRetryable": true, "message": "Inventory service timed out"}
questions.explanation: A category, a retryable flag and a human-readable description let the agent decide between retrying, rephrasing, explaining or escalating. Generic messages and stack traces do not tell it which recovery fits. The category and retryable fields are an application convention carried in the result; the protocol itself defines only the failure flag.

questions.question: A refund tool rejects a request because the item was bought 120 days ago and the refund window is 90 days. Which result should the tool return?
options: A generic failure so that the agent will try again with different arguments next time
A business error marked non-retryable, with a customer-friendly explanation
A success response whose text explains that no refund was issued and why
A transient error so that the agent keeps retrying until the policy window changes
questions.explanation: A policy violation is a business error: retrying cannot change the answer, so it should be flagged non-retryable and come with wording the agent can use to explain the decision or offer alternatives. Reporting it as success or as transient misleads the agent.

questions.question: One subagent runs a database query that returns zero rows. Another subagent runs the same kind of query but it times out. How should each outcome be reported to the coordinator?
options: Both as failures, so that the coordinator retries both of them automatically
Both as empty results, to keep the report format uniform for the downstream agents
Zero rows as a failure, because no data means that something went wrong in the query
Zero rows as a successful empty result, and the timeout as a flagged error with details
questions.explanation: A query that ran and found nothing is a valid answer, while a timeout means the question was never answered and may need a retry decision. Merging the two either hides outages as "no data" or triggers pointless retries for legitimate empty results.

questions.question: A booking tool receives the check-in date "next Tuesday" and returns only "Invalid input". The agent retries with the same text. Which error would work better?
options: A validation error that names the date field and the expected format (YYYY-MM-DD)
A permission error, so that the agent stops trying and tells the user to ask for access
A transient error with a note to wait ten seconds before retrying the same request
A longer "Invalid input" message that apologizes to the user for the inconvenience
questions.explanation: Validation errors should say which input was wrong and what a valid value looks like, so the model can correct and retry. Mislabeling the failure as permission or transient sends the agent down the wrong recovery path, and an apology adds no information.

questions.question: In the MCP specification, which failure should a server report inside the tool result with the failure flag set, so the model can self-correct?
options: A request that names a tool that does not exist
A request that does not match the call schema at all
An internal crash of the server process
A date argument supplied in the wrong format
questions.explanation: Tool execution errors, such as bad input values, API failures and business-rule violations, are returned in the result so the model can adjust and retry. Unknown tools, malformed requests and server faults are protocol errors reported through JSON-RPC, where the model is less likely to recover.

questions.question: One agent is given 18 tools covering search, databases, email, calendar and document editing, and it increasingly picks the wrong one. What is the best architectural response?
options: Keep all 18 tools but add a paragraph to the system prompt ranking them by importance and frequency
Split the work across specialized agents with four or five role-specific tools each, under a coordinator agent
Switch to forced tool selection so that the model has to name its tool before every single step of the task
Rename the 18 tools with numeric prefixes so that they sort in the order they are normally used
questions.explanation: A long tool list raises decision complexity and degrades selection. Dividing the work among role-specific agents with small, relevant toolsets restores reliability. A ranking paragraph and numeric prefixes leave the same crowded decision space, and forcing selection does not help the model choose correctly.

questions.question: A report-writing agent often needs the current exchange rate while drafting. It has no tools, so each time it hands the question to the coordinator, which calls the finance agent. Occasionally it needs real market analysis. Which design is best?
options: Give the report agent the finance agent's entire toolset so that it never has to wait on anyone else
Let the report agent state exchange rates from memory and mark them clearly as approximate
Give the report agent a narrow get_exchange_rate tool, and route real market analysis via the coordinator
Pre-fetch rates for every currency pair at the start of each run and attach all of them to every prompt
questions.explanation: A scoped cross-role tool removes round trips for the frequent, simple need while the rare complex case still flows through the coordinator. Handing over the whole finance toolset breaks specialization, memory-based rates are unreliable, and pre-fetching everything bloats every prompt.

questions.question: A research subagent has a fetch_url tool that can retrieve any address, and it sometimes fetches login pages, ads and search-result pages instead of source documents. Which change is best?
options: Add a prompt line telling it to avoid login pages, ads and search-result pages when fetching
Give it a second, slower fetch tool that it can fall back on when the first returns junk
Increase the tool timeout so that pages finish loading completely before they are read
Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates the address and returns text
questions.explanation: Replacing a broad generic tool with a constrained one builds the guardrail into the interface. A prompt request is probabilistic, a backup fetcher shares the same flaw, and a longer timeout does nothing about fetching the wrong kind of page.

questions.question: An intake service defines one extraction tool per document type (invoice, receipt, contract), and the type of an incoming file is unknown. Sometimes the model replies "This looks like an invoice" in plain text and calls nothing. Which setting guarantees a structured tool call?
options: tool_choice set to any, so some tool must be called and the model picks the matching one
tool_choice set to auto, which leaves the model free to decide whether to call anything at all
tool_choice forced to the invoice extraction tool, since invoices are the most common type
tool_choice set to none, with instructions asking for JSON in the text of the reply
questions.explanation: Requiring some tool call while leaving the choice to the model fits an unknown document type. Automatic choice allows plain text, forcing the invoice tool is wrong for other types, and disabling tools removes structure altogether.
