questions.explanation: When problems interact, sequential fixes can undo or invalidate one another, so one message that explains the whole picture lets Claude plan a consistent solution. Separate messages or sessions hide the dependencies and risk conflicting changes.

questions.question: A developer has corrected Claude three times about the same misunderstanding, and its answers keep drifting back. The session is long and full of discarded attempts. What is the best move?
options: Keep correcting, using stronger wording and more capital letters each time the mistake reappears
Compact the conversation and continue, since the summary will keep only what is useful
Clear the session and start again with a more specific prompt that includes what was learned
Switch to a different permission mode so that Claude pays closer attention to the corrections
questions.explanation: After repeated failed corrections the context is cluttered with wrong approaches, and a fresh session with a sharper prompt usually outperforms patching. Compaction would carry the clutter forward in summary form, emphasis does not fix a misunderstanding, and permission modes do not affect attention.

questions.question: Claude reported that a new CSV importer was finished, but it breaks on fields that contain quoted commas. Which change best prevents this in future tasks?
options: Ask Claude to review its own work carefully before it says that it is done
Tell Claude to be more careful about edge cases at the start of every prompt
Read every diff by hand before accepting any change from Claude
Provide runnable verification, such as tests with representative inputs including quoted fields, and have Claude run them until they pass
questions.explanation: A check Claude can run closes the loop, so it keeps working until the evidence says the job is right. Asking for care or self-review relies on the same judgment that missed the case, and reading every diff by hand does not scale and leaves you as the verification loop.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to implement a rate limiter with specific burst and refill behavior. Which workflow most reliably produces a correct implementation?
options: Write tests for the expected behavior, edge cases and performance first, then have Claude implement and iterate on the failures
Have Claude write both the limiter and its tests in a single pass, then trust the passing result
Describe the burst and refill behavior in detail and verify the implementation by reading the code
Ask Claude to implement the limiter now and add tests only after users report problems
questions.explanation: Tests written first define the target independently of the implementation, and sharing failures steers each iteration. Letting Claude write both in one pass can encode the same misunderstanding in code and tests, reading code is a weaker check than running it, and adding tests after complaints comes too late.

questions.question: Which two actions fit test-driven iteration with Claude Code? (Choose two.)
options: Ask Claude to delete tests it considers redundant before it starts
Disable a failing test temporarily so that Claude can finish the feature
Write tests that cover expected behavior and edge cases before the implementation exists
Describe failures in general terms to avoid anchoring Claude on one case
Paste the failing test output back to Claude after each attempt
questions.explanation: Tests first and failures shared back are the two halves of the loop: a target, then concrete feedback. Disabling tests, vague failure descriptions and letting Claude prune tests all weaken the signal the loop depends on.

questions.question: When several bugs interact, describing them together in one detailed message is generally better than fixing them one at a time.
questions.explanation: Fixes to interacting problems can invalidate each other, so Claude needs the whole picture. Independent problems, by contrast, can be handled one after another.

questions.question: In the interview pattern, the developer must write a complete specification before Claude is allowed to ask any questions.
questions.explanation: The pattern is the reverse: Claude asks questions first to surface considerations the developer may have missed, and the answers become the spec.

questions.question: A CI step posts Claude's review as inline pull-request comments by parsing the prose with regular expressions, and it breaks whenever the wording changes. What is the best fix?
options: Tell Claude to always write findings in one fixed sentence template and keep the regular expressions
Run in print mode with JSON output and a schema for the findings, then read the structured_output field
Switch to streaming output and parse the individual tokens as they arrive from the model
Run the review twice and post only those findings whose wording matches in both runs
questions.explanation: A schema-constrained result gives the pipeline machine-readable fields such as file, line and severity, so wording no longer matters. A template is still free text, token-level parsing is even more fragile, and comparing wording across two runs only discards findings.

questions.question: In a pipeline, the same Claude session that wrote a feature is then asked to review it before merge. Its reviews rarely find anything. What is the best change?
options: Tell the same session to take a more critical stance and to look harder for problems
Ask the same session to think for longer before it approves its own change
Run the review in a separate, fresh invocation that sees only the diff and the criteria
Run the same session's review twice and require both runs to find the same issues
questions.explanation: A session that wrote the code still holds its own reasoning and tends to defend its decisions, whereas an independent instance questions them. Instructions to be critical, extra thinking time and repeated self-review do not remove that bias.

questions.question: After every new commit to a pull request, the review job posts the same nine comments again plus one new one, and developers have started to ignore the bot. What is the best change?
options: Delete all of the bot's earlier comments before each run and then post the complete list again
Run the review only when the pull request is merged instead of on each commit
Ask Claude to shorten each comment so that the repeated ones take up less space
Include the earlier findings in the prompt and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
questions.explanation: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline must supply the earlier findings and ask for only what is new or unresolved. Deleting and reposting still repeats everything, moving the review to merge time loses the feedback loop, and shorter comments leave the duplication in place.

questions.question: A CI job that generates test suggestions keeps proposing scenarios the suite already covers. What is the best fix?
options: Provide the existing test files in the context and tell Claude to avoid scenarios they already cover
Ask for fewer suggestions per run so that the duplicates are less noticeable to reviewers
Run the job less often so that developers see fewer repeated suggestions over the month
Cap the number of turns for each run so that Claude stops earlier and proposes less
questions.explanation: Claude cannot avoid duplicates it cannot see, so the existing tests must be in context. Asking for fewer suggestions, running less often or capping turns only hides the symptom.

questions.question: Tests generated in CI are trivial, such as getters and framework behavior, and they ignore the project's fixtures. The job runs claude -p inside the repository. Which change is most effective?
options: Add the phrase "write high-quality tests" to the end of every CI prompt
Document the testing standards, what makes a test worth writing, and the available fixtures in the project's instruction file
Generate three times as many tests and discard those that do not increase coverage
Move the job to the Message Batches API so that the model has more time to think per test
questions.explanation: The instruction file is how project context reaches a non-interactive run, so recording the standards, the criteria for valuable tests and the fixtures steers generation. A generic quality request adds no information, filtering by coverage keeps trivial tests that still raise coverage, and batch processing changes cost and latency, not guidance.

questions.question: A nightly job on a shared runner that holds production credentials runs claude -p to fix lint errors, and runs sometimes end early because a step the job needs was never pre-approved. What is the best configuration?
options: Run with bypassPermissions so that nothing can ever prompt, since the job is unattended anyway
Pipe the word "yes" into the job's standard input so that every prompt is accepted
Pre-approve the exact tools needed with --allowedTools and use dontAsk mode so that anything else is denied
Add "do not ask for permission" to the prompt text so that Claude proceeds without waiting
questions.explanation: The allowed list pre-approves what the task needs, and dontAsk makes every other action a plain denial, so the policy is explicit and nothing waits for a prompt that no one can answer. Bypassing all checks on a runner with production credentials is unsafe, because that mode is meant for isolated environments; piped input does not reliably answer permission dialogs; and prompt text cannot switch permission behavior off.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to review every pull request automatically when it is opened, without anyone mentioning @claude. How should the GitHub Action step be configured?
options: Leave the prompt empty, because the action reviews every pull request on its own once it is installed
Ask developers to comment @claude on each pull request so that the action wakes up and starts
Raise the maximum number of turns so that the action keeps listening for newly opened pull requests
Give the action a prompt input that describes the review, and trigger the workflow on pull-request events
questions.explanation: With a prompt input the action runs in automation mode on whatever event triggers the workflow. Without a prompt it waits for the trigger phrase, so an empty prompt reviews nothing, relying on manual mentions defeats the automation, and a turn limit has nothing to do with triggering.

questions.question: Reviews in CI began ignoring the project's conventions after the team added --bare to the claude -p command for reproducibility. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: Bare mode skips automatic loading of instruction files, so the guidance must be passed explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file
Print mode never reads instruction files, so the conventions must be moved into the settings file instead
Bare mode disables the model's ability to follow instructions, so the flag should be removed permanently
Instruction files are read only from the home directory in CI, so they must be copied there first
questions.explanation: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files so that runs are reproducible, and context must then be supplied through flags such as an appended system prompt file. Without bare mode, print mode loads the project's instruction file as usual.

questions.question: A team's committed .claude/settings.json sets the default model for the repository. One developer prefers a different model in this repository only and does not want to commit a change. Where should she put the override?
options: In ~/.claude/settings.json, because user settings always override project settings
In .claude/settings.local.json, which ranks above the shared project file and stays out of version control
In the committed .claude/settings.json, then ask teammates to override it back if they disagree
In CLAUDE.local.md, since it is also a personal file that sits next to the project settings
questions.explanation: The project-local settings file sits above the shared project file in precedence and is kept out of git, so only her sessions change. User settings rank below project settings, editing the committed file changes it for everyone, and a CLAUDE.local.md file holds instructions for Claude, not settings.

questions.question: A project's settings contain a deny rule for Bash(aws *) and, from another file, an allow rule for Bash(aws s3 ls). What happens when Claude tries to run aws s3 ls?
options: The call runs, because the narrower allow rule is more specific than the broad deny
The call runs only if the user's settings file sets the allow rule, since user rules outrank project rules
The call is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and the first match decides
Claude Code asks for confirmation each time, because the two rules cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Rules are checked in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first match wins, so a broad deny cannot be carved out by a narrower allow. Specificity does not change the order, file origin does not make an allow outrank a deny, and the rules do not cancel.

questions.question: Which two practices help CI-invoked Claude Code generate useful tests? (Choose two.)
options: Ask for the largest possible number of tests to maximize coverage
Let the job pause for interactive approval before each test file is written
Document the project's testing standards and available fixtures where the run can read them
Provide the existing test files so that suggestions avoid scenarios already covered
Strip out all project context so that every run starts from an identical blank state
questions.explanation: Seeing what already exists and knowing the conventions are what make suggestions new and fitting. Maximizing quantity produces low-value tests, interactive pauses stall an unattended job, and removing context removes exactly the information needed.

questions.question: Which two statements about running Claude Code in a pipeline are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The --ci flag switches Claude Code to the Message Batches API at half price
When no terminal is attached, permission prompts are answered automatically with the safest option
Setting CLAUDE_NONINTERACTIVE=1 is the documented way to avoid hangs
With --output-format json and --json-schema, the structured result is returned in the structured_output field
The -p flag runs a single prompt non-interactively, prints the result and exits
questions.explanation: Print mode and the structured-output flags are documented, parseable pipeline features. The other three describe things that do not exist or that Claude Code does not do: there is no such flag or variable, and permission requests nobody can answer are denied, or must be pre-approved, rather than auto-answered.

questions.question: A session that generated code is just as effective at reviewing its own changes as a fresh, independent Claude instance.
questions.explanation: The generating session retains its own reasoning and is less likely to question its decisions. An independent instance reviewing only the diff and criteria catches subtler issues.

questions.question: When a review is rerun after new commits, including the earlier findings in the prompt and asking for only new or unresolved issues reduces duplicate comments.
questions.explanation: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline has to supply the earlier findings.

questions.question: Running Claude Code with --bare skips automatic loading of CLAUDE.md, so project guidance must then be supplied another way.
questions.explanation: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files. Pass what you need with flags such as an appended system prompt file.

questions.question: Your team's pull-request bot reviews Python services for security problems. Its prompt ends with: "Only report issues you are highly confident are real vulnerabilities." Engineers still get many warnings about harmless code, such as parameterized queries and input validated upstream, and have started ignoring the bot. Which change is most likely to improve precision?
options: Strengthen the wording to "only report issues you are 95% certain are exploitable", so the model applies a much higher bar before it speaks up
Have the model attach a confidence score between 0 and 1 to every warning and let code drop any warning scoring below 0.8
Define what to report (string-built SQL, hard-coded secrets, missing authorization checks) and what to skip (parameterized queries, validated input)
Switch to the largest available model, which should be better at telling harmless code from real vulnerabilities in a large service
questions.explanation: A request for confidence adds no decision boundary: the model already believes the findings it makes, so a stronger phrase or a score cutoff changes little, and self-reported confidence is not calibrated precision. Defining what counts as reportable and what to skip changes the decision itself. A larger model still does not know your team's definition of a reportable issue.

questions.question: A CI job asks Claude to "check that the README examples are accurate". Its comments are full of complaints about wording, missing detail and tone, and maintainers now skim past them. Which rewritten instruction should cut the noise most?
options: Flag an example only when running it as written would fail or print something different from what the README shows
Check each example carefully, but be conservative and avoid nitpicking about wording, tone or missing detail
Rate every example from 1 to 10 for accuracy and report only the examples that score below 5
Flag any example that a first-time user could plausibly find confusing, and sort the flags by importance before posting them
questions.explanation: Flagging an example only when running it would fail is a test the model can answer yes or no, so the bar no longer depends on its own taste. "Accurate" and "conservative" leave the bar undefined, a numeric rating only moves that ambiguity into a number, and "confusing" widens the net to exactly the wording complaints you want to drop.

questions.question: Your review assistant posts findings in four categories. After a month, measured precision is 93% for security, 88% for bugs, 31% for performance and 22% for naming. Developers have begun dismissing every finding unread, including the security ones. What should you do first?
options: Keep all four categories running and add a banner saying that some findings may be wrong, so developers read each one carefully
Lower the severity label on every finding, so that developers feel less pressure to act on any of them
Shut the assistant down until all four categories reach 90% precision, then relaunch it as a whole
Pause the performance and naming categories while their criteria are rewritten, and keep security and bugs running
questions.explanation: False positives in one category teach developers to ignore the assistant as a whole, so the accurate categories lose their value too. Pausing only the noisy categories restores trust quickly and keeps the useful findings flowing; the paused categories return once their measured precision is acceptable. A banner asks developers to do the filtering, lowering severity hides real problems, and a full shutdown throws away the accurate categories.

questions.question: Your review prompt asks the model to label each finding critical, major or minor. Running the same diff twice gives different labels for similar defects: an unchecked null return is critical in one run and minor in the next. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add a sentence to the prompt telling the model to keep its severity labels consistent from one finding to the next
Define each severity level in the prompt and attach a short code example of a typical finding at that level
Ask for a 0 to 100 severity score in place of labels, and convert score ranges to labels in code
Run every review three times and report the label that occurs most often for each finding
questions.explanation: The labels drift because the boundaries between levels are undefined. Concrete definitions with an example for each level anchor the judgment, so like defects get like labels. Asking for consistency supplies no boundary, a numeric scale moves the same ambiguity into a number, and voting reduces noise at triple the cost without making the labels match your team's definitions.

questions.question: A colleague proposes adding "only report findings you are highly confident about" to a review prompt as a quick way to cut false positives. Why is this unlikely to work as well as categorical criteria?
options: Models skip over intensifying words such as "highly", so the instruction has no effect on the output at all
A review prompt can hold only one filtering rule, so the confidence rule would displace the severity rules that were already there
It defines no standard for what counts as reportable, so the model still rates its own flagged findings as confident
Confidence filtering only takes effect when the prompt also caps how many findings the model may report
questions.explanation: The instruction sounds careful but provides no criterion. The model believes the findings it makes, so the same wrong ones are still reported with confidence, and self-reported confidence is not a calibrated measure of precision. Categories of what to report and what to skip change the decision itself. The other explanations invent limits: models do read such words, a prompt can carry many rules, and a cap on count is a separate tactic.

questions.question: A review assistant keeps reporting that a function "mutates its argument" because of the function's name, and developers spend time disproving the claim each time. Which prompt addition most directly reduces these false positives?
options: Require each behavior claim to quote the line of code that demonstrates it, and skip claims resting only on names
Add a line to the reviewer instructions telling the model to be skeptical of function names when it judges behavior
Ask for a confidence percentage with each claim and show developers only the claims rated above 70 percent
Tell the model that false claims waste developer time and that it should try hard to avoid making them
questions.explanation: An evidence requirement is an explicit, checkable criterion: the claim either points at code that shows it or it is not reported. Skepticism, confidence percentages and reminders about wasted time all leave the model to decide for itself what is convincing.

questions.question: Which two revisions turn a vague review instruction into explicit criteria? (Choose two.)
options: Flag a retry loop only when it has no upper bound on the number of attempts
Be conservative and avoid raising false alarms
Skip comments about naming and formatting when they match the conventions already used in the same file
Only report issues that you are very confident about
Think carefully about whether each issue is important enough to mention
questions.explanation: Each correct revision is a condition the model can decide yes or no on: a retry loop either has an upper bound or it does not, and a naming comment either matches local convention or it does not. The other three describe an attitude (conservative, confident, careful) without saying which issues belong in the review.

questions.question: Adding "only report findings you are highly confident about" to a review prompt cuts false positives about as well as defining which categories of issue to report and which to skip.
questions.explanation: A confidence instruction supplies no criterion, so the model keeps flagging the same borderline patterns. Explicit categories of what to report and what to skip change what gets flagged.

questions.question: A review category that produces many false positives can lead developers to distrust the categories that are accurate.
questions.explanation: False positives teach people to dismiss findings by habit, and once that habit forms, correct findings in other categories are dismissed too. That is why a noisy category can be paused while its prompt is improved.

questions.question: Pairing each severity level with a concrete code example helps the model give the same label to similar issues.
questions.explanation: Definitions alone leave the boundaries between levels open to interpretation. A representative example for each level anchors them, so similar defects receive similar labels from run to run.

questions.question: Your review assistant's findings arrive in many shapes: some name a file and line, some only a function, some give a severity word and some do not. The prompt already describes the required format in three paragraphs of prose. What is the most effective next step?
options: Repeat the format rules in capital letters at the end of the prompt, label them as mandatory and add a warning about deviations
Add two or three complete example findings that show the exact shape: location, issue, severity and suggested fix
Lower the temperature so that the model repeats the same structure on every single run of the review
Parse each finding with regular expressions and discard any finding that lacks a file name and line number
questions.explanation: Examples show the format instead of describing it, which is the strongest fix when detailed written instructions still produce inconsistent output. Emphasis adds no information, temperature changes randomness rather than the model's understanding of the format, and discarding findings throws away useful output instead of making it consistent.

questions.question: Your reviewer flags every broad exception handler as a defect, yet the team deliberately uses one at the top of each worker loop to log the error and continue. A prompt list of the files where this is allowed keeps missing new workers. What is the best approach?
options: Keep extending the list of allowed files in the prompt each time a new worker module is added to the codebase
Remove exception handling from the review scope, since the model cannot tell the acceptable and harmful cases apart
Tell the model to flag broad handlers only when it is certain that the handler is hiding a real bug in the code
Add example pairs, each with a reason: a worker handler that logs and continues versus one that swallows an error
questions.explanation: Pairs of acceptable and genuinely problematic code teach the principle behind the distinction, so the model can judge new workers it has never seen. An allow-list covers only what it names, dropping the category loses real bugs, and a certainty instruction supplies no criterion.

questions.question: A pipeline extracts the list of cited sources from research papers. Papers with inline (author, year) citations work well, but for papers that put numbered references in a bibliography at the end, the model often returns an empty list. What should you try first?
options: Add a few examples of correct extraction from both layouts, one of them a paper that has only a bibliography
Mark the cited_sources field as required, so that the model must always produce at least one entry for each paper
Retry every empty result up to five times with the unchanged prompt and keep the first list that is not empty
Split each paper into 500-word fragments, so that the bibliography is easier for the model to locate
questions.explanation: The sources are present, but the model has not learned to recognize where they live in the second layout; examples of that layout teach it. A required field would push the model to invent entries for papers that really have none, unchanged retries reproduce the same miss, and fragmenting a paper can separate the reference list from the citations that point to it.

questions.question: A recipe-digitizing system extracts ingredient quantities. Source text says things like "a good glug of oil" and "about a handful of basil", and the model keeps returning precise numbers such as 15 ml and 10 g. Which change best reduces this invented precision?
options: Tell the model in capital letters never to make up measurements, and repeat the warning at the end of the prompt
Make the numeric quantity fields required, so that every ingredient is guaranteed to have a value
Add examples in which informal quantities are kept as written and the numeric fields are left null
Instruct the model to round every quantity to the nearest 5 ml or 5 g so that the values look consistent
questions.explanation: Examples demonstrate how to record an informal measurement faithfully instead of converting it into false precision, which is how few-shot examples reduce hallucination in extraction. A bare prohibition is easy to overlook, a required numeric field forces a number to exist, and rounding still invents a value the recipe never gave.

questions.question: You are writing few-shot examples for a classifier that labels support emails as billing, technical or account. Several emails are borderline, for instance a failed password reset caused by an expired card. Which set of examples is best?
options: Thirty clear-cut emails, ten for each label, so that the model sees every label many times
A few examples that include borderline emails, each with a short reason why the chosen label beat the alternative
One example per label picked at random from last month's inbox, with no explanation attached to any of them, to avoid bias
Examples for the two most frequent labels only, since the third label is rare and will be picked up anyway
questions.explanation: Targeted examples of hard cases, with the reasoning for the choice, teach where the boundaries lie and carry over to new borderline emails. Many easy examples add little, unexplained random picks do not show why a label won, and leaving out a label biases the classifier against it.

questions.question: A CI job asks Claude to point out missing tests. It reliably lists functions that have no tests, but it never notices a function whose error branch is untested because another test already calls the function. What is the best way to close this gap?
options: Require 100% line coverage in the prompt and have the job fail whenever the reported coverage is lower
Tell the model to be more thorough and to look harder for missing tests in every file it receives
Move the job to the Message Batches API so that the model has more time to examine each file
Add examples of a tested function with an untested branch and show how the gap is described
questions.explanation: The model is treating "has a test" as the signal. Examples of the borderline case, a function that is tested but has an uncovered branch, show it what to notice and how to report it, and the lesson carries over to other branches. "Be more thorough" adds no information, a prompt cannot enforce a coverage number, and the Batches API changes cost and latency, not what the model looks for.

questions.question: Which two problems are most directly addressed by adding well-chosen few-shot examples? (Choose two.)
options: Findings arrive in inconsistent formats even though the prompt describes the format in detail
A date field comes back empty for invoices that print the date in a footer layout the prompt never mentions
A required clause is not present anywhere in the contract text that was supplied
Some documents are too long to fit in the model's context window
A nightly job takes up to a day to finish and nobody is waiting on it
questions.explanation: Examples show the model what the output should look like and where to find a value in a layout it did not recognize. They cannot supply information that the source lacks, shrink a document, or change how long asynchronous processing takes.

questions.question: Which two practices make a set of few-shot examples more effective? (Choose two.)
options: Choose examples that mirror real inputs, including awkward layouts and borderline cases
Make every example share one layout, so that the pattern is unmistakable
Wrap each example, and the whole set, in clearly named tags so that the model can tell examples from instructions
Include as many examples as will fit, since quantity matters more than variety
Omit the reasons from ambiguous-case examples so the model works them out for itself
questions.explanation: Relevant, varied examples in clear tags are what the prompting guidance recommends. Identical layouts teach the model to expect that layout, volume does not replace variety, and for borderline cases the stated reason is the part that transfers to new situations.

questions.question: Well-chosen few-shot examples can lead the model to apply a demonstrated judgment to patterns that do not appear in the examples, rather than only matching the cases shown.
questions.explanation: Examples convey the principle behind a decision, so the model extends it to new cases. That is why a few examples can outperform an exhaustive rule list, which only covers the cases it names.

questions.question: Few-shot examples are useful only for fixing output format; they cannot improve how the model handles ambiguous cases.
questions.explanation: Examples that show the chosen action and the reason it beat a plausible alternative are among the most effective ways to teach ambiguous-case handling. Format demonstration is only one of their jobs.

questions.question: Adding examples of an unusual document layout can reduce empty extractions that happen because the model did not recognize where a field appears in that layout.
questions.explanation: When the information is present but placed differently, examples of that layout show the model where to look. They cannot help when the information is genuinely absent from the document.

questions.question: A pipeline asks the model to "return only JSON" in plain text and parses the reply with a JSON parser. About one response in 200 fails to parse because of a stray comment or a missing bracket. Which change most reliably removes these syntax failures?
options: Define the extraction as a tool whose input schema is the target JSON Schema, mark it strict, and read the tool input
Add "your reply must be valid JSON and nothing else" to both the start and the end of the prompt
Wrap the parser in error handling that asks the model to answer again whenever a reply fails to parse
Set the temperature to 0 so that the model stops producing unusual, unexpected or badly formed output
questions.explanation: A strict tool schema constrains generation so that the tool input always conforms to the schema, which eliminates syntax errors rather than detecting them afterwards (the JSON outputs option does the same for the reply itself). Repeating the instruction and lowering the temperature reduce the failure rate without guaranteeing zero, and re-asking only recovers after a failure has already happened.

questions.question: An invoice schema marks po_number as required. About a third of suppliers do not use purchase-order numbers, and the results for their invoices contain realistic but invented numbers. What is the best fix?
options: Keep the field required and add "never invent a purchase-order number" to the system prompt
Keep the field required and have a validator retry until the number exists in the purchasing database
Make po_number optional or nullable, and tell the model to return null when an invoice shows none
Add few-shot examples that all show invoices with a purchase-order number, so that the format is learned
questions.explanation: A required field pushes the model to produce something, so the schema has to allow honest absence. A prompt prohibition works against that pressure, retrying cannot make a missing number appear, and examples that all contain a number reinforce the expectation that one is always there.

questions.question: A contract-intake schema has a document_type enum with nda, msa, sow and amendment. Each week a few documents of other kinds, such as data-processing addenda, arrive and are quietly labeled with the nearest value, which distorts reports. Which schema change is best?
options: Replace the enum with a free-text string, so that the model can return any label it likes
Add an "other" value and a companion text field in which the model describes the actual type
Make document_type optional, so that the model can leave it out for unfamiliar documents
Add a new enum value each time an unfamiliar type turns up, and re-run the affected documents
questions.explanation: An other-plus-detail pattern keeps the field constrained for known types while capturing new ones with a description, so nothing is mislabeled silently and frequent types can be promoted to real enum values later. Free text loses consistency, omission throws away the fact that the document exists and what it is, and chasing new values leaves every not-yet-seen type mislabeled until someone notices.

questions.question: A ticket-extraction schema has a category enum with billing, technical, account and other. Many tickets say only things like "it's not working", and the model picks a category with confidence anyway. The wrong picks route tickets to the wrong team. What is the most appropriate schema change?
options: Add a required confidence field and route automatically only the tickets with a value above 0.9
Remove "other" from the enum, so that the model is forced to pick the closest category
Add a longer description of each category to the prompt, so that vague tickets clearly match one
Add an "unclear" value for tickets that cannot be classified, and send those tickets to a person
questions.explanation: An explicit unclear option lets the model say that the source is ambiguous instead of guessing, and downstream code can route those tickets for review. Self-reported confidence is a weak proxy, removing options forces even more guesses, and longer category descriptions do not make a vague ticket specific.

questions.question: A strict-schema invoice extraction always returns valid JSON with correct types. Even so, the finance team finds invoices whose line items add up to 1,204.00 while the extracted total is 1,240.00, and some whose ship-to address landed in the bill-to field. What explains this, and what is the right response?
options: Strict schemas guarantee structure, not correct values; add validation code with cross-checks and retry on failure
The tool is not really strict, and switching strict mode on for the extraction tool will stop these mismatches
The numeric types are too loose; change the total to a string with a regular-expression pattern so that it is checked
The response budget is too small for the model to finish its arithmetic, so raising max_tokens will stop the mismatches
questions.explanation: Constrained output guarantees valid structure and types; it cannot check that values are true or placed in the right field. Arithmetic and placement errors need validation code, with failures fed back for correction. The output here is already valid and typed, a pattern on a string does not check a sum, and a larger token budget does not change which values the model chooses.

questions.question: A strict-schema extraction call returns HTTP 200 with JSON that is cut off: the last optional fields are missing and the final string ends mid-word. The schema is valid and the request was accepted. What is the most likely cause and the right response?
options: The model refused the request; rephrase the system prompt and send the request again
The grammar failed to compile; remove strict from the tool and parse the reply leniently
The output hit the max_tokens limit; check the stop reason and retry with a higher limit
Optional fields are dropped once a schema contains several of them; make every field required
questions.explanation: A cut-off result with a normal 200 status points to the output-token limit: the stop reason is max_tokens, and constrained output may then be incomplete. Check the stop reason before trusting parsed output and retry with a larger limit. A refusal has its own stop reason and is not a half-written object, a schema that cannot be compiled is rejected with an error before any output, and optional fields are not silently dropped for being optional.

questions.question: An extraction schema types amount as a number and currency as an enum. Source invoices write amounts as "1.234,50 EUR", "$1,234.50" and "USD 1234.5". The output is valid but sometimes wrong: "1.234,50" occasionally becomes 1.234. What helps most?
options: Raise max_tokens so that the model has more room to work out what the separators in each amount mean
Keep the strict schema and add normalization rules to the prompt for separators and currency symbols
Drop the schema for this field and let the model write each amount in whatever format it finds most natural
Make amount optional, so that ambiguous values come back as null instead of coming back as wrong numbers
questions.explanation: The schema fixes the shape of the answer, not how messy source values are interpreted. Explicit normalization rules, ideally with an example or two, handle the interpretation. More tokens do not help, removing the schema gives up the structure, and nulls would hide values that are in fact present.

questions.question: An extraction service runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and sets tool_choice to {"type": "any"}, so that the model must call one of its extraction tools. Every request now fails with a 400 error. Which approach keeps a structured-output guarantee?
options: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so that the reply must start as JSON, then close it in code
Turn on manual extended thinking for the requests, which allows forced tool calls on this model
Remove the schemas and ask for a JSON reply in the prompt, with a retry whenever the reply fails to parse
Leave tool choice on auto, mark the tools strict, and treat a response with no tool call as a failure to retry
questions.explanation: The current documentation says the newest models, including Sonnet 5.5, reject the "any" and named-tool settings with a 400 error, and so does manual extended thinking. Automatic choice with strict tool use still guarantees that any call matches the schema, and the application checks that a call was actually made (or uses the JSON outputs option when the reply itself is the data). Prefilled replies are not supported on these models either, and prompt-only JSON gives up the guarantee.

questions.question: Which two problems can still occur when an extraction tool enforces its schema with strict mode? (Choose two.)
options: Line items that do not add up to the total printed on the document
A tool input that is missing its closing brace
A string where the schema requires an integer
A value placed in the wrong field, such as a ship-to address in the bill-to field
A required field that is absent from the tool input
questions.explanation: Strict mode constrains syntax, types and required fields, so malformed JSON, wrong types and missing required fields are removed. It cannot verify that values are true or sensibly placed, so arithmetic mismatches and misplaced values remain, which is why validation code is still needed.

questions.question: Which two schema choices reduce the risk of fabricated values? (Choose two.)
options: Make a field optional or nullable when some source documents will not contain it
Mark every field required so that each output is always complete
Add an "unclear" value to categorical fields where the source can be ambiguous
Fill every gap with a default value defined in the prompt, such as "N/A" or 0
Replace enums with free text so that the model is never pushed into a category
questions.explanation: Nullable fields and an explicit unclear option give the model an honest way to report that information is missing or ambiguous. Required fields do the opposite, default fill values look like real data downstream, and free text gives up the consistency of an enum without addressing why the model guessed.

questions.question: Strict tool use guarantees that tool inputs match the schema, but it does not guarantee that the extracted values are correct.
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding enforces structure and types. Whether a total is right or a value sits in the correct field is a semantic question that needs validation in code.

questions.question: When an extraction schema marks a field as required, the model may supply an invented value if the source document does not contain one.
questions.explanation: A required field must be filled in, so a plausible guess is the only way to comply when the data is absent. Fields that may be missing should be optional or nullable.

questions.question: The JSON outputs option constrains the model's reply itself to a JSON Schema, while strict tool use constrains the inputs of tool calls.
questions.explanation: Both rely on constrained decoding. JSON outputs are set with the output_config format option and shape the response text; strict: true on a tool definition shapes tool inputs. They can be used separately or together.

questions.question: An extraction fails your validator: the line items add up to 412.50 but the extracted total is 421.50. Which follow-up request has the best chance of producing a corrected result?
options: Resend the original request unchanged, since model output varies from one attempt to the next
Send only the validator message, so that the model is not distracted by the long source document and the request stays short
Send the document, the failed extraction and the validator message naming the mismatch, and ask for a correction
Send the failed extraction and ask the model to adjust it until the numbers are consistent again
questions.explanation: A correction needs three things: the source to re-read, the attempt that failed and the exact error. Without the document the model can only adjust numbers until they agree, which risks fudging values; an unchanged request repeats the odds of the original mistake; and an error with no document or attempt gives the model nothing to correct.

questions.question: Your validator rejects 3% of contract extractions because governing_law is null. Each affected contract says the governing law is "as set out in Schedule 4", and Schedule 4 was never uploaded. Retrying with the error feedback fails every time. What should the pipeline do?
options: Stop retrying after a small cap, mark the field unavailable, and route the contract to someone who can get the schedule
Raise the retry limit to ten and vary the temperature on each attempt, so that one of them eventually succeeds
Tell the model to infer the governing law from the parties' addresses whenever the referenced schedule is missing
Make governing_law a required field in the schema so that the model treats the retry error message as more urgent
questions.explanation: The needed information is not in the supplied text, so no retry can find it; retries repair format and structure errors. Capping attempts and routing the case to a person who can obtain the schedule is the only productive path. More retries waste cost, inference from addresses invents a legal fact, and a required field only adds pressure to fabricate.

questions.question: A validation-retry loop appends the validator error to each retry. Which failure is it most likely to repair?
options: A warranty period that is stated only in a separate product brochure the pipeline never fetched
An expiry date that is missing because the page holding it was not scanned
A customer name that is empty because the person left that line blank on the form
A date returned as "03/04/26" in a field where the validator requires the ISO 8601 form (year-month-day)
questions.explanation: A format mismatch is a mistake the model can fix once it is told what the validator expects, because the information is in the source. The other three failures share one cause, absent information: the data is in a document the pipeline never supplied, on a page nobody scanned, or nowhere at all. No wording of a retry can produce it.

questions.question: Developers dismiss about a third of the findings your review assistant posts, but you cannot tell which kinds of code lead to the dismissed findings. What is the most useful change to the findings schema?
options: Add a confidence field to every finding and review only the findings that carry the lowest confidence values
Add a detected_pattern field naming the code construct that triggered each finding, and group dismissals by it
Add a long free-text reasoning field to every finding and read a sample of those explanations each week
Record how many findings each developer dismisses and discuss the highest counts with those developers
questions.explanation: A structured field naming what triggered each finding turns dismissals into data: grouped by pattern, they show which criteria produce false positives, so those criteria can be fixed. Confidence says nothing about which constructs cause trouble, free-text reasoning is hard to aggregate, and per-developer counts measure people rather than patterns.

questions.question: Some supplier invoices print a total that does not match their own line items, and you want the pipeline to surface these rather than hide them. Which output design works best?
options: Extract only the sum of the line items, since the model's arithmetic is more dependable than a number printed by a supplier
Extract only the printed total and trust the supplier's arithmetic, flagging nothing for review
Extract the printed total as stated_total and the sum of the line items as calculated_total, then flag any mismatch
Ask the model to correct the printed total whenever it disagrees with the line items on the invoice
questions.explanation: Capturing both numbers keeps the discrepancy visible, and a simple comparison in code flags it for review. Using only one of them silently decides which is right, and having the model rewrite the printed total alters a fact in the source.

questions.question: A lease states its start date as 1 March on the cover page and as 1 April in the terms section. Your extractor currently keeps whichever date it meets first, so conflicts pass silently. Which schema change handles inconsistent source data best?
options: Add a conflict_detected boolean and capture both values, so that downstream code can route the record for review
Tell the model to prefer the date in the terms section whenever the two dates in a document disagree, since that section is the binding one
Make start_date optional, so that a record with conflicting dates produces null instead of a date
Run the extraction twice on each document and keep whichever date appears in both of the runs
questions.explanation: A conflict flag with both values makes the contradiction visible and lets a person or a rule decide. A fixed preference silently resolves it, nulls discard information that is in the document, and two runs of the same extractor tend to repeat the same choice, so agreement between runs proves little.

questions.question: Your validation-retry loop re-asks until validation passes. A few unusual documents keep it running for dozens of attempts, costing many times the average. What is the best fix?
options: Accept the second extraction for any document that fails twice and mark it as validated, so that the queue clears and the costs stop growing
Cap the number of attempts and send documents that still fail to human review together with their validation errors
Double max_tokens on each retry so that the model has more room to get the answer right this time
Add a timeout and quietly drop any document that exceeds it, so that one bad file cannot block the rest
questions.explanation: A bounded loop controls cost, and routing the leftovers to a person with the error details means no document is lost or falsely accepted. Marking a failing extraction as validated defeats the purpose of validating, more tokens do not repair a validation error, and silently dropping documents loses data.

questions.question: Which two situations is a retry with the validation error appended most likely to fix? (Choose two.)
options: A currency returned as "US$" where the validator accepts only USD, EUR or GBP
A tax identifier that appears only on a certificate that was never supplied
A ship-to address written into the bill-to field, caught by a cross-check against the document
A signature date that is missing because the signature page was not included in the file
A customer name that is blank because the form field was left empty
questions.explanation: Both are mistakes in how information that is in the document was written out, and the error message tells the model what to correct. The other three describe information that is not in the supplied source, which no retry can supply.

questions.question: Which two additions to an extraction schema make inconsistencies in the source documents visible to downstream code? (Choose two.)
options: A calculated total stored next to the stated total
A free-text field summarizing the model's overall impression of the document
A boolean that marks records whose source contains contradicting values
A counter recording how many attempts the extraction needed
A generated document title for display in the review queue
questions.explanation: Comparing a calculated total with the stated one exposes arithmetic discrepancies, and a conflict flag exposes contradictions. An impression, a retry counter and a title describe the extraction process or its presentation, not whether the source is consistent.

questions.question: Retrying an extraction with the validation error appended can be expected to recover a value that is not anywhere in the supplied document.
questions.explanation: Retries repair format and structure errors. If the information is absent, for example because it lives in an attachment that was never provided, the model cannot find it, and the better response is to route the case for follow-up.

questions.question: Cross-field business rules, such as an end date that must come after the start date, are checked by validation code rather than guaranteed by the output schema.
questions.explanation: Schemas constrain structure and types but do not express relationships between fields like these. A validator, for example a Pydantic model, checks the rule, and a failure can drive a retry that includes the specific error.

questions.question: An agent reviews insurance claims by calling a client-side lookup_policy tool, reading the result and deciding what to do next, sometimes over several rounds. The team wants the batch discount for 50,000 overnight claims. What is the main obstacle?
options: The Batches API rejects every request that includes tool definitions, whether the tools run on the client or on the server
A batch can hold only one request per claim type, so 50,000 claims would need thousands of batches
Batch requests cannot include a system prompt, so the claim-review instructions would be lost entirely
A batch request is one asynchronous call, so there is no way to return a client-side tool result mid-request
questions.explanation: In a batch, each request is answered in one asynchronous pass, so a loop that runs a client-side tool and sends the result back cannot happen inside it (the exam guide states this as no multi-turn tool calling within a single batch request). Keep such agents on the synchronous API, or redesign the work so that the single pass needs no mid-request tool result. Batches do accept tool definitions and system prompts, and one batch can hold very many requests.

questions.question: A batch of 20,000 invoice extractions has ended, and 340 requests came back errored or expired. What is the most efficient recovery?
options: Use custom_id to identify the failed requests, fix their causes, and submit only those in a new batch
Resubmit all 20,000 requests so that the whole set of results comes from one consistent run
Match the failures to their inputs by position in the results file, then resend those inputs
Rerun the 340 failures one at a time on the synchronous API, accepting the standard price for them
questions.explanation: Results carry the custom_id you assigned, so failed and expired requests can be isolated exactly and resubmitted, with fixes applied where the cause is known. Resubmitting everything repeats work that already succeeded, results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order so position is unreliable, and synchronous reruns give up the discount for work that is not urgent.

questions.question: Among the failed requests, 60 invoices errored because they exceed the model's context limit. How should they be resubmitted?
options: Unchanged, but with a higher max_tokens value so that the longer input is able to fit in the request
Truncated to their first ten pages, which usually hold the header and the totals of an invoice
Split into chunks, each with a custom_id that encodes the source document, and merge the chunk results afterwards
Unchanged, but in a batch of their own so that they cannot be affected by any of the other requests that were submitted with them
questions.explanation: Oversized input is a cause you can fix by changing the input: split the document into chunks and put the document and part into each custom_id so that the results can be reassembled. max_tokens limits output, not input; truncation can drop line items; and isolating the requests does not change their size.

questions.question: Invoices arrive continuously. A batch can take up to 24 hours to finish, and the business needs every invoice extracted within 33 hours of arrival. What is the least frequent submission schedule that still guarantees this in the worst case?
options: Submit a batch every 9 hours
Submit a batch every 12 hours
Submit a batch every 24 hours
Submit a batch every 33 hours
questions.explanation: In the worst case an invoice arrives just after a submission, waits for the next one and then spends up to 24 hours in processing. So the interval plus 24 hours must not exceed 33 hours, which gives 9 hours. Every 12 hours allows 36 hours in the worst case, every 24 hours allows 48, and every 33 hours allows 57.

questions.question: You are about to submit 60,000 product-sheet extractions as one batch. The prompt and schema have been tried on only three hand-picked sheets. What should you do first?
options: Submit the whole batch now and resubmit whatever fails, since resubmission is cheap at the discounted price
Split the job into 600 batches of 100 sheets, so that a problem in the prompt can be spotted early
Switch the whole job to synchronous calls, so that every failure shows up immediately and can be fixed
Run a representative sample through the same request shape, fix prompt and schema problems, then submit the batch
questions.explanation: A sample run catches systematic problems, such as a misread layout or a schema that pushes the model to invent values, before they are repeated 60,000 times, which raises first-pass success and avoids paying for rework. Submitting blindly means outputs that are wrong but "succeeded" never show up as failures, many small batches each still take up to a day to finish, and synchronous calls give up the discount.

questions.question: After a batch is submitted, how should the application find out that its results are ready?
options: Poll the batch's processing status until it reports that processing has ended, then retrieve the results
Wait exactly 24 hours, because results are only released when the processing window closes
Read the results straight away and use the entries that have arrived so far, in the order they were submitted
Hold a streaming connection open and read each result as soon as it completes
questions.explanation: A batch moves from in progress to ended, and results are retrieved once it has ended, so polling the status is how the application finds out. Most batches finish well inside 24 hours, so a fixed wait wastes time; results do not come back in a guaranteed order; and streaming is not supported for batch requests.

questions.question: You will resubmit chunks of oversized documents and later reassemble each document's results. Which custom_id scheme best supports that?
options: The position of the request in the submitted list, because results come back in that order
The same batch name on every request, since all of the requests belong to one job
A unique, stable ID built from the document and the chunk, such as inv-4417-c3
The timestamp taken when each request was added to the batch, so that every value is different
questions.explanation: Each custom_id must be unique within the batch, and one that encodes the document and part lets you pair results with inputs and resubmit specific items without a lookup table. Position is unreliable because results can come back in any order, a shared name cannot tell requests apart, and a timestamp changes whenever a request is rebuilt.

questions.question: Which two workloads are best suited to the Message Batches API? (Choose two.)
options: Regenerating unit tests overnight for every module merged that day
A pre-merge check that blocks a developer until it passes
Scoring 30,000 archived contracts against a policy checklist in a weekly audit
A chat assistant that answers a customer who is waiting for a reply
An agent loop that calls a client-side tool after every model turn
questions.explanation: Nobody waits on nightly test generation or a weekly audit, so the cost saving is worth the processing window. A pre-merge check and a live chat reply are blocking workflows that need predictable latency, and an agent loop that must return client-side tool results mid-request cannot run inside a single batch request.

questions.question: Results in a finished batch come back in the same order as the requests were submitted, so a result's position identifies its request.
questions.explanation: Results can arrive in any order, which is why every request carries a custom_id that you use to match each result to its input.

questions.question: Because the Message Batches API offers no guaranteed completion time, it is a poor fit for a check that blocks developers from merging.
questions.explanation: Most batches finish within an hour, but up to 24 hours is allowed and nothing is guaranteed, so a blocked developer could wait a day for a check that takes seconds on the synchronous API. The 50% saving does not justify an unbounded wait.

questions.question: Tuning the prompt on a small representative sample before submitting a large batch helps avoid costly resubmissions.
questions.explanation: Fixing systematic problems on a sample raises the share of requests that succeed on the first pass. Request parameters in a batch are also validated asynchronously, so checking the request shape on the synchronous API first avoids discovering mistakes only after the batch has ended.

questions.question: A code-generation agent writes a database migration and, in the same session, is asked to review it. It approves its own work, but a teammate later finds a subtle ordering bug. Which change would most improve the automated review?
options: Ask the same session to review the migration again, this time with a harsher and more skeptical tone
Run the review in a separate Claude instance that receives only the migration and the review criteria
Give the same session a larger thinking budget for the review step so that it examines the migration longer
Ask the same session to restate its reasoning for the migration before it starts the review
questions.explanation: The authoring session still holds the reasoning that produced the migration, so it tends to defend it. A fresh instance without that context questions decisions the author would not. A harsher tone, more thinking time and restating the reasoning all keep the same biased context in play.

questions.question: You are setting up a separate reviewer instance for AI-written changes. Which input gives it the best chance of finding subtle problems?
options: The diff plus the full transcript of the authoring session, so that the reviewer understands the intent
The diff plus the author's own summary of why the change is correct and which tests it passes
The diff plus the author's list of risky areas, so that the reviewer does not repeat them
The diff and the review criteria, with nothing from the authoring session's reasoning
questions.explanation: Anything derived from the author's reasoning primes the reviewer with the same assumptions and weakens the independence that makes a second instance valuable. Intent can be conveyed through the criteria and a plain description of the change; a transcript, a self-justification and a self-assessed risk list all carry the author's blind spots.

questions.question: A pull request changes 18 files in a billing service. One review pass over the whole diff gives thorough comments on the first few files and little on the rest, and it misses that a refund helper now returns cents while its callers still expect dollars. Which restructured review is best?
options: Review each file in its own pass for local problems, then run a separate pass on how data flows between the files
Run the same single pass with a model that has a larger context window, so that all 18 files fit comfortably
Review each file in its own pass and merge the findings, since local passes already cover cross-file issues
Run only an integration pass, since cross-file problems are the most serious and local issues will surface in it anyway
questions.explanation: Per-file passes give every file the same depth, and a dedicated integration pass looks at how files connect, which is where a cents-versus-dollars mismatch lives. A bigger window does not fix uneven attention, local passes alone cannot see the callers in other files, and an integration-only pass dilutes attention across the whole diff again.

questions.question: A single-pass review of a 25-file change fits within the model's context window but gives uneven depth across the files. A colleague proposes moving to a model with a much larger window. Why is that unlikely to solve the problem?
options: Larger windows are available only through the Batches API, which would make the review asynchronous and slower to deliver
The window size limits how much output the model can write, not how much input it can read
Fitting everything in the window does not guarantee even attention across it, whereas focused passes do
Models with larger windows are trained on longer documents and review short inputs less accurately
questions.explanation: The problem is attention dilution, not capacity: with many files in one pass, depth varies and verdicts can contradict each other. Narrower passes address that directly. The other statements are false: larger windows are not limited to batch processing, the window covers the input as well as the output, and larger windows do not make models worse on short inputs.

questions.question: A verification pass asks the model to attach a confidence from 0 to 1 to each review finding. A manager wants findings above 0.9 posted automatically and the rest sent to a human queue starting tomorrow. What should you do before relying on those thresholds?
options: Nothing, because model-reported confidence is calibrated by design, so 0.9 means nine in ten are correct
Compare the confidence values with known outcomes on a labeled sample and set cutoffs from the measured accuracy
Ask the model to give a second confidence value for each finding and average the two values together
Raise the automatic posting threshold to 0.99, since a higher cutoff is always the safer choice for a bot that comments on other people's code
questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence is a useful routing signal, but what a value means has to be measured: on labeled findings, check how often each band is actually right and set the cutoffs from that. A second self-report has the same weakness, calibration is not guaranteed by design, and an extreme threshold sends almost everything to humans without evidence that quality improves.

questions.question: Which two approaches give a review that is independent of the author's reasoning? (Choose two.)
options: A fresh Claude instance that sees only the code and the review criteria
The authoring session, asked to review the same change as if it were a different engineer
A verification subagent started with clean context to try to refute each reported finding
The authoring session with extended thinking enabled for the review step
The authoring session, asked to list its own assumptions and then check them
questions.explanation: Independence comes from a context that does not contain the author's reasoning: a fresh instance, or a verifier that starts clean and tries to disprove a finding. Role-play, extra thinking and self-audits all happen inside the context that produced the work.

questions.question: Which two are benefits of splitting a large review into per-file passes plus an integration pass? (Choose two.)
options: Each file receives a similar depth of attention instead of tailing off across the diff
Total token use falls, because no file is read more than once
Cross-file data-flow problems get a dedicated pass that looks at how the files connect
The review no longer needs any filtering for false positives
Human reviewers are no longer needed for risky changes
questions.explanation: Focused passes counter attention dilution, and the integration pass supplies the cross-file view that local passes lack. The approach reads some material more than once, so it does not save tokens, and it removes neither false positives nor the need for people.

questions.question: A model asked to review its own output in the same session keeps the reasoning that produced it, which makes it less likely to question its own decisions.
questions.explanation: The earlier reasoning stays in context and supports the original choices. An independent instance without that context is a stronger check.

questions.question: Enabling extended thinking for the review step is as effective at catching subtle issues as sending the code to a separate reviewer instance.
questions.explanation: Extra reasoning time happens inside the same context that produced the code, so the bias toward its own decisions remains. A separate instance without that context is more effective.

questions.question: A support agent summarizes the conversation every few turns to stay within budget. In a long refund chat, the early detail "refund of $84.50 for order A-7731, promised by Friday" has shrunk to "customer wants a refund", and the agent now asks the customer to repeat the amount. What is the best fix?
options: Instruct the summarizer to keep every important detail and never to shorten a sentence that contains a number or a date
Summarize more often, so that each summary covers only a handful of turns and drops less detail from each one
Move to a model with a larger context window so that long conversations rarely need summarizing at all
Keep amounts, dates, order numbers and promises in a facts block sent with every prompt, apart from the summarized history
questions.explanation: Each round of summarizing trades precision for brevity, so figures, dates and promises are the first things to blur. A case facts block holds those transactional facts exactly and puts them in every prompt, while the summary is free to stay loose. Asking the summarizer to be careful still leaves the facts inside a lossy process, summarizing more often means more rounds of loss, and a bigger window does not prevent compression once it happens (accuracy also falls as the context fills).

questions.question: In a returns workflow, each lookup_order call returns about forty fields, but a return decision needs only the status, the item list, the amounts and the delivery date. After several lookups the agent loses track of earlier details and the cost per conversation is climbing. What is the best change?
options: Add a prompt rule telling the agent to ignore every order field that has no bearing on returns
Cut each result down to the return-relevant fields in code before it is added to the conversation
Raise max_tokens so that the long order records fit alongside the agent's replies
Keep the full records and have the agent summarize the whole conversation after every lookup
questions.explanation: A tool result stays in the conversation and is re-read on every later turn, so the cheapest tokens are the ones that never enter it. Filtering to the relevant fields in code (in the tool wrapper or a post-execution hook) cuts cost and distraction at the same time. An instruction to ignore fields leaves every token in place, max_tokens limits the length of the reply rather than the input, and summarizing after each lookup still ingests the whole record and adds a lossy step.

questions.question: A synthesis agent receives about 30 pages of aggregated findings from five research subagents. Final reports keep leaving out findings that sit in the middle of the input, although the earlier and later sections are well covered. Which change addresses this best?
options: Put a short key-findings summary at the start and give each detailed section a clear header
Ask for a longer final report so that every finding has room to appear in the output
End the prompt with a line in capital letters telling the model not to skip the middle sections
Order the sections by the time each subagent finished, so that the layout is the same every run
questions.explanation: Models tend to use the start and end of a long input more reliably than the middle, so the fix is structural: surface the key findings where they will be read and make the rest navigable with explicit headers. A longer report does not make the model attend to material it overlooks, an emphatic sentence is still a prompt-wording hope, and finishing order is arbitrary, so it does not move important material to a well-read position.

questions.question: A document-analysis subagent returns several paragraphs of narrative reasoning for each document. The synthesis agent has a limited context budget and runs out of room when it combines five of these results. What is the best way to fix this?
options: Cut every incoming result to its first 500 words before it reaches the synthesis agent, whatever it contains
Raise max_tokens on the synthesis agent so that it can read and write at greater length when combining results
Add another agent that rewrites each narrative as one shorter paragraph before synthesis begins
Change the analysis subagent to return key facts, citations and relevance scores in a structured form
questions.explanation: Fix the producer: when a downstream agent has a small budget, upstream agents should return compact structured data (facts, citations, relevance scores, with dates and source locations) instead of prose and reasoning chains. Cutting at 500 words discards whatever comes later, max_tokens bounds output rather than input, and an extra rewriting step adds one more lossy summary that strips figures and sources.

questions.question: A customer disputes three separate orders in one long conversation. Near the end, the agent applies the refund amount from the second order to the third and misquotes a delivery date. Which design change best prevents this?
options: Keep a structured record for each issue (order ID, amount, status) as a separate context layer included in every prompt
Merge the three disputes into one running narrative so that the agent sees a single coherent story
Ask the customer to restate each order's details every few turns so that the agent can refresh its memory
Drop the oldest turns once the customer moves on to the next order, so the context holds only the current dispute
questions.explanation: In a multi-issue session the facts for each issue must stay separate and exact. A structured per-issue layer outside the running history works as a ledger the model can consult for each dispute. One merged narrative is exactly how details tangle, making customers repeat themselves is poor service and still leans on the transcript, and deleting old turns throws away facts that may be needed again, for example in a final summary.

questions.question: A synthesis agent must compare statistics reported by several subagents, and the subagents currently return only a paragraph of prose each. Which two additions to their structured output most help the synthesis agent interpret the figures correctly? (Choose two.)
options: The date each figure was published or collected, and where in the source it appears
The subagent's full chain of reasoning behind each finding
A note saying which subagent finished its work first
The methodological context, such as the sample size and how the figure was measured
A one-word label describing how confident the source sounds
questions.explanation: Dates, source locations and methodological context let downstream synthesis tell a real disagreement from a difference in time, population or method. A reasoning chain adds bulk without helping comparison, finishing order says nothing about the data, and a tone label is not evidence about how a number was produced.

questions.question: Telling the model to ignore the irrelevant fields in a long tool result removes those fields from the context window.
questions.explanation: An instruction changes what the model attends to, not what is in the window. The unused tokens stay in the history and are processed again on every later turn, so large results should be trimmed in code before they are appended.

questions.question: Models tend to handle material at the start and end of a very long input more reliably than material in the middle, so a key-findings summary placed first and clear section headers can help.
questions.explanation: This position effect is why aggregated inputs should open with the key findings and organize the details under explicit headers. For long documents, the usual guidance is to put the material first and the question last.

questions.question: Because the Messages API keeps each conversation on the server, a follow-up request only has to contain the newest user message.
questions.explanation: The API is stateless: Claude knows only what each request contains. To keep a conversation coherent, the request must carry the earlier turns, including tool requests and their results, which is exactly why trimming and structuring what goes into the history matters.

questions.question: A customer writes: "I have been charged twice. Please just transfer me to a person." The agent replies that it will first pull up the account and both transactions to see whether it can fix the problem. What should the agent have done?
options: Offered to resolve the duplicate charge and transferred the customer only if the request was repeated
Checked the charges first, then transferred the customer if it could not refund the duplicate within a few steps
Transferred the customer to a human agent right away, with a summary of what is already known
Asked the customer to explain why a human is needed, so that it can judge whether a transfer is justified
questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human is honored immediately: the customer has already made the decision, and investigating first or demanding a justification overrides it. The acknowledge-and-offer pattern is for frustration without such a request. Passing on what is already known keeps the handoff useful.
