questions.question: A customer writes: "This is the third time my parcel is late and I am furious." They do not ask for a person. Under the standard policy the agent can arrange a redelivery or a shipping credit. What is the best response?
options: Escalate to a human at once, because strongly negative sentiment is a reliable signal of a serious case that needs a person
Process the standard credit quietly, without mentioning the customer's frustration, to keep the reply short
Acknowledge the frustration, offer the redelivery or credit, and escalate only if the customer still wants a person
Ask the customer whether they would like to be transferred to a person before doing anything else for them
questions.explanation: Frustration alone is not a trigger. When the problem is within the agent's reach, acknowledging the feeling and offering a concrete fix resolves it, and a repeated wish for a human is honored at that point. Sentiment does not track difficulty, so escalating on tone sends solvable cases to people; ignoring the emotion is cold, and asking about a transfer first delays the fix.

questions.question: The price-adjustment policy covers only price drops on the company's own site within 14 days of purchase. A customer asks the agent to match a cheaper listing from a competitor, a case the policy does not mention. What should the agent do?
options: Escalate to a human with the details, because the policy is silent on this request
Decline the request, since the policy only authorizes adjustments to the company's own prices
Grant the price match to keep the customer and record the exception for later review
Ask for a screenshot of the competitor's listing and approve the match if it looks genuine
questions.explanation: When the policy is silent or ambiguous about a request, the agent should not invent policy in either direction: a refusal and an approval are both improvised decisions. A gap, rather than mere difficulty, is the trigger for a human. Asking for a screenshot treats a missing rule as a verification problem.

questions.question: The get_customer tool returns three accounts for the name "Maria Lopez". The agent picks the account with the most recent activity and begins processing a refund. Which change to the agent's instructions is best?
options: Rank the matches by order value and pick the account that is most likely to own the disputed order, then proceed
Escalate to a human whenever more than one account matches a name, instead of trying to resolve it
Choose the most recent account but tell the customer which one was used so that they can object
Ask the customer for another identifier, such as an email address or order number, before continuing
questions.explanation: Choosing among candidates by heuristic risks acting on the wrong person's account, which is far worse than one extra question. Asking for an additional identifier resolves the ambiguity cheaply. Ranking by order value is just another heuristic, objecting after the fact happens when the refund is already under way, and escalating turns a routine ambiguity into an unnecessary handoff.

questions.question: A support lead proposes adding this rule to the escalation policy: "Escalate any message that contains three or more separate problems, because those cases are complex." How should the proposal be judged?
options: Adopt it, since complex cases carry the highest risk of mistakes and humans handle them best of all
Drop it and escalate only on a customer request, a policy gap or a lack of progress
Adopt it, but apply it only when the customer's tone is negative, to avoid unnecessary handoffs
Adopt it, but skip the escalation whenever the agent reports high confidence in its own answer
questions.explanation: Complexity by itself is not an escalation trigger: three routine problems can be resolved one by one and answered together. Escalation should follow an explicit request, a policy gap or inability to progress. Adding a tone condition or a self-reported confidence condition brings in two unreliable proxies for difficulty.

questions.question: Which three situations justify handing a case from the agent to a human? (Choose three.)
options: The customer asks to speak to a person.
A sentiment score for the customer's latest message is strongly negative.
The customer's request falls into a gap that the written policy does not address.
The agent reports a confidence of 6 out of 10 in its own proposed answer.
Repeated attempts have left the agent unable to make meaningful progress on the issue.
questions.explanation: The three sound triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy gap or ambiguity, and inability to make progress. Detected sentiment and self-reported confidence are weak proxies: sentiment says little about how complex or risky a case is, and a model is often most confident on exactly the cases it gets wrong.

questions.question: A model's self-reported confidence score is a dependable signal for deciding which cases to escalate to a human.
questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated: models are often most confident on exactly the hard cases they get wrong. Escalation should follow explicit criteria (a customer request, a policy gap, inability to progress), and confidence becomes usable for routing only after it has been calibrated against labeled outcomes.

questions.question: An agent that has tried its available tools and still cannot make meaningful progress on a request should hand the case to a human, even if the customer has not asked for one.
questions.explanation: Inability to make progress is one of the sound escalation triggers; looping on a stuck request wastes the customer's time. The handoff should say what was tried and what is known.

questions.question: A research coordinator receives two reports. The patent subagent says: "Query ran against the patent database; 0 matches." The regulatory subagent says: "Request to the regulatory database timed out after 30 seconds; no data returned." How should the coordinator treat them?
options: Treat both as "no information available", since neither source returned any data, and leave both sources out of the final report
Treat the patent result as a real "nothing found" and the regulatory result as a gap needing a retry or another source
Treat both as failures and rerun both subagents until each of them returns at least one result
Treat both as successful searches, since neither subagent raised an unhandled exception in its code
questions.explanation: A valid empty result is an answer: the source was reached and had nothing to offer. An access failure is missing information: the source was never reached, so absence cannot be concluded. Only when the two are reported differently can the coordinator choose well (retry, alternative source, or a coverage note if the gap remains). Merging them hides gaps, and forcing a result out of a legitimately empty search never ends.

questions.question: A web-search subagent occasionally receives a brief 503 error from its search provider, and a retry a second later nearly always succeeds. How should the subagent handle this?
options: Report every such error to the coordinator immediately, so that the coordinator decides about every retry and every skip
Retry locally with a short backoff, and report upward only if that fails, with the attempts and any partial results
Retry without any limit until the call succeeds, so that the coordinator never has to see a failure of any kind
Skip the query and return an empty result so that the research continues without any delay to the other agents
questions.explanation: Transient failures are cheapest to fix where they happen. The subagent recovers locally and escalates only what it cannot resolve, with the attempts and partial results needed for a decision. Forwarding every blip floods the coordinator, endless retries can hang a run on a permanent fault, and an empty result silently suppresses the error.

questions.question: Two of five planned sources, both paywalled journals, could not be accessed during a research run. The other three produced solid findings. How should the synthesized report handle this?
options: Present the findings as complete, since the missing journals would most likely have agreed with the three that were read
Open every report with a general line saying that results may be incomplete, without naming any gaps
Annotate coverage: mark which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps because sources were unavailable
Withhold the report until every planned source has been reached, however long that takes, so nothing is partial
questions.explanation: A coverage annotation lets readers rely on the strong sections and see exactly where the weak ones are. Presenting partial work as complete misleads, a boilerplate warning does not say which areas are affected, and refusing to deliver wastes the findings that are solid (and may wait forever on a source that stays unavailable).

questions.question: A document-analysis subagent processes 40 PDFs. The 23rd file is corrupted and throws an exception; the orchestration code catches it at the top level and stops the whole research workflow, discarding 22 finished analyses. What is the best redesign?
options: Record a structured error for that file and carry on, so the coordinator can retry or note the gap
Return an empty analysis for the corrupted file and mark it successful so that the workflow keeps going
Retry the corrupted file in a loop until it parses, and only then continue with the remaining files
Check all 40 files in advance and refuse to start the run unless every single one of them opens correctly
questions.explanation: One bad input should not erase the value of the other 39. Containing the failure and reporting it as structured error context lets the coordinator decide what to do (retry, try an alternative extraction route, or skip with a note). An empty success hides the problem, a corrupted file will never parse however often it is retried, and demanding perfect inputs only moves the abort earlier.

questions.question: A research report states that "no published studies exist" on a topic, yet a manual search finds plenty. The logs show that the search subagent timed out on every query and returned an empty list with the status "success". What is the right fix?
options: Tell the synthesis agent to double-check every empty result by running its own searches before it writes the report
Raise the search timeout to two minutes so that queries are much less likely to fail in the first place, whatever the load
Add a rule to the report template that forbids absolute claims such as "no studies exist"
Return a timeout as a structured failure with the attempted query and partial results, not as an empty success
questions.explanation: The defect is upstream: an access failure was reported as a valid empty result, so neither the coordinator nor the synthesis agent could know that anything had gone wrong. Fixing the report at its source makes recovery possible. Downstream verification duplicates work and still cannot tell failure from absence, a longer timeout only reduces how often the bug fires, and a template rule hides the symptom.

questions.question: A reviewer is auditing the error handling of a multi-agent research pipeline. Which two behaviors should be fixed because they weaken recovery? (Choose two.)
options: A subagent retries a transient timeout locally before it reports a failure
A subagent returns an empty result marked as successful after its source timed out
A failure report includes the attempted query and the partial results gathered so far
A single failed subagent call terminates the whole workflow and discards the finished work
The final report notes which topic areas lacked sources
questions.explanation: Silent suppression hides that anything went wrong, and aborting on one failure throws away recoverable work; both remove the coordinator's ability to choose a sensible response. Local retries, informative failure reports and coverage notes are the recommended behaviors.

questions.question: A search that runs successfully and finds no matching documents should be reported to the coordinator as an error, so that the coordinator can retry the query.
questions.explanation: A valid empty result is a legitimate answer, not a failure. Reporting it as an error would trigger pointless retries and blur it with real access failures such as timeouts. The two outcomes should be distinguishable.

questions.question: A subagent should handle transient failures such as brief timeouts itself and propagate only the errors it cannot resolve.
questions.explanation: Local recovery keeps the coordinator focused on decisions that need its wider view. What does travel upward should include what was attempted and any partial results.

questions.question: Three hours into mapping a legacy accounting system, an agent starts to answer with lines like "a typical layered design would put posting logic in a service class" instead of naming the LedgerPostingService it found in the first hour. What is the best way to counter this?
options: Have the agent record key findings (class names, paths, call chains) in a scratchpad file and reread it when needed
Add a reminder to every question telling the agent to name specific classes instead of typical patterns and to be precise
Start a fresh conversation for each new question and let the agent rediscover the code every single time it is asked
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the early discoveries stay in range for the rest of the session
questions.explanation: In long sessions, early specifics blur into generic patterns. A scratchpad moves the key findings outside the window, where they can be reread exactly whenever a question needs them. A reminder cannot restore details the model no longer uses reliably, restarting throws away hours of discovery, and a larger window does not stop recall from degrading as the context fills.

questions.question: In a repository with thousands of files, an engineer asks the main agent to find every test file and then to trace the dependencies of the refund flow. The raw search output is filling the main conversation. What is the most effective approach?
options: Run the searches in the main conversation and clear it with /clear once the answer has been found and noted
Cap every search at its first twenty matches so that the output stays small enough for the main conversation
Delegate each question to a subagent whose verbose output stays in its own context, returning only a summary
Tell the agent to remember only the file names and to forget the rest of each result as soon as it has read it
questions.explanation: A subagent works in a separate context window, so the bulky reads never reach the main conversation; the main agent keeps the high-level picture and receives a compact answer. Clearing discards the findings, a twenty-match cap can miss files, and an instruction to forget has no mechanism behind it.

questions.question: A codebase review runs in two phases. In phase one, subagents map the modules and their dependencies. In phase two, a new set of subagents will examine the riskiest modules in depth. How should the phase-two agents benefit from phase one?
options: Rely on the phase-two agents to inherit the phase-one conversation automatically
Have the phase-two agents rediscover the structure themselves so that their conclusions stay independent
Pass the complete phase-one transcripts to every agent so that nothing is left out
Summarize the key findings of phase one and place that summary in each phase-two agent's starting prompt
questions.explanation: Subagents start with an empty context, so earlier findings must be put in their prompt. A concise summary of what phase one learned avoids both rediscovery and the cost of dragging whole transcripts forward. Automatic inheritance does not exist, rediscovery is slow and duplicative, and full transcripts bring back the verbosity that delegation was meant to keep out.

questions.question: A multi-agent analysis of a large codebase crashes four hours in. When restarted, the coordinator begins from scratch and repeats all the earlier work. Which design best supports recovery?
options: Increase the timeout of every agent in the system so that long-running work is much less likely to crash before it has finished
Have each agent export state to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects the state
Keep all agent state in memory and rely on the model to recall the earlier progress after a restart, however long ago it was made
Store the raw transcript of every agent and replay all of them into one prompt on restart so nothing is missing
questions.explanation: Recovery needs durable, structured state outside any agent's memory: each agent writes its state to an agreed place, and the coordinator reads a manifest to learn what is finished and what remains, then injects the relevant state into the resumed agents. Longer timeouts only postpone failure, in-memory state is lost in a crash, and replaying raw transcripts is huge and would refill the context with the very bulk that caused trouble.

questions.question: During a long Claude Code session exploring a payments module, the context is filling with verbose discovery output and replies are becoming less precise. The engineer wants to keep working on the same task. What is the best action?
options: Run /clear and ask Claude to explore the module again from the start, so that the context is clean
Run /compact with a focus on the payment classes and call paths, then keep going in the same session
Paste the conversation so far into a new session so that nothing is lost, then continue the exploration there
Keep working until automatic compaction runs, and accept whatever it decides to keep from the session so far
questions.explanation: /compact summarizes the session so far and continues it, freeing space, and a focus instruction steers the summary toward what you still need. /clear discards the conversation and forces rediscovery, pasting the transcript into a new session recreates the bloat, and waiting leaves the choice of what to keep to the automatic pass.

questions.question: An agent built directly on the Claude API runs long, tool-heavy tasks, and stale tool results are filling its context window. Which two features directly help manage that growth? (Choose two.)
options: Prompt caching, which stops cached tokens from counting toward the context window
Context editing's tool result clearing, which removes the oldest tool results once a threshold is passed
Server-side compaction, which replaces earlier turns with a summary so that the conversation can continue
Raising max_tokens, which enlarges the room available for the conversation history
Strict tool use, which keeps the output of each tool smaller
questions.explanation: Tool result clearing removes stale tool output by rule, and server-side compaction (currently in beta) replaces older turns with a model-written summary. Prompt caching changes what repeated prefixes cost, but cached tokens still occupy the window; max_tokens limits the length of a reply, not the room for history; and strict tool use guarantees schema-valid tool inputs without shrinking anything.

questions.question: A developer plans a long Claude Code session and expects to use /compact. Which two statements about compaction are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Optional focus instructions steer what the summary keeps
Instructions given only in a chat message are guaranteed to survive word for word
Compaction deletes the conversation and starts again with an empty context
The project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk afterward, so its instructions keep applying
Every file the session read is restored in full, exactly as it was
questions.explanation: A focus such as "/compact focus on the auth bug fix" tells the summarizer what matters, and the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-injected from disk, which is why standing instructions belong there rather than in a one-off message. Chat-only instructions are summarized like the rest of the conversation, deleting everything is what /clear does, and only a few recently modified files are re-read after compaction.

questions.question: A subagent that investigates a question should return its full raw search output to the main agent so that no detail is lost.
questions.explanation: The point of delegation is to keep verbose exploration output inside the subagent's own context. The main agent should receive a concise, structured summary, which leaves its window free for coordination.

questions.question: In Claude Code, /compact summarizes the conversation so far and continues the same session, whereas /clear starts again with an empty context.
questions.explanation: Compaction frees space while keeping a summary of the work; clearing discards the conversation, which suits unrelated tasks or a restart after repeated failed corrections.

questions.question: An invoice-extraction pipeline reports 97% field accuracy across all documents, and management wants to drop human review. A breakdown shows 99% on typed invoices (80% of volume), 96% on scanned receipts (15%) and 68% on handwritten forms (5%). What is the best next step?
options: Remove review everywhere, since 97% exceeds the target and the weak segment is only 5% of the volume
Automate the segments that meet the target and keep human review for the weak one while it improves
Keep human review for all documents until overall accuracy reaches 100%, because anything less is a risk
Take a random sample of 3% of all documents and decide from the overall error rate that sample shows
questions.explanation: An overall figure averages away weak segments, so accuracy has to be validated by document type and field before review is reduced. Segments that pass can be automated while the failing one stays under review. Dropping review everywhere would let about a third of handwritten forms through wrong, demanding perfection is impractical, and a flat random sample is dominated by easy typed invoices, so it would barely see the problem.

questions.question: A team auto-approves every extraction with a confidence above 0.9 and no longer reviews them. Three months later a supplier changes its invoice layout, and the resulting errors go unnoticed until a customer complains. Which practice would have caught the problem earlier?
options: Review every extraction rated above 0.9 as well, so that nothing in the pipeline is automated any more
Lower the auto-approval threshold from 0.9 to 0.8 so that a larger share of documents is reviewed by people
Review a stratified random sample of the auto-approved extractions every week and track errors by segment
Ask the model to explain, for every extraction it approves, why it is confident in the values it extracted
questions.explanation: Automation removes the checking that would reveal a new failure pattern. Regular stratified random sampling of high-confidence outputs keeps measuring their true error rate by segment, such as supplier or document type, and surfaces new patterns like a layout change. Reviewing everything defeats the purpose of automating, a lower threshold still trusts the model's confidence on layouts it misreads, and a self-explanation is not an independent measurement.

questions.question: An extraction prompt now asks the model to report a confidence score for each field. How should the team choose the thresholds that decide which fields go to human review?
options: Use 0.9 for every field, because that is the conventional cut-off for high confidence in extraction work
Ask the model to justify its scores and set each threshold where the justification sounds convincing enough
Copy the thresholds from another team's pipeline, since confidence scores mean the same thing everywhere
Calibrate against a labeled validation set and set thresholds from how often each field is right at each level
questions.explanation: A raw score is only the model's opinion. It becomes a routing signal once it is checked against labeled data: if fields scored 0.9 are right nine times in ten, then 0.9 means something. A conventional cut-off, a persuasive justification and borrowed thresholds all skip that measurement, and scores differ by model, prompt, field and document mix.

questions.question: Reviewers can check about 500 extractions per day, but 1,200 land in the review queue. Which prioritization makes the best use of reviewer time?
options: Review in order of arrival until the day's capacity is used, so that no document waits longer than another
Review the lowest calibrated confidence first, with documents whose sources conflict or are ambiguous
Review a random 500 each day, so that every document has an equal chance of being checked by a person
Review the largest documents first, since they contain the most fields that could be wrong in them
questions.explanation: With limited capacity, reviewers should see the extractions most likely to be wrong first: low calibrated confidence, or ambiguous or contradictory source documents. Arrival order and random selection ignore risk, and size is a weak proxy for it. A separate stratified sample of confident outputs still runs alongside to catch what the scores miss.

questions.question: Two documents attached to the same insurance claim state different dates of loss. The extraction model outputs one of the dates with a confidence of 0.96. What should the pipeline do?
options: Accept the date, since 0.96 is above the review threshold and the pipeline can send the claim straight on
Reject the claim automatically and ask the customer to resubmit documents that are consistent with each other
Route the claim to human review, because the sources contradict each other whatever the confidence
Keep the date from the document that was uploaded most recently, as it is probably the corrected one
questions.explanation: Contradictory or ambiguous sources belong with a person: a high score cannot settle a disagreement between documents, and choosing either date is a guess. Accepting by score, choosing by upload time or rejecting automatically each skip the human judgement that the conflict needs.

questions.question: A team wants to know whether it is safe to expand the automated acceptance of extractions. Which two measures give the most reliable evidence? (Choose two.)
options: A single overall accuracy figure computed across every document
Accuracy broken down by document type and by field on a labeled set
Accuracy measured only on the extractions that the model scored as low confidence
The model's own written assessment of how reliable its extractions have been
Ongoing review of stratified random samples of the high-confidence extractions
questions.explanation: Per-segment accuracy reveals the weak document types and fields that an average hides, and ongoing stratified sampling measures the true error rate among the outputs that automation no longer checks while exposing new patterns. An overall figure masks weak segments, sampling only low-confidence items says nothing about the confident ones being accepted, and self-assessment is not independent evidence.

questions.question: A 97% overall accuracy figure shows that every document type and every field is also close to 97% accurate.
questions.explanation: An overall number is an average weighted by volume, so a large, easy segment can hide a small, weak one. Accuracy has to be checked by document type and field before human review is reduced.

questions.question: Stratified random sampling draws samples separately from each segment, such as each document type, so that small segments are represented in the measurement of error rates.
questions.explanation: Sampling within each stratum guarantees that rare but important segments are checked, which a single pooled random sample might skip. It supports ongoing error-rate measurement and the detection of new failure patterns.

questions.question: Two credible sources report different 30-day readmission rates for heart-failure patients: a national registry says 21% and an insurer's claims analysis says 24%. What should the synthesis agent do?
options: Report the registry's figure alone, because registries are generally regarded as more authoritative sources
Report the average, 22.5%, as the best single estimate of the true readmission rate for these patients
Report both figures, each labeled with its source and, if known, its method, and flag that they differ
Leave the statistic out of the report altogether, because the sources disagree about what the rate is
questions.explanation: When credible sources conflict, the honest output keeps both values with attribution, so the reader can weigh them; differences often come from definitions, populations or years. Silently choosing one hides the disagreement, an average is a number that no source reported, and omitting the statistic discards useful evidence.

questions.question: A synthesis agent flags a "contradiction": one source says 12% of firms use a technology, another says 31%. The 12% figure comes from a 2021 survey and the 31% figure from a 2025 survey, but the subagents' outputs did not show dates. Which change best prevents false contradictions like this?
options: Require subagents to include the publication or data-collection date in each structured finding
Instruct the synthesis agent to always prefer the most recent figure and ignore older ones
Have each subagent settle disagreements with the other subagents before returning its findings
Tell the synthesis agent never to describe any difference between sources as a contradiction
questions.explanation: Without dates, a change over time looks like a conflict. With a date on every finding, the synthesis agent can present the figures as a trend, 12% in 2021 and 31% in 2025. Always preferring the newest figure hides that trend, subagents work in isolation and cannot see each other's findings, and banning the word contradiction would also hide real conflicts.

questions.question: To fit a downstream budget, an intermediate agent condenses 60 findings into 15 bullets. Three of the findings made the same claim, each from a different report. Which representation of the merged claim best preserves provenance?
options: The claim once, with a note that three sources agree
The claim once, with the source of only the first finding, to keep the bullet short
The claim once, with no sources, because corroboration makes citations unnecessary
The claim once, with all three source URLs and a supporting excerpt from each
questions.explanation: Claim-source mappings must be preserved and merged when findings are combined: the merged record keeps every source and its excerpt, so each can be audited and the corroboration is visible. A bare count cannot be traced, one source throws away the other two, and dropping sources removes the very thing that makes a claim checkable.

questions.question: A final report covers 20 findings. Twelve are supported by several agreeing sources, and eight involve sources that disagree on method or numbers. How should the report be structured?
options: Rank all 20 findings in one list by publication date, newest first, so that readers see recent work at the top
Include only the twelve established findings so that the report speaks with one clear and confident voice
Present all 20 in a single list and add hedging words such as "some say" to each of the disputed ones
Separate established from contested findings, keeping each source's own characterization and methods
questions.explanation: Separating established from contested findings shows readers where confidence is high and where it is not, and keeping the sources' own wording and methods lets them weigh the disagreement. A date-ordered list mixes the two, omitting the contested eight conceals the uncertainty, and hedging words do not say who disagrees or why.

questions.question: A synthesis agent converts everything it finds into bullet points. Quarterly revenue figures for four companies become hard to compare, and a news story loses its narrative thread. What is the best fix?
options: Render each type in its natural form: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists
Present all content as tables, because tables are the most precise way to show any kind of information to a reader
Present all content as continuous prose, so that the whole report reads as a single coherent narrative from start to end
Output everything as JSON and leave the decision about how to display it to a downstream formatter at a later stage
questions.explanation: Different kinds of content carry their information differently, so forcing one uniform format destroys some of it. Tables suit comparisons of numbers, prose suits narrative, and structured lists suit technical points. A single table format flattens stories, prose buries numbers, and passing the decision to a hypothetical formatter leaves the problem unsolved.

questions.question: A document-analysis subagent finds two different values for the same metric in two reports. Which two actions fit the recommended pattern? (Choose two.)
options: Include both values in its structured output, each annotated with its source and date
Keep only the value from the report with more pages, since it is probably more thorough
Let the coordinator decide how to reconcile the values before the findings go to synthesis
Average the two values and report the result as the finding
Leave the metric out entirely, since the reports disagree
questions.explanation: The analysis agent reports the conflict openly, with both values annotated; the coordinator, which sees the whole task, decides how to reconcile it before synthesis. Picking by page count, averaging and omitting the metric each resolve the disagreement silently, on weak grounds, or by throwing the evidence away.

questions.question: When two credible sources give different figures for the same statistic, the synthesis step should choose one value so that the report reads cleanly.
questions.explanation: Silently choosing hides a real disagreement. The report should keep both values, annotate each with its source (and method or date where known), and let the reader or coordinator reconcile them.

questions.question: Requiring publication or data-collection dates in subagents' structured outputs helps the synthesis step tell a real conflict from a change over time.
questions.explanation: A statistic that moved between 2021 and 2025 describes a trend, not a contradiction. Dates on every finding let the synthesis step interpret differences correctly.

lessons.title: The Agentic Loop and Task Decomposition
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.1 and 1.6: how an agent loop runs on stop_reason, how tool results reach the next step, which termination shortcuts fail, and when to use a prompt chain versus adaptive decomposition.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.1 (agentic loops) and 1.6 (task decomposition). An agent is a loop wrapped around a model. You give Claude a goal, a list of tools and the conversation so far. It answers either with a final reply or with a request: run this tool with these arguments. Claude never runs your tools itself. Your code, or the Claude Agent SDK, which ships the loop ready-made, runs the tool, adds the output to the conversation and asks again. That repeat-until-done cycle is the agentic loop.

The control flow hangs on one field of every API response, stop_reason. When it is "tool_use", the response contains one or more tool_use blocks, each with an id, a tool name and an input object. You execute them and send a new user message holding one tool_result block per request, matched by id and placed before any text. When it is "end_turn", Claude is finished and the loop exits. "max_tokens" means the reply was cut off; if it ends in a half-written tool request, retry with a larger limit instead of running the fragment. The Messages API is stateless, so every request carries the whole history: the assistant message with its tool requests and the user message with the results. That appended history is how Claude "remembers" what a tool returned. If one response asks for several independent tools, return all results together; read-only calls may run concurrently.

This design is model-driven: Claude reads the latest results and decides what to call next, or whether to stop. The alternative is a pre-configured decision tree, where your code fixes the order of tools. Trees are predictable and fine when the steps really are known, but they cannot react to what a result reveals. The exam expects you to spot three anti-patterns for ending a loop. Scanning Claude's prose for "all done" breaks when the wording changes. Treating the existence of text as completion fails because Claude often writes a sentence beside a tool request. Making an iteration cap the primary stop cuts off tasks that need more steps. Caps still belong as a safety net: the Agent SDK's maxTurns and budget limits end a run with an error result (error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd), so check the subtype before reading the text; only success carries a final answer.

Task statement 1.6 asks how to break big work into steps. A prompt chain is a fixed sequence of focused calls: extract, then validate, then summarize. Use it when the steps are predictable and repeat on every input. For code review the standard chain is a per-file pass for local problems, then a separate integration pass on data flow across files. The reason is attention dilution: when a model reviews many files at once, depth becomes uneven, bugs slip through and the same pattern gets contradictory verdicts. A bigger context window does not cure that; narrower passes do.

Open-ended work needs the opposite, dynamic and adaptive decomposition. To add tests to a legacy billing system nobody understands, a checklist written before looking at the code is wrong within the hour. Map the structure first, find the high-impact or risky areas, write a prioritized plan, and revise it whenever a new dependency appears. Predictable steps call for a chain; unpredictable discoveries call for a plan that adapts.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agentic loops? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a contractor who has no hands of her own and works through an assistant on the phone. She says "measure the kitchen window", the assistant does it and reports back, and she decides what to ask next. She hangs up only when she says "that is everything I need". A fixed checklist would be a script the assistant follows whatever the measurements show. The loop is the phone call, and the closing sentence is the signal that ends it; listening to the assistant's chatter for hints that she must be finished would be the mistake.
commonTraps: Ending the loop because a reply contains text, or because it says "done", is wrong; the stop reason decides.
A turn or iteration cap is a safety net that ends the run with an error result, not the normal way an agent finishes.
The API is stateless, so leaving out the assistant's tool requests or the matching results makes the agent lose its place.
A bigger context window does not fix inconsistent multi-file reviews; focused per-file passes plus an integration pass do.
lessons.scenario: A team builds a returns assistant on the Messages API. Their first loop stopped whenever a response contained text and often quit mid-task. They now continue while the stop reason is tool_use, finish on end_turn, resend the full history each time, and keep a maximum-turns guardrail that returns a clear error. For a weekly audit of return policies they use a fixed chain of extract, validate and summarize, while for investigating odd refund patterns they let the agent plan adaptively.
lessons.onTheJob: Log the stop reason of every response and the number of loop iterations per task; a sudden change in either is the earliest warning that a prompt or tool change broke something. Keep guardrails such as a turn limit, a spending cap and timeouts, but make each produce a specific, handled outcome so a capped run can be resumed rather than silently going wrong. Reach for a fixed chain first when the work is predictable: it is cheaper, easier to test and easier to explain than an agent. Add adaptivity only where discoveries really change the plan.

lessons.title: Coordinators, Subagents and Context Passing
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.2 and 1.3: hub-and-spoke orchestration, subagent definitions and isolation, explicit context passing, parallel spawning, and the coordinator's decomposition, selection and refinement duties.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.2 and 1.3. A single agent has one context window and one toolbox. When a job is broad, such as a cited research report, you split it across specialists: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes, one writes the report. The common shape is hub-and-spoke. A coordinator agent receives the request, decomposes it, delegates to subagents, collects what they return and decides what happens next. Subagents never talk to each other; everything passes through the coordinator, which gives you one place to log, one place to handle errors consistently and one place to control what each agent sees.

A subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window, system prompt and tool list. In the Agent SDK you describe each type with an AgentDefinition (a description that tells the coordinator when to use it, a system prompt, and the tools it may use) and the coordinator starts instances by calling the subagent-launching tool. The exam guide calls that tool Task and expects the coordinator's allowed tools to include it; current SDK documentation calls it Agent and still accepts the old name. The key fact is isolation. A subagent does not inherit the coordinator's conversation, earlier tool results or other subagents' work. The only channel from parent to child is the prompt string, and the only channel back is the child's final message. A delegation prompt must therefore be self-contained: the goal, the quality bar, the actual findings to build on, the output format and any constraints. "Summarize what the search agent found" fails if those findings were never pasted in.

Pass structured records rather than prose. If each finding carries the claim, an evidence excerpt, the source URL or document name, the page and the date, attribution survives every hand-off, whereas a flowing paragraph is where citations die. Write coordinator prompts as goals and quality criteria rather than rigid step lists, so a subagent can adapt when a site is blocked or a source is empty.

The coordinator earns its keep in four jobs. It decomposes: if it splits "the future of urban transport" into three subtasks that all concern e-scooters, every subagent can succeed and the report still ignores buses, rail and cycling. When a report has gaps and the subagents look healthy, read the coordinator's subtask list first. It selects: a quick factual lookup should not trigger the full pipeline. It partitions scope, by subtopic, region or source type, so parallel agents do not duplicate each other. And it refines: after synthesis it checks for gaps, sends targeted queries to the search and analysis agents, and re-runs synthesis until coverage is adequate.

Speed comes from parallelism. If the coordinator needs four independent lookups, it should emit four launch calls in a single response; they run concurrently and the total time approaches the slowest one. Launched over four turns, the time is the sum. At the session level, a fork copies a session's history into an independent branch so two approaches can start from the same analysis. Two anti-patterns recur: shared mutable state between subagents, such as a common scratchpad both write to, and peer-to-peer messaging that bypasses the hub.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to multi-agent systems? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a newsroom editor running a story on regional flooding. She does not write everything herself: she sends one reporter to the council records, one to interview engineers, and one to check insurance data. Each reporter works alone and can only use the notes on the assignment sheet she hands over, because none of them sat in her planning meeting. When they return, the editor reads their notes, notices that nobody covered funding, sends someone back with a precise question, and only then lets the writer draft the piece.
commonTraps: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history; a short prompt such as "use the earlier results" leaves them blind.
Gaps in a report whose subagents all succeeded usually mean the coordinator's decomposition was too narrow.
Parallelism needs several launch calls in one response; one call per turn is sequential.
Shared scratchpads and agent-to-agent messaging bypass the hub and hide failures.
lessons.scenario: A policy research firm asks its coordinator how small cities are preparing for extreme heat. The coordinator picks three partitions (cooling infrastructure, public health programs, funding sources) and launches the three search subagents in one response. It passes each the goal, scope and a required record format with source URL and date. The first synthesis lacks anything on funding, so the coordinator sends one targeted follow-up query and re-runs synthesis before the report agent is invoked.
lessons.onTheJob: Read the coordinator's decomposition before you read anything else when output quality drops; most coverage bugs are visible there. Write delegation prompts as if the subagent were a smart contractor who has never seen the project: objective, boundaries, the material, the output format, and what to do when data is missing. Keep a subagent's final report short and structured, because that message is all the coordinator receives. Limit each specialist to the tools of its role, and log every launch and return at the hub so you can replay a run.

lessons.title: Enforcement, Hooks and Human Handoffs
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.4 and 1.5: prompt guidance versus programmatic enforcement, prerequisite gates, pre- and post-execution hooks, result normalization, structured handoffs and multi-concern requests.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.4 and 1.5. Some rules are style: be concise, apologize for delays. If the model occasionally forgets, little is lost. Other rules are obligations: verify the customer before touching money, never approve a payment above a limit, never send privileged documents to an outside service. For these the exam draws a hard line. Prompt instructions, however emphatic, and few-shot examples are probabilistic. The model follows them almost always, which still means sometimes not. Where one miss costs money or exposes data, enforce the rule in code.

Two code-level tools carry most of the weight. A prerequisite gate sits in the layer that executes tools. When the model asks for process_refund before get_customer has returned a verified customer id, the gate refuses and returns an error saying what to do first; the model then calls the verification tool. Hooks are callbacks the Agent SDK runs at fixed points in the loop. A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool executes and can allow, deny, ask about or rewrite the call (the decision field is permissionDecision, and rewriting arguments uses updatedInput). A deny blocks the call and its reason is returned to the model, so write the reason as a redirect: "refund exceeds the limit; escalate to a human with a case summary". When several hooks answer differently the strictest wins, so deny beats defer, ask and allow. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool returns and can add context or replace the result before the model reads it.

Two details trip people up. First, a hook's matcher selects by tool name, such as Bash, Write|Edit, or a pattern for every tool of one MCP server, never by arguments. To act on an amount or a file path, read the tool input inside the callback. Second, timing: prevention and argument rewriting belong before execution, while normalization and enrichment belong after. A post-execution hook cannot undo a payment. Hooks run in your application process, so they use no context tokens and the model cannot argue its way past them.

Normalization is the classic post-execution job. Suppose three MCP tools return a date as a Unix timestamp, an ISO 8601 string and a numeric status code. Rather than explaining every format in the prompt, convert them in a post-execution hook so that the model only ever sees one convention.

Humans enter through escalation. A human agent often cannot see the AI conversation, so the handoff must stand alone: customer id, root cause, amounts, actions already taken and a recommended next step. Make the escalation tool's input schema require those fields so a thin handoff cannot be produced. And when a customer message holds several problems, split it into distinct items, investigate them in parallel using the same verified customer context, and reply once with a unified resolution.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to enforcement and hooks? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A bank teller is trained to check ID before any withdrawal. That is guidance. The vault door that will not open until a manager turns a key is enforcement. A good bank uses both: training for judgment, the door for the rule that must never be broken. When the door refuses, a note on it says "needs manager approval, ring the bell", so the teller knows the next step. A pre-execution hook is that door, and its denial reason is the note.
commonTraps: Few-shot examples and stronger wording never provide a guarantee; if the stem mentions money or security, choose the code-level control.
Pre-execution hooks prevent and rewrite; post-execution hooks transform results. A post-execution hook cannot stop a payment.
Matchers match tool names, not arguments; the argument check happens inside the callback.
A denial without a reason strands the agent, so point to the alternative workflow in the message.
A raw transcript or a vague note is a weaker handoff than a structured summary.
lessons.scenario: A telecom billing agent has lookup_account, apply_credit and escalate_to_human tools. The team adds a gate so apply_credit is rejected until lookup_account has returned a verified account id, and a pre-execution hook that denies credits above $200 with the message "above limit; escalate with case summary". A post-execution hook converts the three date formats returned by legacy systems. The escalate tool requires account id, root cause, amount, actions taken and recommended action.
lessons.onTheJob: Start by listing which rules are obligations and which are preferences; only the first group needs hooks and gates, and over-engineering the second group adds maintenance for no benefit. Write every denial message for the model: what was blocked, why, and what to do instead. Test enforcement by trying to break it, for example by asking for a refund before identifying yourself. Keep a log of denials; a rising count shows where the prompt and the policy disagree. Treat hook callbacks like production code, with timeouts and error handling, since a failing hook can block real work.

lessons.title: Sessions: Resume, Fork or Start Fresh
lessons.summary: Covers task statement 1.7: named sessions and resumption, fork_session for divergent approaches, and choosing between resuming with a change note and starting fresh with an injected summary.
lessons.reading:
Task statement 1.7 is about continuity. A session is the saved conversation of an agent run: your prompts, every tool call, every result and every reply. Claude Code and the Agent SDK write it to disk so you can return later with the context intact. Two facts matter more than the mechanics. First, a session stores the conversation, not your files: it remembers what the agent read, not whether the file has changed since. Second, you must choose on purpose between three ways forward: resume, fork, or start fresh.

Resuming continues an existing session with its whole history. In Claude Code you name a session (claude -n auth-refactor at startup, or /rename inside the session) and later reopen it with claude --resume auth-refactor, while claude --continue reopens the most recent session in the directory. In the SDK you capture the session id from the final result message and pass it as resume, and the continue option picks the most recent one automatically. Use the targeted form whenever several sessions exist, for example one per customer or one per investigation. Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves both conversations into one transcript, so do not.

Forking starts a new session as a copy of an existing one: the fork_session option in the SDK, or --fork-session and /branch in Claude Code. The copy gets its own id and the original stays as it was. This is how you explore divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline. Spend an hour mapping a payment module once, then fork twice to compare two testing strategies or two refactorings. Remember what a fork does not branch: files. If both branches edit code in the same directory, the edits collide, so give edit-heavy experiments separate worktrees or copies.

The hard judgment is staleness. A resumed session still holds the outputs of old Read and Bash calls. If a teammate rewrote four files overnight, the agent may reason confidently from contents that no longer exist. You have two good options. When most earlier work is still valid, resume and tell the agent exactly which files changed, so it re-reads those instead of repeating the whole exploration. When many things changed, or the history is long and mostly obsolete, start a new session and inject a structured summary of the findings you still trust. The SDK documentation makes a similar point about moving sessions between machines: capturing results as state and passing them into a fresh prompt is often more robust than shipping transcripts around.

A rule of thumb ties it together. Mostly valid context: resume, plus a note about what changed. Mostly stale context: start fresh with a summary. Several alternatives to try from the same understanding: fork.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to sessions? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A resumed session is like returning to a half-finished jigsaw puzzle on the dining table. Your earlier progress is all there, but someone may have moved pieces while you were away. Forking is photocopying your progress notes so two people can try different strategies; the pieces on the table are still shared, so anything that moves pieces needs a second table. Starting fresh with a summary is sitting down at a clean table with a note that says "the border and the sky are done".
commonTraps: Sessions store conversations, not files, so a resumed or forked agent does not know that files changed unless it is told.
The continue option reopens the most recent session, which may not be the one you want; use resume with a name or id.
Resuming the same session in two places mixes the histories; fork to branch.
Trusting a long, mostly outdated history is riskier than starting fresh from a short summary.
lessons.scenario: An engineer names a session "billing-test-plan" and maps the billing module over two days. A teammate then refactors five files. She resumes the session, lists the five changed files, and the agent re-reads only those before proposing tests. Later she forks the session twice to compare a contract-test strategy with a snapshot-test strategy, each in its own git worktree. After a quarter-end merge touches most modules, she begins a new session seeded with a one-page summary of the findings that survived.
lessons.onTheJob: Name sessions the moment you start anything that may span days, and put the task in the name. Before resuming, check what changed in version control since the session was last active and decide whether a change note will do or a restart is cleaner. Keep a short findings file or summary as you work; it doubles as the seed for a fresh session and as protection against context loss. Fork only when you genuinely want to compare alternatives, and give each branch its own worktree if it will write code.

lessons.title: Tool Descriptions, Error Responses and Tool Distribution
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3: writing descriptions that separate similar tools, structured MCP error responses, scoping tools to roles, and what tool_choice guarantees.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3. When Claude chooses a tool it consults only what you show it: the tool's name, its description and its input schema. It never sees your code, so the description does the selecting. A line such as "Retrieves customer information" beside "Retrieves order details" produces unreliable picks when both take similar identifiers. A strong description says what the tool does, which inputs it accepts with an example format, what it returns, the edge cases, and the boundary: when to use it instead of a similar tool.

Overlap is the enemy. If analyze_content and analyze_document read almost the same, rename and rewrite them so each has a distinct purpose, for example one built for extracting web results. A generic tool that extracts, summarizes and fact-checks, with a different output shape for each, should be split into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts. (The documentation also advises grouping closely related operations; the shared principle is that every tool has one clear purpose.) Then read the system prompt: "always check billing history for billing questions" can wire a keyword to a tool and override good descriptions.

Errors are the other half of the contract. In MCP a failed call comes back inside a normal result with isError set to true, so the model sees the failure as data it can act on; faults in the request itself, like an unknown tool, are JSON-RPC errors. Inside the result, a useful convention, which the exam calls structured error metadata, is a category, an isRetryable flag and a readable message (the field names are yours; the protocol defines only isError). Transient errors such as timeouts deserve a retry. Validation errors need a corrected input. Business errors, such as a refund outside the window, are final: mark them not retryable and include wording the agent can pass to the customer. Permission errors need other access or a human. A uniform "Operation failed" hides all of this, and an empty result returned for an outage is worse: zero matches is a valid answer, a timeout is not.

Where tools live matters as much as how they are written. Give one agent eighteen tools and its selection degrades; give a specialist the four or five its role needs. Out-of-role tools get misused, like web search in a synthesis agent. When a specialist has a frequent, simple need, add one narrow tool (a verify_fact lookup for the synthesis agent) and route rare heavy cases through the coordinator. Swap risky generic tools for constrained ones, such as a validating load_document instead of fetch-any-URL.

Finally, tool_choice. "auto" lets the model answer in text or call tools. "any" requires some tool call and lets the model choose which, which suits several extraction tools when the document type is unknown. Naming a tool forces that call, which suits "run extract_metadata first", with later turns back on auto. Forcing prefills the reply, so no explanation comes before the call. Not every model or setting accepts the forced modes: manual extended thinking rejects them, and current documentation lists newer models where the substitute is automatic choice with strict tool use, which makes inputs match your schema (valid shape, not necessarily sensible values).
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to tool design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A tool description is the label on a drawer in a workshop. A label reading "Tools" tells an apprentice nothing, but "Phillips screwdrivers, sizes 0 to 3, for electronics; for wood screws use the next drawer" lets a newcomer pick correctly without asking. If two drawers carry nearly the same label, even a skilled apprentice guesses. It also helps to hand the apprentice only the drawers needed for today's job instead of the entire warehouse.
commonTraps: Few-shot examples or a routing layer are not the first fix for confusion between similar tools; fix the descriptions and names first.
A business-rule failure is not retryable, and retrying it only wastes calls.
An outage reported as "no results" is silent error suppression, whereas a genuine empty result is a success.
tool_choice auto can return plain text; only requiring a tool (any, or a named tool) guarantees a call, and both skip the explanatory preamble.
More tools for one agent is not more capability: past a handful, selection reliability falls.
lessons.scenario: A logistics assistant has track_shipment and lookup_order, each with a one-line description, and it sends tracking numbers to the wrong one. The team rewrites both descriptions with accepted formats, example queries and an explicit boundary. The refund tool now returns a business error flagged non-retryable, with a customer-friendly sentence, once the window has passed, and a retryable transient error for timeouts. In the research agents, the synthesis agent keeps only a narrow verify_fact tool instead of web search.
lessons.onTheJob: Write tool descriptions the way you would brief a new colleague: what the tool is for, what it is not for, what goes in, what comes out, and one example. Test selection with ambiguous requests such as "check on my order" and read the transcripts; wrong picks usually trace to a thin description or a keyword-heavy line in the system prompt. Standardize one error payload across every tool you own so the agent learns a single vocabulary of failures. When an agent needs a new capability, ask whether another specialist should own it before widening anyone's toolbox.

lessons.title: MCP Servers, Scopes and the Built-in Tools
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 2.4 and 2.5: MCP tools, resources and prompts, project versus user scope, environment variable expansion, descriptions that compete with built-ins, and choosing between Grep, Glob, Read, Write and Edit.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 2.4 and 2.5. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems. A host application creates one client per server, and each server can offer three kinds of capability. Tools are actions the model chooses to invoke. Resources are read-only content addressed by URI, such as documentation pages, database schemas or issue summaries, that the application decides how to surface. Prompts are templates the user selects, usually as slash commands. Servers cannot see the whole conversation or each other, and in the current specification (dated 2026-07-28) every request is self-contained.

Configuration is mostly a question of scope. A project-scoped server lives in .mcp.json at the repository root and is committed, so every teammate gets the same tooling (Claude Code asks for approval first). A user-scoped server lives in your own ~/.claude.json and follows you across projects without touching anyone else, which suits personal or experimental servers. Claude Code also has a local scope, the default for claude mcp add: private to you, tied to the current project, and again stored in ~/.claude.json. If one name is defined in several places, the highest-precedence entry wins whole (local, then project, then user). All configured servers connect together, so a shared GitHub server and your experimental one are usable in the same session. Keep secrets out of the file with environment variable expansion, such as "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" or ${VAR:-default}, and each person supplies the variable.

Claude Code defers MCP tool definitions by default: only names load at the start and full definitions are fetched on demand. MCP tools appear as mcp__server__tool, which is also how permission rules and hook matchers refer to them. Write rich MCP tool descriptions: if the agent keeps using the built-in text search instead of your symbol-aware search tool, the description is probably too thin to compete. And expose catalogs as resources: if the agent wastes calls discovering what exists, publish the documentation hierarchy or schema list as a resource. Prefer an existing community server for a standard integration such as Jira, and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows.

The built-in tools are the other half. Grep searches file contents (callers of a function, an error message, an import). Glob matches file paths (every **/*.test.tsx). Read loads a whole file. Write creates a file or overwrites it with the full content you supply. Edit replaces exact text, which must appear exactly once; if it matches in several places the edit fails, and you either add surrounding lines to make the anchor unique or fall back to reading the file and writing the updated whole. (In some Claude Code setups search runs through the shell; the roles stay the same.)

Do not read all 3,000 files of an unfamiliar service. Search for the entry point (a refund route, an error string), read the file it points to, and follow its imports with more searches. When a function is re-exported through wrapper modules under other names, first list each wrapper's exported names and then search for every one of them; searching only the original name misses the real callers.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to MCP? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: MCP is like a standard wall socket for tools. The host is the building, each server is an appliance plugged into its own socket, and the shared plug shape is the protocol, so any appliance fits. The project-level .mcp.json is the building plan listing the sockets every office has, while your user-level file is the desk lamp you brought from home. The built-in tools are the instruments in your pocket: a magnifying glass for text inside documents (Grep), a directory board for names on doors (Glob), and a pencil for exact corrections (Edit).
commonTraps: Committing a token in .mcp.json is wrong; reference ${VAR} and rotate any secret that leaked.
Project scope is shared through version control and user scope is private, yet tools from all configured servers are available together.
An agent preferring a built-in tool over your MCP tool is a description problem, not a reason to disable the built-in.
Glob finds file names, Grep finds text inside files, and mixing them up is a frequent wrong answer.
A failed targeted edit is fixed with a unique anchor or a read-then-write, not by repeating the edit or using replace-all blindly.
lessons.scenario: A team commits a project .mcp.json that defines a Jira server using ${JIRA_TOKEN}, while one developer keeps an experimental code-search server in her user config. The team also publishes the documentation hierarchy as an MCP resource so agents stop spending calls listing pages. Asked how refunds flow through an unfamiliar service, the agent searches for the refund route, reads the handler and follows the imports; later it finds a wrapper that re-exports a helper under a new name and searches for each exported name.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat .mcp.json like any committed configuration: review it in pull requests, never allow literal credentials, and document which variables a newcomer must set. Put experiments at user scope and promote them to the project file only when the team agrees. Watch transcripts for the agent ignoring a server, which almost always means the description undersells the tool. Teach newcomers the exploration habit of search first and read second, and keep an eye on output size, since huge tool results eat context quickly.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md Hierarchy, Imports and Path-Scoped Rules
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 3.1 and 3.3: where instruction files live and who receives them (user, project, directory), how they combine, @import and .claude/rules/ for modular organization, and path-scoped rules that load only for matching files.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 3.1 and 3.3. Claude Code starts every session knowing nothing about your team, and CLAUDE.md is how you tell it: a plain markdown file of build and test commands, naming conventions and architecture notes, read when a session starts. Two facts frame everything. It is guidance, not enforced configuration, so a line that forbids an action does not block it (use a hook or a deny rule for a guarantee). And every line costs context in every session, so placement matters as much as wording.

Know three levels. The user-level file, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, follows you into every project but lives outside any repository, so teammates never receive it. The project-level file, CLAUDE.md at the repository root or .claude/CLAUDE.md, is committed, so everyone who clones the repository gets the same standards. Directory-level files sit in subdirectories such as packages/api/CLAUDE.md. Files in the working directory and its parents load at launch and are joined rather than overriding, with closer files read later; a subdirectory file loads only when Claude reads or edits a file there. CLAUDE.local.md holds private, gitignored preferences such as a sandbox URL. The classic diagnosis: a new engineer's Claude ignores conventions everyone else sees, because a senior colleague saved them in the user-level file. Move them into the committed project file.

The opposite failure is a monolith: in a 600-line file individual rules get followed less reliably, so aim for under about 200 lines and split by topic. An @import line pulls another file in: writing @docs/standards.md inside packages/payments/CLAUDE.md loads packages/payments/docs/standards.md with it, so each package imports only the standards its maintainers need. Relative paths resolve from the importing file, and imports may nest up to four hops. Imports organize instructions; they do not shrink them, because the imported text loads at launch. The second tool is the .claude/rules/ directory: one small markdown file per topic (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md) in place of one big file. A rule without frontmatter loads at launch.

Path-scoped rules save context. Give a rule file YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns, for example paths: ["terraform/**/*"], and it loads only when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file, so Terraform conventions stay out while someone edits CSS. A glob follows a file type wherever it lives: **/*.test.tsx catches every test file in the repository, whereas directory-level files would need a copy in dozens of folders and would miss the next new one. Use a directory-level file for a convention that belongs to one package, a glob rule for one that cuts across directories. The paths field is the only frontmatter key Claude Code reads in a rule.

When behavior differs between sessions, check what loaded before rewording anything. /memory lists the instruction files in play and opens them for editing; /context shows what fills the window, including the memory files loaded at launch. After /compact the project-root file is re-read from disk, but a path-scoped rule or nested file that arrived mid-session is folded into the summary and returns only when Claude next touches a matching file.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to CLAUDE.md? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a company that gives every new hire a welcome binder. The binder kept at the office (the project file) is identical for everyone, while the sticky notes in your own desk drawer (the user-level file) are yours alone and a new colleague never sees them. Each department also keeps a short folder of its own rules (directory-level files), and the safety rules for the workshop floor are handed out only at the workshop door (path-scoped rules). A binder of 600 pages is one that nobody reads.
commonTraps: Conventions saved in the user-level file never reach teammates; team standards belong in the committed project file.
An instruction file is advice delivered as context. A bold line that says never to touch a folder does not block anything; a hook or a deny rule does.
@import organizes a large file but does not reduce context, because imported text loads at launch. Path-scoped rules are what keep irrelevant conventions out.
A convention that follows a file type across many folders is best written once as a glob rule, not copied into a directory-level file per folder.
A rule is matched by its paths patterns, never by its own file name or folder; a rule with no paths field applies to everything.
lessons.scenario: A payments team shares one monorepo between a web app and an API, and its root CLAUDE.md has grown to 550 lines. A new hire reports that Claude ignores the naming rules everyone else sees, because a senior engineer saved them in a home-directory file. The team moves the shared rules into the committed project file, splits the rest into .claude/rules/testing.md and api-conventions.md, scopes the testing rule to **/*.test.ts, and has packages/payments/CLAUDE.md import the payments standards document.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat the instruction file like code: review changes to it, keep it short and delete rules that no longer apply, because contradictory lines may be followed arbitrarily. When Claude breaks a rule twice, first check whether the rule was loaded (/memory or /context) before rewording it. Put anything with serious consequences into a hook or a permission rule instead of a bolder sentence. Keep personal sandbox URLs in CLAUDE.local.md and add that file to .gitignore.

lessons.title: Skills, Slash Commands and Plan Mode
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 3.2 and 3.4: project and personal commands and skills, SKILL.md frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint), choosing a skill over CLAUDE.md, and when to use plan mode, direct execution and the Explore subagent.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 3.2 and 3.4. A custom slash command is a markdown file whose name becomes the command: .claude/commands/review.md creates /review. Committed in the repository it reaches the whole team; kept in ~/.claude/commands/ it is personal. Commands have since been merged into skills, folders such as .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md with optional extras. Both forms create /review, old command files keep working, and the skill wins if the names clash. Skills have the same scopes plus organization-deployed enterprise skills; if a name exists in several places, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project. To adapt a team skill without changing teammates' copy, save a variant under a different name in ~/.claude/skills/.

YAML frontmatter at the top of SKILL.md configures behavior. The description is what Claude reads to decide when the skill applies; descriptions stay in context while the full body loads only on use. context: fork runs the skill in a separate subagent that starts without your conversation, so a codebase analysis that prints thousands of lines, or a brainstorm of alternatives, leaves only its result behind. The body must contain a real task, because guidelines alone give the subagent nothing to do; the agent field picks the subagent type. allowed-tools lists tools Claude may use without asking while the skill runs, for example Bash(git add *) and Bash(git commit *). In current Claude Code it pre-approves and does not remove other tools, so forbid something with disallowed-tools, a deny rule or a restricted agent. argument-hint shows a hint such as [issue-number] in autocomplete, and what the user types arrives as $ARGUMENTS. disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from starting the skill on its own, the right setting for /deploy.

Skill or CLAUDE.md? Standards that must hold in every session, such as 'use pnpm and run the typecheck before finishing', belong in CLAUDE.md, which is always loaded. A twelve-step release checklist needed twice a month belongs in a skill, so it costs context only when invoked.

Task statement 3.4 is about matching ceremony to uncertainty. Plan mode lets Claude read files, run exploratory commands and write a plan without editing source until you approve; enter it with Shift+Tab, a /plan prefix or claude --permission-mode plan. Choose it for large changes, architectural decisions, several valid approaches and multi-file edits: splitting a service, upgrading a library across about 45 files, or picking WebSockets or polling when each needs different infrastructure. Choose direct execution for well-scoped changes, such as adding one validation check to one function or fixing a bug whose stack trace points at one line. A useful test: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.

The two combine: plan to investigate and design, approve the plan (you can edit it first), then let the same session carry it out. Discovery that would flood the window, such as tracing authentication across a large service, goes to the Explore subagent, a fast, read-only agent with its own context. The files it reads stay there and only a summary comes back, which keeps the main conversation usable through a multi-phase task.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to skills and plan mode? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A skill is a recipe card in the kitchen drawer: it comes out when that dish is on the menu, while the rules on the wall poster (CLAUDE.md) apply to every dish. A forked skill is sending a sous-chef to the stockroom to inventory everything and bring back one summary sheet instead of narrating each shelf. Plan mode is the architect walking the site with a clipboard before any wall comes down, and direct execution is changing a lightbulb without drawing a blueprint.
commonTraps: In current Claude Code, allowed-tools pre-approves tools for the turn; it does not remove the unlisted ones. To prevent a tool, use disallowed-tools, a deny rule or a restricted agent type.
A command in ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. Only files committed to the repository, under .claude/commands/ or .claude/skills/, reach teammates.
context: fork needs an actionable task in the body. A skill that only lists guidelines returns nothing useful from its subagent.
Plan mode for everything is as wrong as direct execution for everything; scale the ceremony to the uncertainty and to the number of files touched.
The Explore subagent is read-only and keeps raw findings out of the main window; it is for discovery, not for making the edits.
lessons.scenario: A platform team ships three workflows. /release-notes reads dozens of merged pull requests and prints long intermediate output, so it is a skill with context set to fork. /deploy sets disable-model-invocation to true so that it runs only when a person types it, and /fix-issue declares an argument-hint of [issue-number]. When the team must replace a message broker used by forty services, it starts in plan mode and lets the Explore subagent map the usage, approves the plan, then executes it; renaming one config key, it simply asks Claude to do it.
