lessons.onTheJob: Write skill descriptions for a colleague skimming a list: put the key use case first, because long descriptions are cut off. Keep SKILL.md focused (under roughly 500 lines) and move reference material into supporting files. Commit shared skills so the team receives them through version control, and test a forked skill by checking what comes back to the main conversation. Scale planning to risk: ask whether you could describe the diff in one sentence; if so, skip the plan, and if not, plan and let the Explore subagent do the reading.

lessons.title: Iterative Refinement and Claude Code in CI/CD
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 3.5 and 3.6: input/output examples, test-driven iteration, the interview pattern and interacting versus independent issues; then running Claude Code in pipelines with -p, --output-format json, --json-schema, CLAUDE.md context, prior findings and independent review.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 3.5 and 3.6. Iterative refinement is the craft of getting from a first attempt to a correct one. When a prose description is read differently on each run, show the transformation instead: give two or three concrete input/output pairs, such as '(555) 010-9999' becoming '+15550109999'. Prefer test-driven iteration: write tests for expected behavior, edge cases and performance first, ask Claude to implement, then paste the failing output back and repeat. Tests give Claude a check it can run instead of a vague sense of being done. To fix one edge case, hand over a specific case with input and expected output, for example a migration row with a null in a legacy column and the result you want.

In unfamiliar territory you may not know what to ask for. Use the interview pattern: have Claude question you before it builds. For a cache it might ask about invalidation, staleness limits and failure behavior; your answers become a spec, ideally executed in a fresh session. For feedback, separate interacting problems from independent ones. If a rounding bug, a currency-order bug and a discount-stacking bug all change each other's results, describe them together in one detailed message so Claude can design one coherent fix; independent problems are fixed one after another. And once you have corrected the same point more than twice, the context is cluttered with failed attempts: clear the session and restart with a sharper prompt.

Task statement 3.6 puts Claude Code in a pipeline. A CI job has no human, so any prompt would hang it. The -p (or --print) flag runs non-interactively: it processes the prompt, prints the result and exits, with a non-zero exit code on failure. Add --output-format json to receive one JSON object with the result, session id and usage metadata, and add --json-schema with a schema to receive validated data in the structured_output field. A review job can request an array of findings, each with file, line, severity and message, that a script posts as inline pull-request comments. Scraping free-form prose with regular expressions breaks whenever the wording changes.

Give the run context and limits. Testing standards, fixture conventions and review criteria belong in CLAUDE.md, which a plain claude -p run loads. The --bare option skips hooks, skills, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md for reproducible runs; if you use it, supply that guidance yourself, for example with --append-system-prompt-file. Pre-approve exactly what the job needs with --allowedTools and rule syntax such as Bash(git diff *), and consider --permission-mode dontAsk, which denies anything not pre-approved.

Two quality rules finish the topic. Independence: the session that wrote code is a weak reviewer of it, because it still carries its own reasoning, so review in a fresh instance that sees only the diff and the criteria. No repetition: when a review reruns after new commits, include the earlier findings and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues, or developers see the same nine comments again. Likewise, include existing test files when generating tests so that scenarios are not duplicated.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to iterative refinement and CI? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a tailor. Describing the fit in words (a bit looser) gets a different garment each time, but laying two finished suits on the table (examples) settles it, and the fitting-room mirror (tests) shows exactly where the cloth pulls. The interview is the tailor asking about occasions and weather before cutting. A CI run is the night shift in a locked shop: nobody can answer the phone, so the tailor works from written instructions and leaves a report in a fixed form, and a different tailor inspects the suit instead of the one who sewed it.
commonTraps: Without -p, a pipeline step can sit waiting for input that never arrives; the flag is what makes the run non-interactive.
Prose findings cannot be posted reliably as inline comments; request --output-format json with --json-schema so the script receives fields instead of sentences.
The session that generated the code is a weak reviewer of it; independence comes from a fresh instance given only the diff and the criteria.
Re-running a review without the earlier findings repeats comments; pass them in and ask for new or still-unaddressed issues only.
Independent bugs can be fixed one at a time, but interacting bugs need one message; mixing the two up wastes iterations.
lessons.scenario: A team builds a pipeline in which Claude Code reviews every pull request and drafts tests. The job runs claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema describing findings, and a script posts each finding as an inline comment. CLAUDE.md lists the fixtures and what a worthwhile test looks like, the test prompt includes the existing test files, and on each new commit the review prompt includes the earlier findings and asks only for new or unresolved ones. The review runs in a separate invocation from the one that wrote the code.
lessons.onTheJob: Define the contract between Claude and your script, then enforce it: validate the structured output and fail the job on a schema error or a non-zero exit code instead of silently posting nothing. Start restrictive, pre-approving only the Bash patterns the job needs and capping turns, and loosen deliberately. Keep CI instructions in the repository, in CLAUDE.md or a prompt file under version control, so changes get reviewed. When iterating by hand, resist long chains of corrections: after two misses, write down what you learned, clear the session and re-prompt with examples and a test.

lessons.title: Precise Criteria, Few-Shot Examples and Schema-Enforced Output
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3: explicit report-and-skip criteria and severity examples, few-shot examples for format, borderline cases and varied layouts, and structured output through extraction tools, strict schemas, tool_choice and schema design.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 4.1 to 4.3. Consider a pull-request review bot. A prompt such as "check that comments are accurate" or "be conservative" leaves the model to invent its own bar, so it keeps flagging harmless code: words like conservative and confident change the tone, not what counts as a problem. Give it a criterion it can answer yes or no to: flag a comment only when the behavior it describes contradicts the code; report bugs and security flaws; skip minor style and patterns that match the surrounding code. Ask for evidence, such as the quoted line.

Precision is also about trust. If one category is wrong most of the time, developers learn to dismiss the bot, and then they dismiss its accurate security findings too. Switch the noisy category off for now, keep the good ones running, and re-enable it once its criteria hold up. Treat severity the same way: define each level and attach a code example of a typical finding, so one kind of defect always gets one label.

Task statement 4.2 is few-shot prompting. When written rules still give inconsistent results, worked examples are the strongest remedy, because they show rather than describe. A complete example finding with location, issue, severity and suggested fix settles the format. A borderline case, with the action chosen and why it won, teaches judgment. A pair such as a worker-loop handler that logs and continues beside one that swallows an error teaches acceptable versus genuine, where an allow-list covers only the places it names. Examples of an unusual layout, such as a bibliography-only paper, fix fields that come back empty. Keep examples relevant and varied, and tag them so they are not mistaken for instructions. The guide says two to four; Anthropic's docs say three to five. Examples cannot supply information the document lacks.

Task statement 4.3 is output you can parse without fear. Asking for "JSON only" mostly works, which is the problem. Instead define an extraction tool whose input schema is the JSON Schema you want, and read the data from the tool-use block. With strict: true the input is constrained to match the schema, and the JSON outputs option (output_config.format) does the same for the reply itself. That removes syntax errors and wrong types, not semantic ones such as line items that do not sum to the total. Check the stop reason too: a refusal or a max_tokens cut-off can leave output that does not match.

tool_choice decides whether a call happens. With auto the model may answer in plain text; any requires a call but lets the model choose the tool, which suits several extraction schemas and an unknown document type; naming a tool forces it. The current docs add a caveat: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, and with manual extended thinking, any and a named tool return an error, so use auto with strict tools and treat a reply with no tool call as a failure. Design schemas so absence is honest: optional or nullable fields for data some documents lack (a required field invites an invented value), an unclear value for ambiguous sources, and other plus a detail string for unforeseen categories. Put normalization rules, such as ISO 8601 dates, in the prompt: the schema fixes the shape, not how messy values are read.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to prompting and structured output? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture briefing a new proofreader. "Be careful" tells them nothing, while "flag a sentence only when it contradicts the figure in the table above it, and ignore house-style quibbles" lets them start. Two marked-up sample pages teach more than a page of rules, especially for borderline cases. A form with boxes that must all be filled in makes people write something even where they know nothing, while a form with a "not stated" option gets honest answers. And a form printed with fixed boxes guarantees tidy handwriting, not correct numbers.
commonTraps: Phrases such as "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" sound careful but add no criterion; categorical report-and-skip rules are the fix.
Few-shot examples teach format and judgment, but they cannot supply information the document does not contain.
Strict schemas remove syntax and type errors, not wrong values: totals that do not add up and misplaced fields still need validation.
A required field makes the model produce a value even when the source has none; use optional or nullable fields, an unclear option, and other plus detail.
tool_choice any or a named tool is rejected on the newest models and with manual extended thinking; use auto with strict tools and check that a call came back.
lessons.scenario: A fintech team's invoice reader returns unparseable JSON about once in every two hundred calls, invents purchase-order numbers for suppliers who do not use them, and labels vague tickets with confident guesses. They replace the "JSON only" prompt with a strict extraction tool, make the purchase-order field nullable, and add an unclear category value. The companion review bot, which developers had stopped reading, gets explicit report-and-skip criteria and a few example pairs of acceptable and genuine code.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a small labeled set of real documents and diffs and re-run it after every prompt or schema change; precision and format consistency are measurable, so measure them. When something misbehaves, change one thing at a time: criteria first, examples second, schema last. Take examples from real failures rather than invented ones, and keep each short with its reason attached. Log the stop reason with every structured call, and count nulls and unclear values per field: a field that is never null in production is probably being invented.

lessons.title: Validation, Retries, Batch Processing and Independent Review
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6: retry with error feedback and its limits, self-check fields, matching the Message Batches API to latency-tolerant work, custom_id and deadline scheduling, and independent, multi-pass and confidence-routed review.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 4.4 to 4.6: what happens after the first answer. Treat extraction output as a candidate and validate it in code, with a Pydantic model or a JSON Schema validator, for rules a schema cannot express, such as an end date after the start date or line items that sum to the total. When validation fails, retry with error feedback: send the original document, the failed extraction and the specific errors ("line items sum to 412.50, total says 421.50"). A bare "try again" repeats the mistake. Retries repair format and structure errors. They cannot repair absence: if the governing-law clause sits in a schedule nobody supplied, no retry finds it, so cap the attempts and route the case to a person.

Design the output so problems show themselves. Extract calculated_total beside stated_total and flag any mismatch. Add a conflict_detected boolean for sources that contradict themselves, so the model does not silently choose. Give review findings a detected_pattern field naming the construct that triggered them; when developers dismiss findings, you can group the dismissals and fix the criteria behind the worst patterns.

Task statement 4.5 is the Message Batches API: half price because requests are processed asynchronously. Most batches end within an hour, but up to 24 hours is allowed and nothing is guaranteed, so batch work nobody waits for (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation) and never a blocking step such as a pre-merge check. Give every request a custom_id, because results return in any order; poll the batch status until it ends, then match results to inputs by custom_id. One batch request is a single asynchronous call, so a client-side tool loop cannot run inside it; keep those agents on the synchronous API. Deadlines become schedules: a document may wait for the next submission and then take 24 hours, so a 36-hour deadline needs a submission at least every 12 hours. When some requests fail or expire, resubmit only those after fixing the cause, for example by splitting an oversized document into chunks. Tune the prompt on a small representative sample first.

Task statement 4.6 is review with more than one pass or instance. A model that has just written code still holds the reasoning behind it, so asked to review it in the same session it tends to defend it; a harsher tone or extra thinking time does not remove that. A second Claude instance given only the diff and the criteria catches subtler problems. Large reviews fail differently: with many files in one pass, depth becomes uneven and verdicts contradict one another (attention dilution), and a bigger context window does not cure it. Run a per-file pass for local issues and a separate integration pass for data flow across files. A verification pass can attach a confidence to each finding to route doubtful ones to closer review, but raw confidence is only a hint until you calibrate it against labeled examples.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to extraction pipelines and review? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a bank clearing cheques. A second clerk checks the first clerk's entry without seeing the first clerk's working, because a person who has just written a number tends to see what they meant. A cheque with a smudged amount goes back with a note saying exactly what is wrong. A cheque with no date on it cannot be fixed by sending it back again, so an officer handles it. The overnight clearing run is cheaper because nobody is waiting, but it is not used for the cheque a customer is watching being cashed at the counter.
commonTraps: A retry only helps when the answer is in the source; absent information, such as a value in an attachment nobody supplied, needs routing, not more attempts.
A bare "try again" is not feedback; the retry needs the document, the failed extraction and the specific errors.
Batch is wrong for blocking work such as pre-merge checks because nothing guarantees completion, and results come back in any order, so custom_id is how you match them.
Worst-case batch latency is the submission interval plus up to 24 hours, and a client-side tool loop cannot run inside one batch request.
Asking the same session to review harder, or think longer, does not make it independent; a fresh instance without the author's reasoning does.
lessons.scenario: An insurer extracts policy data from 40,000 scanned documents a week. Each result is validated in code; failures are retried once with the document, the failed output and the exact error, and anything still failing goes to an adjuster with the errors attached. The weekly run uses the Batches API with custom_ids such as pol-1182-c2, after a 100-document sample run to settle the prompt. A separate Claude instance reviews every change to the extraction code, first file by file and then across files.
lessons.onTheJob: Cap retries at two or three and record which validation errors a retry fixed and which never get fixed; the second list shows where the prompt, the source feed or the schema needs work. Put the batch status, the count of each result type and the age of the oldest request on a dashboard, so a stuck job shows up before the deadline. Keep custom_ids stable and meaningful so a resubmission can reuse them. Give the independent reviewer the diff and your written criteria, nothing about how the author reasoned, and check its confidence numbers against labeled findings before using them to route work.

lessons.title: Context Facts, Escalation and Error Reports
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3: keeping exact facts alive in long conversations, trimming and ordering what enters the context window, when an agent should hand a case to a human, and how failures travel from subagents to a coordinator.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 5.1 to 5.3. Everything Claude knows during a task sits in its context window: instructions, conversation, tool results and pasted documents. It is working memory, and more is not automatically better: accuracy and recall slip as it fills (context rot). The Messages API is also stateless, so every request must carry the history, or the agent forgets.

The first danger is progressive summarization. Long support chats are compressed to fit the budget, and each round trades precision for brevity: "refund of $84.50 for order A-7731, promised by Friday" becomes "customer wants a refund", and the agent can no longer keep the promise. The cure is a case facts block, a short structured list of amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses and the customer's stated expectations, placed in every prompt outside the summarized history. With three disputed orders in one chat, keep one record per issue so that figures never mix. Summarize the talk, never the numbers.

The second danger is bulk. A lookup_order call may return forty fields when a return decision needs five. That result is re-read on every later turn, so trim it in code (in the tool wrapper or a post-execution hook); telling the model to ignore the other fields leaves the tokens in place. Position matters too: models read the start and end of a very long input more reliably than the middle, so open an aggregated input with a key-findings summary, give each section a clear header, and put long documents before the question. If a downstream agent has a small budget, change the producer: upstream agents return key facts, citations and relevance scores, with dates and source locations, not prose.

Task statement 5.2 asks when an agent should hand over. Three triggers are sound: the customer asks for a human, the policy is silent or ambiguous about the request (a competitor price match, when the policy covers only own-site prices), and the agent cannot make meaningful progress. A request for a person is honored at once, without investigating first. Mere frustration is different: if the problem is within reach, the agent acknowledges the feeling, offers the fix, and escalates only if the customer then asks for a person. Sentiment and self-reported confidence are poor triggers: anger does not mean difficulty, and models are often most sure when wrong. Write explicit criteria with examples of both outcomes into the system prompt; if a lookup returns several matches, ask for another identifier.

Task statement 5.3 follows a failure through a multi-agent system. A subagent that meets a transient error such as a timeout retries locally and reports upward only what it cannot fix, as structured context: the failure type, the query attempted, any partial results and possible alternatives, so the coordinator can retry, switch source or carry on. Keep two outcomes apart: an access failure (the database never answered) and a valid empty result (it answered and found nothing). Two anti-patterns recur: silent suppression (an empty list passed off as success, so a gap looks like a finding) and aborting the whole workflow over one failed step. The final report marks which areas are well supported and which have gaps because a source was unavailable.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to context management? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a hotel front-desk clerk who works a long shift with only a small notepad. At the end of each hour she rewrites it as short notes, and over the day "Mr. Okafor wants the 6:30 airport taxi charged to his room" shrinks to "guest needs a taxi". A smarter clerk keeps a separate card per guest with room number, amounts and promised times, and never rewrites the cards. She knows which requests she may grant herself, passes on at once any guest who asks for the manager, and calls the manager when a request falls outside the hotel's written rules. When the kitchen line is dead she does not tell a guest that no food exists; she says the kitchen cannot be reached and offers alternatives.
keyTerms: Valid empty result versus access failure
commonTraps: A bigger context window, more frequent summaries or a "be careful" instruction does not stop summarization from blurring exact figures; keep the facts in a block that is never summarized.
Telling the model to ignore fields leaves the tokens in the window; trim the tool result in code before it is appended.

An explicit request for a human is honored at once, whereas plain frustration earns an acknowledgment and an offer first; sentiment, self-reported confidence and mere complexity are not escalation triggers.
An empty result marked as success after a timeout, and aborting everything after one failed step, are both anti-patterns; return structured error context and let the coordinator decide.
lessons.scenario: A retailer's support agent handles a customer who disputes three orders in one chat. A facts block records each order's ID, amount, status and promised delivery date, trimmed from forty-field lookup results to five fields. When the customer asks for "a real person" about the second order, the agent transfers at once with those facts. In the nightly research pipeline, a subagent that times out on a pricing database retries twice, then reports the failure type, the query and the partial results, and the final report marks pricing coverage as incomplete.
lessons.onTheJob: Decide what is a fact and what is conversation before you build anything: facts (amounts, dates, IDs, statuses, promises) go into a structure you rebuild from tool results, and only the talk may be summarized. Measure how many tokens each tool returns and trim the biggest offenders first; one noisy lookup often accounts for most of the growth. Write escalation criteria from real transcripts, including cases that should not escalate, and review a sample of both outcomes every month. Give every subagent a standard error shape so the coordinator never has to guess whether silence means nothing found or could not look.

lessons.title: Long Sessions, Human Review and Provenance
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6: keeping a long codebase exploration coherent with scratchpads, subagents, manifests and compaction, designing human review with calibrated confidence and sampling, and preserving sources and dates through multi-source synthesis.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6. They share one theme: keeping an agent system trustworthy when the work is long, the volume is high and the answer is assembled from many sources.

In a long exploration of an unfamiliar codebase, context degrades. Hours in, the agent gives inconsistent answers and talks about "typical patterns" instead of the actual classes it found at the start. Four habits counter this. A scratchpad file: the agent writes key findings (class names, paths, call chains) to a notes file and rereads it when a later question needs them. Delegation: a narrow question such as "find every test file" goes to a subagent, whose verbose output stays in its own context while only a summary returns. Phase summaries: subagents inherit nothing, so the findings of one phase are summarized into the starting prompt of the next. Recoverable state: each agent exports its state to a known place and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume, so a crash does not mean starting over. In Claude Code, /compact summarizes the session and keeps going (add a focus, such as /compact focus on the payment module), while /clear starts empty. For agents you build on the API, server-side compaction (beta) summarizes older turns, tool result clearing drops the oldest stale tool results, and the memory tool lets Claude keep files in a /memories directory that your application controls.

Task statement 5.5 puts people in the loop. An extraction pipeline can report 97% accuracy overall and still get only 68% on handwritten forms, because a big easy segment drowns out a small hard one. Before reducing review, measure accuracy by document type and by field, and automate only the segments that pass on their own. Have the model output a confidence score per field, then calibrate: run a labeled validation set, check how often each confidence level was right, and set review thresholds from those rates. A raw score is not a probability. Send low-confidence fields, and documents whose sources conflict or are ambiguous, to reviewers first, since their time is limited. Keep checking the confident ones too: a weekly stratified random sample from each segment measures the true error rate and catches new problems, such as a supplier's new template.

Task statement 5.6 protects provenance, the trail from a claim back to its source. Attribution disappears when findings are summarized without their sources, so subagents return claim-source mappings (the claim, the URL or document name, a short excerpt and the publication or collection date), and every later step preserves and merges them: if three findings make the same claim, the merged record lists all three sources. When credible sources disagree, say 21% versus 24% for a readmission rate, keep both values with source, method and date, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile them; do not pick one or average. Dates often dissolve a conflict, since a 2021 figure and a 2025 figure may describe a trend. Finally, structure the report to separate well-established findings from contested ones, keep the sources' own wording about methods, and render each kind of content naturally: financial figures as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to long-running agents? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A detective working a case for weeks keeps an evidence board and a case notebook, because memory fades and key facts belong on the board. For a narrow question, such as who bought a ticket that night, she sends a junior colleague, who comes back with one page rather than a box of receipts. If the office floods, the filing system shows which boxes were already examined, so work resumes where it stopped. The captain does not close the case because 97 percent of the paperwork checked out; she asks which kinds of paperwork were wrong, and pulls a few certain-looking files at random to be sure. In the final report every claim carries its source and date, and when two witnesses disagree, both statements appear.
commonTraps: An overall accuracy of 97% says nothing about each document type or field; validate the segments separately before reducing review.
A raw confidence score needs calibration against labeled data before it can route review, and sampling only the low-confidence items never reveals errors among the confident ones.
Subagents inherit nothing: findings from an earlier phase must be summarized into their prompts, and a long multi-agent run needs a manifest to resume.
Choosing one of two conflicting figures, or averaging them, silently destroys evidence; keep both with source and date and let the coordinator reconcile.
lessons.scenario: An engineering team maps a million-line billing system with a coordinator and five exploration subagents. Each agent writes findings to a notes file and exports its state to a manifest; when the run crashes on day two, the coordinator loads the manifest and injects the saved state into the agents that must continue. Their invoice extractor reports 97% overall, but a per-type breakdown shows handwritten forms at 68%, so those stay under review while a weekly stratified sample audits the auto-approved rest. The research summary lists both a 21% and a 24% readmission rate, each with its source and year.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat the scratchpad as part of the design, not an afterthought: agree a file name and a simple structure (finding, file, evidence) and require agents to update it as they learn. Prefer several narrow subagent questions over one broad one, and ask for short structured answers. For review, build the labeled validation set before the dashboard, track accuracy per segment from the first day, and schedule sampling as a recurring job so that it survives a busy quarter. For research output, make claim, source, excerpt and date required fields in the schema the subagents return, so that a missing citation fails validation instead of reaching the report.

cheatSheet.heading: Agentic loop and task decomposition (1.1, 1.6)
points: Loop: send history and tools, then read stop_reason. "tool_use" means run every requested tool, append the assistant message and ONE user message holding a tool_result per id (results first, text after), and call again. "end_turn" means finished.
max_tokens with a half-written tool request: retry with a larger limit and never run the fragment. The Messages API is stateless, so the full history is resent on every call.

Termination anti-patterns: parsing prose for "done", treating any text as completion, and using an iteration cap as the primary stop. Caps (maxTurns, budget) are guardrails that end in error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd; only subtype success carries a result.
Model-driven decisions adapt to tool results; pre-configured decision trees and fixed tool sequences are predictable but cannot adapt.
Parallel tool calls: return all tool_result blocks together in one user message. Read-only tools may run concurrently; Edit, Write and Bash run one at a time.

Prompt chaining = fixed, sequential steps for predictable multi-aspect work. For big reviews use a per-file local pass plus a cross-file integration pass; a larger context window does not cure attention dilution.
Dynamic decomposition for open-ended work: map the structure, find high-impact areas, build a prioritized plan, and revise it as dependencies surface.

cheatSheet.heading: Multi-agent orchestration (1.2, 1.3)
points: Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator decomposes, selects subagents by query complexity, delegates, aggregates, and judges coverage. ALL communication goes through it. No peer-to-peer messaging and no shared mutable scratchpad.
Subagents have isolated context: no parent history, no earlier tool results, no memory between invocations. The prompt is the only channel in; the final message is the only channel out.

The spawning tool is Task in the exam guide; current SDK and Claude Code docs call it Agent and still accept Task. The coordinator must be allowed to use it. An AgentDefinition holds a description, a system prompt and a tool list (optionally a model).
Pass complete findings in the prompt as structured records: claim, evidence, source URL or document, page, date. Keep content separate from metadata so attribution survives.
Parallel subagents = several launch calls in ONE coordinator response. One call per turn is sequential and costs the sum of the durations.
Coordinator prompts state goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step scripts. Partition scope (subtopic, region, source type) to avoid duplication.
Refinement loop: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, send targeted queries to search and analysis, re-run synthesis, and stop on a coverage criterion.
Report has gaps but every subagent succeeded? Read the coordinator's decomposition first.

cheatSheet.heading: Enforcement, hooks, handoffs and sessions (1.4, 1.5, 1.7)
points: Obligations with money, identity or security consequences need programmatic enforcement (prerequisite gates, hooks). Prompts, few-shot examples and capital letters are probabilistic.

PreToolUse hook: allow, deny, ask or defer via permissionDecision; updatedInput rewrites arguments. Deny beats defer, which beats ask, which beats allow. Put the redirect in the denial reason, such as "escalate to a human".
PostToolUse hook: runs after the tool and can add context or replace the result, for example normalizing Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates and numeric status codes. It cannot undo a side effect.
Matchers match tool names (Write|Edit, an mcp__server__ prefix), not arguments: inspect the tool input inside the callback. Hooks run outside the context window.
Human handoff when the human cannot see the transcript: customer id, root cause, amounts, actions taken, recommended next step. Make them required fields of the escalation tool.
Multi-concern message: split into distinct items, investigate in parallel with the same verified context, and synthesize one reply.

Sessions store the conversation, not files. claude -n or /rename names a session, claude --resume <name> reopens it, claude --continue reopens the most recent; the SDK uses resume with an id and fork_session to branch.

Mostly valid context: resume and tell the agent which files changed. Mostly stale: start fresh with a structured summary. Alternatives from one baseline: fork (give each branch its own worktree if it edits).

cheatSheet.heading: Tool design, errors and tool_choice (2.1, 2.2, 2.3)
points: Descriptions drive tool selection: purpose, accepted input formats with examples, outputs, edge cases, and a boundary against similar tools. Fix thin or overlapping descriptions and names before adding routers or few-shot examples.

Split overloaded generic tools into purpose-specific ones with clear contracts, and namespace names (github_list_prs). Review the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that override descriptions.

MCP: isError true in the result is a model-visible failure; unknown tools and malformed requests are JSON-RPC protocol errors. Categories: transient (retry), validation (fix the input), business (final, customer-friendly text, not retryable), permission (other access or a human). errorCategory and isRetryable are a convention, not protocol fields.
Never return a uniform "Operation failed" or an empty success for an outage: zero matches is a valid result, a timeout is an access failure.
Subagents retry transient failures locally and propagate only what they cannot fix, with what was attempted and partial results.

Too many tools (18 versus 4-5) degrade selection. Scope tools per role, add a narrow cross-role tool (verify_fact) for frequent small needs, and replace risky generic tools with constrained ones (load_document instead of fetch_url).

tool_choice: auto (default, text possible), any (must call some tool), a named tool (forced), none. Forced and any prefill the reply, so no preamble. They are rejected with manual extended thinking and, per current docs, on several newest models; strict tool use (strict: true) guarantees schema-valid inputs, not sensible values.

cheatSheet.heading: MCP integration and built-in tools (2.4, 2.5)
points: MCP primitives: tools (model-controlled actions), resources (read-only content by URI that the application surfaces; catalogs cut exploratory calls), prompts (user-selected templates).

Scopes: project = .mcp.json, committed and shared; user = ~/.claude.json, private across projects; local (default for claude mcp add) = private to this project, also in ~/.claude.json. Same name in several scopes: the highest-precedence entry wins whole (local, then project, then user).
Secrets: ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expansion works in command, args, env, url and headers. Never commit tokens; rotate any that leaked.
Tools of all configured servers are available together. Tool search loads names first and fetches definitions on demand. MCP tools are named mcp__server__tool.

Agent prefers Grep over your MCP tool? Enrich the MCP tool description (capabilities, outputs, when to prefer it). Use community servers for standard integrations such as Jira; build custom ones only for team-specific workflows.
Built-ins: Grep = text inside files (callers, errors, imports); Glob = file paths (**/*.test.tsx); Read = whole file; Write = full overwrite; Edit = exact text that must be unique.
Edit fails on non-unique text: add surrounding lines for a unique anchor, or Read then Write. Never repeat the same edit or use replace-all blindly.
Explore incrementally: search for entry points, Read, follow imports. For wrapper modules, list the exported names and search for each one.

cheatSheet.heading: CLAUDE.md hierarchy, imports and rules (3.1, 3.3)
points: Three levels. User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: only you, every project, never in version control. Project-level CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md: committed and shared with the team. Directory-level CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory: loads when Claude reads or edits files there. Also CLAUDE.local.md (private, gitignored) and an organization-managed policy file.

Files are concatenated, not overridden: the working directory and its parents load at launch (root first, closest last). Contradictory lines may be followed arbitrarily, so prune them. Aim for under about 200 lines per file.
A teammate is missing conventions that everyone else gets? They were saved at user level. Move them into the committed project file.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement: a line that forbids something does not block it. Use a hook or a permission deny rule when you need a guarantee.
@path/to/file imports a file at launch: relative to the importing file, nested up to four hops. It organizes (each package imports only its own standards) but does not reduce context.
.claude/rules/*.md holds one topic per file (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md), found recursively. A rule with no paths field loads at launch like the main file.

Path-scoped rule: YAML frontmatter paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"] (a list or a comma-separated string; paths is the only field read). It loads when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file, which saves context. A glob such as **/*.test.tsx follows a file type across directories, which directory-level files cannot do cheaply.

Diagnose with /memory (lists and edits the instruction files in play, toggles auto memory), /context (what fills the window, including loaded memory files) and /init (drafts a starter file). After /compact the root file reloads; path-scoped rules and nested files return when a matching file is touched again.

cheatSheet.heading: Skills, commands and plan mode (3.2, 3.4)
points: Commands: .claude/commands/ in the repository is shared through version control; ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. Skills (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, personal ones in ~/.claude/skills/) have absorbed commands: both create /name and the skill wins a name clash. Precedence: enterprise, then personal, then project.

SKILL.md frontmatter: description (when to use it; key use first), context, agent, allowed-tools, disallowed-tools, argument-hint, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, model. Descriptions stay in context; the body loads only when the skill runs.

context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent that starts without your conversation, and only the result returns. Use it for verbose analysis or brainstorming alternatives. The body needs a concrete task, not just guidelines; agent picks the subagent type.

allowed-tools lists tools Claude may use without asking while the skill runs, for example Bash(git commit *). Current docs: it pre-approves and does not remove other tools (restrict with disallowed-tools, deny rules or a restricted agent). The exam guide words it as limiting tool access, so know both framings.
argument-hint is an autocomplete hint such as [issue-number]; what the user types arrives as $ARGUMENTS. disable-model-invocation: true means only a person can start the skill (deploys, commits).

Skill versus CLAUDE.md: standards that always apply go in CLAUDE.md (always loaded); task-specific procedures go in skills (loaded on demand). A personal variant is a copy of a team skill saved under a different name in ~/.claude/skills/.

Plan mode: Claude reads, explores and writes a plan, with no source edits until you approve. Enter with Shift+Tab, a /plan prefix or claude --permission-mode plan. Use it for large or architectural work, multi-file edits and several valid approaches (service split, 45-file library migration, choosing an integration).
Direct execution suits small, well-scoped changes (one validation check, a single-file bug with a clear stack trace). If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.

Combine them: plan to investigate and design, approve, then execute in the same session. The Explore subagent is fast, read-only and has its own context, so discovery output stays there and only a summary returns.

cheatSheet.heading: Iterative refinement, headless mode and CI (3.5, 3.6)
points: Refinement toolkit: two or three concrete input/output examples when prose is read inconsistently; tests first (behavior, edge cases, performance) and then share the failures; one specific edge-case example, such as a null value and its expected result, to fix a bug.
Interview pattern: in an unfamiliar area, have Claude ask you questions (cache invalidation, failure modes), capture a spec, then build, preferably in a fresh session.
Interacting problems go in one detailed message; independent problems are fixed one after another. After about two failed corrections, clear the session and restart with a better prompt.

Non-interactive mode: claude -p "prompt" (or --print) processes the prompt, prints the result and exits; a non-zero exit code means failure. Without -p a pipeline step can hang waiting for input. Piped stdin is capped at 10 MB.

Structured output: --output-format text, json or stream-json. json returns the result with session id and usage; add --json-schema (print mode only) to get validated data in the structured_output field, which a script can post as inline pull-request comments.

Context for CI: CLAUDE.md (testing standards, fixtures, review criteria) loads in a plain claude -p run. --bare skips CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, MCP servers and auto memory for reproducibility, so pass guidance with --append-system-prompt-file or --settings.

Permissions in CI: --allowedTools "Bash(git diff *),Read" pre-approves (it does not restrict); --permission-mode dontAsk denies whatever is not pre-approved. GitHub Action: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1. With a prompt input it runs automatically; without one it answers @claude mentions. Keep keys in GitHub Secrets.

Quality rules: review in a fresh, independent instance, not the session that wrote the code; on reruns include prior findings and ask for only new or unaddressed issues; include existing tests when generating tests; document test standards and fixtures in CLAUDE.md.

cheatSheet.heading: Criteria, few-shot examples and structured output (4.1, 4.2, 4.3)
points: Vague instructions ("be conservative", "only high-confidence findings", "check that comments are accurate") do not change what gets flagged. Write explicit categorical criteria: what to report (bugs, security) and what to skip (minor style, local patterns), as tests the model can answer yes or no. Ask for evidence (quote the line) before a claim is posted.

False-positive trust erosion: one noisy category makes developers ignore the accurate ones. Temporarily disable the noisy category, improve its criteria, then re-enable it. Define every severity level with a concrete code example so labels stay consistent.

Few-shot examples are the strongest fix when detailed instructions still give inconsistent output. The guide says 2-4 targeted examples for ambiguous cases (Anthropic docs: 3-5), each showing the action chosen and why it beat the alternative. Make them relevant and varied, wrapped in example tags inside an examples tag.

Jobs for examples: demonstrate the format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix); settle ambiguous cases; pair acceptable and genuine code to cut false positives while generalizing; cover varied layouts (inline citations versus bibliography, informal measurements) to fix empty or invented values. Examples cannot supply information the document lacks.

Structured output: define an extraction tool whose input schema is the JSON Schema and read the tool-use input. strict: true (or the JSON outputs option, output_config.format) constrains decoding: no syntax errors, correct types, required fields present. It does NOT catch semantic errors (totals that do not sum, values in the wrong field). Check stop_reason: refusal and max_tokens can leave non-conforming output.

tool_choice: auto (default; the model may reply in text), any (must call some tool, the model picks: unknown document type), a named tool (forced: run extract_metadata first). Forcing prefills the reply, so there is no preamble. Current docs: any and a named tool return a 400 error on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 (and Mythos 5.1) and with manual extended thinking; use auto with strict tools and treat a reply with no tool call as a failure.

Schema design: optional or nullable fields for data some documents lack (a required field invites invented values); an "unclear" enum value for ambiguous sources; "other" plus a detail string for extensible categories; keep always-present fields required. Put format normalization rules (dates, currency, units) in the prompt next to the strict schema.

cheatSheet.heading: Validation, batches and multi-pass review (4.4, 4.5, 4.6)
points: Validate in code (Pydantic or a JSON Schema validator) for semantic and cross-field rules. Retry with error feedback: send the original document, the failed extraction and the specific errors. A bare "try again" repeats the mistake. Cap the retries and route leftovers to human review.

Retries fix format and structure errors (wrong date format, value in the wrong field). They cannot fix information that is absent from the supplied source (a clause in an attachment never provided): stop, record it as missing, and route it.

Self-check design: extract calculated_total beside stated_total and flag differences; add a conflict_detected boolean (keep both values) for contradictory sources; add detected_pattern to findings so dismissals can be grouped and false-positive patterns fixed.

Message Batches API: 50% cheaper, asynchronous, up to 24 hours (most batches finish within an hour), no guaranteed latency. Use it for overnight, weekly and nightly work; never for blocking steps such as pre-merge checks. Poll the processing status until it ends, then fetch the results.

custom_id (unique and stable, such as inv-4417-c3) correlates requests and results, which come back in any order. Result types: succeeded, errored, canceled, expired. Resubmit only the failed or expired requests after fixing the cause (for example chunk oversized documents). Tune the prompt on a small representative sample first.

A batch request is one asynchronous call: a client-side tool loop (run the tool, return the result, continue) cannot run inside it, so use the synchronous API for those agents. Deadline maths: worst case = submission interval + 24 hours, so a 36-hour deadline needs a submission at least every 12 hours.

Self-review is weak: the same session keeps the reasoning that produced the work, and extended thinking or a harsher prompt does not remove the bias. Use an independent Claude instance given only the diff and the criteria (writer/reviewer pattern), or a clean-context verification subagent that tries to refute findings.

Large reviews: per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow; this fixes attention dilution (uneven depth, contradictory verdicts), which a bigger context window does not. A verification pass can carry self-reported confidence to route findings, but calibrate it on labeled data before trusting thresholds. Requiring several runs to agree can suppress real bugs that are caught only intermittently.

cheatSheet.heading: Context facts, escalation and error propagation (5.1, 5.2, 5.3)
points: Context is working memory: accuracy and recall fall as it fills (context rot), so curate what enters. The Messages API is stateless, so every request carries the full history.

Progressive summarization blurs amounts, dates, order numbers and promises. Keep a case facts block (and one structured record per issue in multi-issue sessions) in every prompt, outside the summarized history.

Tool results pile up and are re-read every turn: trim to the relevant fields in code (tool wrapper or PostToolUse hook), for example 5 of 40 fields. A prompt telling the model to ignore fields leaves the tokens in place.

Position effects ("lost in the middle"): put a key-findings summary first, use explicit section headers, and place long documents before the question. Upstream agents return key facts, citations, relevance scores, dates and source locations instead of prose.

Escalate on an explicit request for a human (at once, no investigation first), a policy gap or ambiguity, or no meaningful progress. Do not escalate on sentiment, self-reported confidence or mere complexity.

Frustration without a request and a fixable issue: acknowledge, offer the resolution, escalate only if the customer repeats the wish. Several lookup matches: ask for another identifier and never pick by heuristic.

Wrong escalation calibration: fix it first with explicit criteria plus few-shot examples of escalating and of resolving in the system prompt. Classifiers and confidence thresholds are heavier and less reliable.

Errors: retry transient failures locally and propagate only what cannot be fixed, as structured context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives). An access failure (could not look) differs from a valid empty result (looked, found nothing).

Anti-patterns: an empty result marked as success (silent suppression), a generic "unavailable" status, and aborting the whole workflow on one failure. Final reports carry coverage annotations: well-supported findings versus gaps from unavailable sources.

cheatSheet.heading: Long sessions, human review and provenance (5.4, 5.5, 5.6)
points: Long sessions degrade: inconsistent answers and "typical patterns" instead of specific classes. Counter with scratchpad files that are reread, subagents for narrow questions (only summaries return) and phase summaries injected into the next agents' prompts.
Crash recovery: each agent exports state to a known location, and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and injects the state into the agents' prompts. Subagents inherit nothing.

Claude Code: /compact (optionally with a focus) summarizes and continues the session; /clear starts empty. The project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after compaction; instructions given only in chat can be lost.

API tools for long runs: server-side compaction (beta) summarizes older turns; context editing clears old tool results or thinking blocks by rule; the client-side memory tool stores files under /memories. Prompt caching changes cost, not what occupies the window.
A 97% overall accuracy can hide 68% on one document type. Validate accuracy by document type and field before cutting review, and automate only the segments that pass on their own.

Field-level confidence is calibrated on a labeled validation set. Route low-confidence fields and ambiguous or contradictory sources to reviewers first, and keep ongoing stratified random sampling of high-confidence outputs to measure error rates and catch new patterns.

Provenance: subagents return claim-source mappings (claim, URL or document, excerpt, publication or collection date) and synthesis preserves and merges them. Prose summaries are where attribution disappears.

Conflicting credible figures: keep both with source, method and date, and let the coordinator reconcile; never silently pick or average. Dates often explain an apparent conflict (a 2021 figure versus a 2025 one).
Structure reports as established versus contested findings, and render content by type: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 60 items (multiple choice and multiple response; each item says how many answers to choose) built from 4 scenarios picked at random from a bank of 6. Time limit 120 minutes, so roughly two minutes per item. Proctored online or at a test center.

Scoring: scaled 100 to 1,000 with a pass mark of 720, measured against a fixed standard rather than other candidates. The score report gives percent-correct per domain, but pass or fail depends on the total score only.

Blueprint weights: Agentic Architecture 27%, Tool Design and MCP 18%, Claude Code Configuration 20%, Prompt Engineering and Structured Output 20%, Context Management and Reliability 15%. Domains 1 and 2 together are 45% of the items.

Questions are scenario-based and ask for the BEST or MOST effective approach: one best answer and three plausible but flawed ones. Read the scenario's constraints first (severity of consequences, latency, who can see what).

Reliable principles: code-level enforcement beats prompt guidance when consequences are severe; descriptions are the first fix for tool misrouting; subagents inherit nothing, so pass context explicitly; fix the root cause, using the proportionate first step.

Eliminate options that rely on prompts where a guarantee is needed, that add heavy infrastructure (routers, classifiers) before a simple fix, that blame downstream agents for an upstream decomposition problem, that run independent work sequentially, that share mutable state between agents, or that return generic errors.

For multiple-response items, check the required count first and make sure every choice stands on its own: each correct option should be a complete, defensible answer, and tempting extras usually contain an absolute or an anti-pattern.

Terminology differs between sources: the guide says Task tool, current documentation says Agent tool. Answer by the mechanism. Skip heavy study of out-of-scope topics such as fine-tuning, API billing, hosting MCP servers, computer use, streaming internals and pricing.

If you stall on an item, choose the best remaining answer and move on; a scenario you know well later is worth more than ten extra minutes here. A failed attempt can be retaken after 14 days, then 30, then 90, with up to four attempts in 12 months.

cliChallenges.prompt: Run Claude Code non-interactively so that it answers the question "What does the auth module do?", prints the answer and exits.
cliChallenges.command: claude -p "What does the auth module do?"
altCommands: claude --print "What does the auth module do?"
cliChallenges.explanation: The -p (or --print) flag makes Claude Code process the prompt, write the result to standard output and exit, with a non-zero exit code if the run fails. It is what keeps an automated step from hanging on interactive input.

cliChallenges.prompt: Run a non-interactive query "Summarize this project" whose output is a single JSON object holding the result text together with the session id and usage metadata.
cliChallenges.explanation: In print mode --output-format accepts text (the default), json and stream-json. The json form returns one object with the answer in the result field plus metadata such as the session id and cost estimate, which a script can read with a tool like jq. stream-json is for newline-delimited events while the answer is generated.

cliChallenges.prompt: Run the non-interactive request "Extract the main function names from auth.py" so that the answer comes back as JSON validated against a schema (an object with a required "functions" array of strings).
cliChallenges.command: claude -p "Extract the main function names from auth.py" --output-format json --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"functions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["functions"]}'
cliChallenges.explanation: --json-schema works in print mode only. Combined with --output-format json, the validated result arrives in the structured_output field next to the usual metadata. This is the CI pattern for machine-parseable findings, for example a list with file, line, severity and message that a script posts as inline pull-request comments.

cliChallenges.prompt: Run the non-interactive request "Look at my staged changes and create an appropriate commit", pre-approving git diff, git log, git status and git commit commands (use the --allowedTools flag) so that no permission prompt appears.
cliChallenges.command: claude -p "Look at my staged changes and create an appropriate commit" --allowedTools "Bash(git diff *),Bash(git log *),Bash(git status *),Bash(git commit *)"
cliChallenges.explanation: --allowedTools takes permission-rule patterns; the space and asterisk at the end of Bash(git diff *) give prefix matching. It pre-approves the listed calls without a prompt but does not remove any other tool. To restrict the built-in tools Claude can use, pass --tools, and to deny calls use --disallowedTools or a deny rule. The hyphenated spelling --allowed-tools is accepted as well.

cliChallenges.prompt: For a reproducible CI run, summarize README.md non-interactively while skipping the automatic loading of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, and pre-approve only the Read tool.
cliChallenges.explanation: --bare starts Claude Code without auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so a scripted run behaves the same on every machine. Because CLAUDE.md is skipped, anything the job needs must be supplied explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file or --settings. Bare mode also never reads subscription logins, so with the Anthropic API it expects an API key, for example in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

cliChallenges.prompt: Start an interactive Claude Code session that begins in plan mode, so that Claude can explore the code and propose a plan without editing files until you approve it.
cliChallenges.explanation: --permission-mode sets the mode a session starts in: default (also called manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions. Inside a session, Shift+Tab cycles the modes and a /plan prefix switches for one prompt. In plan mode Claude reads, explores and writes a plan, and edits wait for your approval.

cliChallenges.prompt: Start an interactive session and give it the display name "auth-refactor", so that it is easy to find in the resume picker and can be resumed by name later.
cliChallenges.explanation: --name (short form -n) sets a display name for the session, shown in the /resume picker and the terminal title. A named session can later be reopened with claude --resume followed by the name. Inside a running session, the /rename command changes the name.

cliChallenges.prompt: Resume the session named "auth-refactor" and send it the prompt "Finish this PR".
cliChallenges.explanation: --resume (short form -r) reopens a specific session by ID or by name, and shows an interactive picker when you give no argument. A prompt after it is sent as the next message. By contrast, --continue (-c) reopens the most recent conversation in the current directory.

cliChallenges.prompt: Resume the session "auth-refactor" but branch it into a new session ID, so that the original conversation stays untouched while you try a different approach.
cliChallenges.explanation: --fork-session, used together with --resume or --continue, creates a new session ID instead of reusing the original, so two approaches can start from the same history while the original session is left as it was. The Agent SDK counterpart is the fork_session option (forkSession in TypeScript).

cliChallenges.prompt: Register the remote HTTP MCP server "notion" at https://mcp.notion.com/mcp so that its configuration is written to the project's .mcp.json and shared with teammates through version control. Use the long option names.
cliChallenges.command: claude mcp add --transport http notion --scope project https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
cliChallenges.explanation: claude mcp add takes --transport (http is the recommended choice for remote servers) and --scope. Local scope is the default: private, this project only. Project scope writes .mcp.json at the repository root so teammates share it, and Claude Code asks each person to approve project servers before using them. User scope makes a private server available in all your projects. The short forms are -t and -s.

madlibs.scenario: The application keeps calling the model while the stop reason is {b1}, and leaves the loop when the stop reason is {b2}. A counter that ends the loop after a fixed number of rounds is acceptable only as a {b3}, not as the primary stop condition.

options: tool_use
end_turn
refusal
end_turn
tool_use
pause_turn
safety net
primary signal
completion check

madlibs.explanation: tool_use means the model wants tools run, so the loop continues; end_turn means it has finished, so the loop exits. A turn or iteration cap guards against runaway behavior but must not be what normally ends a healthy run.

madlibs.scenario: A subagent starts with a {b1} context, so everything it needs must be written into the {b2} the coordinator gives it. To run independent subagents concurrently, the coordinator emits several launch calls in {b3}.

options: fresh
shared
inherited
delegation prompt
tool schema
hook callback
one response
separate turns
the next session

madlibs.explanation: Subagents do not inherit the parent's history, and the prompt is the only channel from parent to child. Parallelism comes from placing multiple launch calls in a single coordinator response; spreading them over turns makes them sequential.

madlibs.scenario: Where a skipped step could cause financial harm, rely on {b1} enforcement such as a prerequisite gate, because prompt-based guidance is only {b2}. A hook that runs {b3} a tool executes can block or rewrite the call.

options: programmatic
prompt-based
optional
probabilistic
deterministic
redundant
before
after
instead of

madlibs.explanation: Code-level gates and hooks give deterministic guarantees, while instructions and examples are followed with high but not perfect probability. Only a pre-execution hook can stop or rewrite a call; a post-execution hook sees the result of something that already happened.

madlibs.scenario: To reopen a named investigation, run claude {b1} followed by the session name. To compare two approaches starting from the same analysis, {b2} the session. A session stores the conversation but not the {b3}.

options: --resume
--print
--fork-session
fork
delete
compact
files on disk
tool names
prompt text

madlibs.explanation: claude --resume <name> reopens a named session. Forking copies the history into an independent branch, so two strategies can start from one baseline. Files are not part of the saved session, which is why changes made since the analysis must be pointed out to a resumed agent.

madlibs.scenario: An MCP tool reports that a call failed by setting the {b1} flag in its result. A timeout is a {b2} error worth retrying, while a refund requested outside the allowed window is a {b3} error that should be marked not retryable.

options: isError
isRetryable
stop_reason
transient
business
permission
business
transient
validation

madlibs.explanation: The protocol defines the isError flag; categories and retryable markers are an application convention carried in the result. Timeouts are transient. A policy refusal is a business error, final for that request, and needs a customer-friendly explanation.

madlibs.scenario: Servers the whole team shares are defined in {b1} at the repository root, personal or experimental servers live in {b2}, and credentials are kept out of the file by {b3}.

options: .mcp.json
CLAUDE.md
~/.claude.json
~/.claude.json
.mcp.json
CLAUDE.md
environment variable expansion
base64 encoding
renaming the key

madlibs.explanation: The project-level .mcp.json is committed and shared; the user-level ~/.claude.json is private. Writing ${VAR} references and supplying the values from each environment keeps secrets out of version control, whereas encoding or renaming does not protect them.

madlibs.scenario: With tool_choice set to {b1}, the model decides for itself whether to call a tool. With {b2} it must call one of the supplied tools but chooses which, and naming a specific tool makes it a {b3} call.

options: auto
any
none
any
auto
none
forced
optional
parallel

madlibs.explanation: auto leaves the decision to the model, any guarantees that some tool is called without naming it, and a named tool is a forced call. none turns tool calling off.

madlibs.scenario: Instructions saved in the {b1} file in your home directory apply to you in every project but are never shared with teammates, so team standards belong in the {b2} file that is committed to the repository. A convention that applies only to files of one type, such as every test file, can be written once as a rule under .claude/rules/ whose {b3} frontmatter field lists glob patterns, so it loads only when Claude touches a matching file.

options: user-level CLAUDE.md
project-level CLAUDE.md
directory-level CLAUDE.md
project-level CLAUDE.md
user-level CLAUDE.md
managed policy CLAUDE.md
paths
scope
match

madlibs.explanation: The user-level file follows you across projects but sits outside any repository, which is why a new teammate does not receive what it contains. The project-level file is committed and reaches everyone who clones. In a rule file, paths is the only frontmatter field Claude Code reads; a rule without it loads at launch for all work.

madlibs.scenario: A skill that prints thousands of lines of analysis should set {b1} so that it runs in an isolated subagent and only the result returns to the main conversation. To let a /commit skill run git commands without a prompt each time, list them in {b2}, which pre-approves tools instead of removing the others. The {b3} field shows a hint such as [issue-number] when a developer types the skill name.

options: context: fork
disable-model-invocation: true
user-invocable: false
allowed-tools
disallowed-tools
argument-hint
argument-hint
description
allowed-tools

madlibs.explanation: context: fork starts a separate subagent without the conversation history, so verbose output stays out of the main session. allowed-tools grants approval for the listed tools during the turn the skill runs; disallowed-tools is the field that removes tools. argument-hint is only an autocomplete hint, and the text the user types reaches the skill body as $ARGUMENTS.

madlibs.scenario: A pipeline step that calls Claude Code should use the {b1} flag so that the run processes its prompt, prints the result and exits instead of waiting for input. Adding --output-format json together with {b2} returns schema-validated findings in the structured_output field. For the review itself, use a {b3} Claude instance that sees only the diff and the review criteria, because the session that wrote the code is biased toward its own work.

options: -p
--verbose
--continue
--json-schema
--input-format
--max-turns
fresh, independent
resumed
forked

madlibs.explanation: -p (or --print) is the non-interactive mode that prevents a pipeline from hanging. --json-schema, which works in print mode, makes the answer structured and validated. A resumed or forked session carries the earlier conversation, including the reasoning that produced the code, while a fresh instance judges the change on the diff and the criteria alone.

madlibs.scenario: To cut false positives, replace "only report high-confidence findings" with explicit {b1} that say which issues to report and which to skip. Few-shot examples work best when they are relevant, {b2} and wrapped in tags so the model does not mistake them for instructions. A field that some documents do not contain should be {b3}, so the model is not pushed to invent a value.

options: confidence thresholds
categorical criteria
temperature settings
identical
as numerous as possible
varied
optional or nullable
required
defaulted to zero

madlibs.explanation: Confidence wording and thresholds supply no decision boundary, whereas categorical criteria define what counts. Examples need variety rather than repetition, and clear tags to separate them from instructions. A required field pushes the model to fabricate, so a field that some documents lack should allow null or omission.

madlibs.scenario: A retry after a failed validation should send the original document, the failed extraction and the specific {b1}. The Message Batches API halves the cost, but a batch can take up to {b2} to finish and nothing guarantees an earlier result. A review that is independent of the author's reasoning needs {b3} that sees only the code and the criteria.

options: previous system prompts
confidence scores
validation errors
10 minutes
24 hours
7 days
a fresh Claude instance
the same session with extended thinking
the same session with a harsher prompt

madlibs.explanation: A retry needs the specific validation errors alongside the document and the failed attempt. A batch is cheaper because it is asynchronous, but it may take up to 24 hours and carries no earlier guarantee. Independence comes from a fresh instance without the author's reasoning; extended thinking or a harsher prompt in the same session keeps the same context.

madlibs.scenario: Exact amounts, dates and order numbers belong in a {b1} that is sent with every prompt, apart from the summarized history, because repeated {b2} turns precise figures into vague phrases. Models read the {b3} of a very long input more reliably than the middle, so aggregated findings should open with a key-findings summary.

options: sentiment score
case facts block
tool description
validation
caching
summarization
beginning and end
middle third
longest sections

madlibs.explanation: A case facts block keeps transactional facts exact in every prompt, because each round of summarization trades precision for brevity. Because models handle the start and end of a long input better than the middle, key findings go first and the detailed sections get explicit headers.

madlibs.scenario: A timeout is an {b1} failure, whereas a query that ran and found nothing is a valid {b2} result. When credible sources disagree, the synthesis presents {b3}, each labeled with its source.

options: access
empty
validation
partial
empty
error
the larger value
the average
both values

madlibs.explanation: An access failure means the source was never reached, so absence cannot be concluded; a valid empty result means the source answered with nothing. The coordinator needs the two reported differently. Conflicting credible values are kept side by side with their sources instead of being replaced by a choice or an average.

sequences.prompt: Put one pass through the agentic loop in order, from sending the request to presenting the answer.
steps: Send the conversation history and the tool definitions to the model
Read the response and check its stop reason
Execute each tool the model requested
Append the assistant message and a user message with one tool_result per request
Call the model again with the extended history
When the stop reason is end_turn, present the final answer
sequences.explanation: The stop reason decides what happens after each response. Tool results are appended together with the assistant message that requested them, and the whole history goes back to the model. Only an end_turn response is presented as the final answer.

sequences.prompt: Order the coordinator's work in an iterative research run.
steps: Analyze the query and decompose it into distinct subtasks
Launch the chosen subagents in parallel with self-contained prompts
Collect the structured findings and aggregate them
Run synthesis on the aggregated findings
Evaluate the synthesis for coverage gaps
Re-delegate targeted queries for the gaps and re-run synthesis
Deliver the report once coverage is sufficient
sequences.explanation: Decomposition and delegation come first, aggregation and synthesis next, and then the coordinator checks coverage. Gaps trigger targeted re-delegation and another synthesis pass; the loop ends on a coverage criterion.

sequences.prompt: A refund below the approval limit passes through a prerequisite gate, a threshold hook and a normalizing hook. Put the events in order.
steps: The model calls get_customer and receives a verified customer id
The model requests process_refund for an amount below the limit
The gate confirms that a verified customer id exists for the session
The pre-execution hook compares the amount with the approval limit
The refund tool executes
A post-execution hook normalizes the result before the model reads it
sequences.explanation: Identity must be verified before the refund call can pass the gate. The pre-execution checks run before the tool, and only a call that passes both reaches execution. Normalization happens afterwards, on the result, before the model sees it.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps in order for continuing work in a fresh session when an older session's results have become stale.
steps: Review what the old session established and which results are still valid
Write a structured summary of the validated findings
Start a new session
Inject the summary into the new session's first prompt
Tell the agent which areas to verify or re-read
Continue the work from the refreshed baseline
sequences.explanation: The summary is only as good as the review behind it, so validation comes first. The summary is then injected into a clean session, the agent is pointed at the areas that still need checking, and work continues without stale tool results.

sequences.prompt: Order what happens when a search subagent hits a persistent timeout.
steps: The upstream service times out inside the tool
The tool returns a result with the error flag set, a transient category and a retryable marker
The subagent retries locally after a short wait
The retries keep failing
The subagent reports to the coordinator what it attempted and any partial results
The coordinator chooses an alternative source or proceeds with a coverage note
sequences.explanation: Structured error metadata lets the subagent recognize a retryable failure and handle it locally first. Only an error it cannot resolve is propagated, together with the attempts and partial results, so that the coordinator can recover intelligently.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of exploring an unfamiliar codebase incrementally in order.
steps: Search file contents for an entry point, such as a route or an error string
Read the file the search points to
Follow its imports with targeted searches
List the exported names of any wrapper modules found on the way
Search the codebase for each of those exported names
Summarize the flow from the files actually read
sequences.explanation: Start with a content search instead of reading everything, read only what the trail leads to, and handle re-exports by searching for every exported name rather than only the original one. The summary reflects what was really read.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for adding a shared MCP server that needs a secret token.
steps: Add the server definition to .mcp.json at the repository root
Reference the token as ${VAR} in the headers or env section
Commit the file to version control
Each teammate sets the variable in their own environment
Approve the project-scoped server the first time Claude Code asks
The agent can now use the server's tools alongside any others
sequences.explanation: The shared file carries only a reference, so it is safe to commit. Each person supplies the secret locally, approves the project server on first use, and then all configured servers are available together.

sequences.prompt: Put a plan-then-execute workflow for a library migration in order.
steps: Enter plan mode and let Claude explore the affected code, delegating noisy discovery to the Explore subagent
Ask Claude to propose a migration plan covering the files, the replacement patterns and the risks
Review the plan, editing it or giving feedback until it fits
Approve the plan so that Claude leaves plan mode and starts editing
Run the test suite and fix failures against the plan
Commit the change with a descriptive message
sequences.explanation: Plan mode separates investigation from execution: Claude explores and proposes, you steer the plan, and only approval allows edits. The same session then carries out the plan, verifies it with the tests and commits. Editing before the plan is approved would defeat the purpose of the mode.

sequences.prompt: Order the interview pattern followed by test-driven iteration for a feature in an unfamiliar area.
steps: Describe the feature briefly and ask Claude to interview you about design considerations before it builds anything
Answer the questions, including edge cases and failure modes you had not thought of
Have Claude write the agreed requirements into a spec file
Start a fresh session and write tests from the spec covering behavior, edge cases and performance
Ask Claude to implement the feature and run the tests
Share the failing test output with Claude and repeat until the tests pass
