sequences.explanation: The interview surfaces considerations the developer had not anticipated and turns them into a spec. A fresh session then starts with clean context focused on the spec, tests define done before any implementation, and each round of failures goes back to Claude as concrete feedback.

sequences.prompt: Order one run of an automated pull-request review built on Claude Code.
steps: A push to the pull request triggers the workflow, which checks out the code
The job collects the diff and the findings already posted on the pull request
A fresh claude -p run starts with the repository's CLAUDE.md and the review criteria, asking for --output-format json with a --json-schema
Claude returns schema-valid findings, reporting only new or still-unaddressed issues
The job reads the structured_output field and checks the exit code
A script posts each finding as an inline comment on the pull request
sequences.explanation: The job gathers its context before calling Claude: the diff and the earlier findings. A fresh non-interactive run with the project standards returns machine-parseable findings, which the job validates and only then posts as inline comments.

sequences.prompt: Put the stages of a validated extraction pipeline in order, from defining the output to handling the leftovers.
steps: Define an extraction tool whose JSON schema has nullable fields and an unclear or other option for categories
Call the model with the document, the tool and the normalization rules in the prompt
Check the stop reason, then read the extraction from the tool-use block
Validate the result in code for semantic rules such as totals and date order
On a fixable failure, retry with the document, the failed extraction and the specific errors
After a small retry cap, route anything still failing to human review
sequences.explanation: The schema comes first because its design prevents fabrication. The stop reason is checked before the output is trusted, and code validation catches the semantic errors that constrained output cannot. A retry carries the document, the failed attempt and the exact errors, and a cap sends the unresolvable cases to a person instead of looping.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of running a large extraction job through the Message Batches API.
steps: Refine the prompt and schema on a small representative sample
Build one request per document, each with a unique custom_id
Submit the batch
Poll the batch status until it reports that processing has ended
Retrieve the results and match each one to its document by custom_id
Resubmit only the failed or expired requests after fixing their causes, for example by chunking oversized documents
sequences.explanation: Tuning on a sample comes first so most requests succeed on the first pass. Each request needs its custom_id before submission, because results return in any order. After polling shows the batch has ended, results are matched by custom_id, and only the failures are rebuilt and resubmitted.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of recovering a long multi-agent codebase analysis after a crash, using a manifest.
steps: Each agent exports its state to a known location as it completes work
The run is interrupted and the coordinator restarts
The coordinator loads the manifest of exported agent states
The coordinator works out which agents finished and which work remains
The saved state is injected into the prompts of the agents that must continue
The resumed agents carry on with the remaining work only
The coordinator merges the earlier and the new results into the final output
sequences.explanation: State must be written before the crash, in a place that outlives any single agent. On resume the coordinator reads the manifest, decides what is left and injects the saved state into the resumed agents, because subagents start with an empty context. Only the remaining work is repeated, and the results are merged at the end.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of building confidence-based human review for an extraction pipeline.
steps: Have the model output a confidence score for each extracted field
Run the extractor on a labeled validation set
Compare the scores with the actual accuracy by document type and field
Set review thresholds from the accuracy observed at each confidence level
Route low-confidence fields and conflicting source documents to human reviewers
Review stratified random samples of the high-confidence extractions
Use the sample results to spot new error patterns and adjust the thresholds
sequences.explanation: Scores are only an opinion until they are checked against labeled data, so calibration comes before routing. Once thresholds exist, reviewers see the doubtful items first, and continuing stratified sampling of the confident ones measures the true error rate and feeds back into the thresholds.

caseStudies.title: Brightwell Home: A Support Agent Stuck at 61% Resolution
caseStudies.scenario: Brightwell Home sells kitchen appliances online and has built a customer support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It resolves returns, billing disputes and delivery problems through four custom MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. The target is 80% first-contact resolution; the agent currently reaches 61%. Transcript reviews show four problems. First, get_customer and lookup_order each have a one-line description, and the system prompt says "for any order question, begin by looking up the customer", so pasted order numbers such as #48213 are often sent to get_customer. Second, lookup_order returns dates as Unix timestamps and a numeric status code, while get_customer returns ISO 8601 dates and text statuses; the agent has twice misjudged return deadlines as a result. Third, company policy allows automatic refunds up to $150 and requires a human for larger ones. The prompt states this, yet a few larger refunds have still gone through. Fourth, when the order service times out, lookup_order returns only the word "Error", and the agent either apologizes at once or retries the call endlessly. The team wants each fix to match its cause.

questions.question: Which change best prevents refunds above the $150 limit from going through without a human?
questions.explanation: Policy limits with financial consequences need deterministic enforcement. A pre-execution hook blocks the call and its reason redirects the agent to the escalation tool. More examples are still probabilistic, an email after the fact is detection rather than prevention, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.
options: A pre-execution hook that denies process_refund above $150 and tells the agent to call escalate_to_human
Two further worked examples in the prompt showing the agent escalating a $300 refund instead of processing it
A post-execution hook that emails finance whenever a refund above $150 has been processed by the agent
A step asking the model to state its confidence before each refund and to escalate below 80%

questions.question: Which change is the most robust fix for the misjudged return deadlines?
questions.explanation: The two tools disagree on formats, which can be fixed deterministically after each call. A post-execution hook converts timestamps and status codes before the model reads them. A prompt note depends on the model applying it every time, double-checking doubles the calls, and a bigger model still faces mixed formats.
options: A note in the system prompt explaining that one tool returns Unix timestamps and the other ISO 8601 dates
A post-execution hook that converts dates and status codes into one format before the model reads results
An instruction to double-check every date by calling both tools again for each order that is discussed
A switch to a larger model so that the agent reasons better about dates in several formats

questions.question: What should lookup_order return when the order service times out?
questions.explanation: A timeout is a transient failure, so the result should carry the error flag, a category, a retryable marker and a short description. That lets the agent retry sensibly or explain the delay. The bare word "Error" caused today's behavior, an empty success hides the outage, and ending the session abandons the customer.
options: The single word "Error", plus a note to the agent to apologize to the customer straight away
An empty list marked as successful, so that the conversation can simply continue without a break
A result with the error flag set, a transient category, a retryable marker and a short description
An exception that ends the whole support session so that nothing further can go wrong

questions.question: Which two changes would best stop pasted order numbers from being sent to get_customer? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Both causes are in the definitions the model reads: one-line descriptions that do not separate the tools, and a keyword-heavy prompt line that ties every order question to the customer lookup. Rewriting the descriptions and the prompt line fixes them. A keyword router overrides the model, merging the tools hides the ambiguity, and temperature does not change what the tools mean.
options: Rewrite both descriptions with accepted identifier formats, example queries and a boundary between the tools
Reword the system-prompt line to say when a customer lookup is needed instead of tying every order question to it
Add a keyword router that overrides the model whenever a message contains the word "order" in any form
Merge all four tools into one tool that handles every kind of request, so there is nothing to choose between
Lower the temperature so that the agent chooses tools more predictably from one conversation to the next

caseStudies.title: Meridian Insights: A Research Assistant That Misses Things
caseStudies.scenario: Meridian Insights, a consulting firm, has built a research assistant with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis and report writing. In a test run on "the economics of battery recycling", the coordinator created three search tasks (collection logistics, recycling costs and recovered-metal prices) and launched them one per turn, so the run took six minutes. It then invoked the synthesis agent with the instruction "combine the findings from the earlier agents". The agent produced a generic overview with no sources, and it kept trying web searches because it had been configured with the same toolset as the search agent. Reviewers also noticed that the report said nothing about regulation or labor, even though each subagent had completed its task. Finally, when the search agent timed out on one task, it returned the message "search unavailable", and the coordinator carried on without noticing that one subtopic had no sources at all.

questions.question: Which change would most reduce the six-minute run time?
questions.explanation: The three searches are independent, so launching them from a single coordinator response lets them run concurrently, and the time approaches that of the slowest one. Merging them into one subagent serializes the work, a smaller model only shortens each step, and a higher turn limit does not change the schedule.
options: Have the coordinator emit all three search launch calls in one response, since the tasks are independent
Merge the three search tasks into one subagent prompt so that only a single launch is needed
Use a smaller model for the coordinator so that each of its turns completes more quickly
Increase the coordinator's maximum number of turns so that it can process more tasks per run

questions.question: Why did the synthesis agent produce a generic overview without sources, and what is the fix?
questions.explanation: Subagents start with an isolated context, so "the findings from the earlier agents" meant nothing to the synthesis agent. The fix is to pass the complete findings in its prompt as structured records that keep source details. Temperature and summary length are unrelated, and letting it search for itself duplicates work and invites out-of-role behavior.
options: Subagent context is isolated, so it never saw the findings; pass them as structured records with sources
Its temperature was too low for synthesis, so raising it would make the writing more specific and detailed
The search agent's summaries were too long to digest, so the search agent should be told to send shorter ones
It lacks the web-search tools it needs, so it should be given them to find the sources on its own

questions.question: How should the synthesis agent's tools be handled?
questions.explanation: The agent searches because search tools are in its toolset. Restricting each subagent to the tools of its role removes the temptation deterministically. A prompt line is probabilistic, more search tools make the problem worse, and a cap of two searches still allows out-of-role behavior.
options: Keep all of its tools and add a prompt line telling it not to search for anything
Add more search tools to its toolset so that each search it performs is more accurate
Restrict it to the tools its role needs, which removes web search from its toolset
Let it keep searching, but cap it at two search calls per run to limit the damage

questions.question: Which two changes address the missing regulation and labor coverage and the unnoticed timeout? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The coverage gap comes from the coordinator's narrow decomposition, so it should enumerate the dimensions of the topic before delegating. The unnoticed timeout needs structured error context so the coordinator can recover. Writing sections from general knowledge loses sourcing, an empty success suppresses the failure, and a call cap does not target either problem.
options: Have the coordinator list the major dimensions of the topic, including regulation and labor, before delegating, and assign them across subagents
Have subagents return structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results) so the coordinator can react to a timeout
Ask the report agent to add sections on regulation and labor from its general knowledge of the subject
Return an empty result marked as successful when a search times out, so that the output format stays uniform
Limit the whole run to three subagent calls so that costs stay predictable from one run to the next

caseStudies.title: Orbit Labs: A Developer Productivity Agent
caseStudies.scenario: Orbit Labs gives its engineers a developer-productivity agent built on the Claude Agent SDK. It uses the built-in Read, Write, Bash, Grep and Glob tools plus three MCP servers: a shared Jira server defined in the repository's .mcp.json, a deploy-calendar server the team wrote for its release rules, and a symbol-aware code-search server that one engineer, Priya, runs privately. The main codebase, ledger-core, has about 2,800 files. Asked "where is the retry logic for payment webhooks?", the agent reads dozens of files before answering and often runs out of context. Priya's search server is described only as "Searches code", and the agent keeps using Grep instead of it. The Jira entry in .mcp.json currently has a personal access token pasted in as plain text. Priya also keeps a named session, webhook-audit, in which she mapped the payment module last week. Since then colleagues have rewritten six of its files, and when she resumed the session yesterday, the agent confidently described functions that no longer exist.

questions.question: What is the best way for the agent to answer the question about the webhook retry logic?
questions.explanation: Building understanding incrementally keeps context focused: search file contents for entry points, then read only the files the results point to. Reading a whole directory wastes context, file-name length says nothing about relevance, and asking the engineer first delays work the agent can start itself.
options: Search for webhook and retry terms to find entry points, then read only the files that matter
Read every file under the payments directory first, in order, so that nothing at all is missed
Use Glob to list all files in the repository and then read the ones with the longest names first
Ask the engineer to point to the right directory before doing anything else in the codebase

questions.question: How should the Jira entry in .mcp.json be changed?
questions.explanation: Environment variable expansion keeps the committed file free of secrets while every engineer supplies the value locally, and the exposed token must be rotated because it is already in history. Moving the file, encoding the token, or ignoring the file each break sharing or leave the secret exposed.
options: Replace the pasted token with ${JIRA_TOKEN}, have each engineer set it, and rotate the exposed token
Move the file into each engineer's home directory so that the token is no longer in the repository
Encode the pasted token in base64 so that it is not readable at a glance to anyone browsing the file
Keep the token as it is but add the file to the ignore list so that it is not committed again

questions.question: The agent keeps using Grep instead of Priya's symbol-aware search server. What is the most effective fix?
questions.explanation: The agent chooses from descriptions, and "Searches code" gives it no reason to prefer the server. Expanding the description with capabilities, outputs and when to prefer the tool addresses the cause. Removing Grep for everyone is heavy-handed, project scope does not change preference, and renaming the tool to match a built-in adds confusion.
options: Expand the server's tool description with what it understands beyond text, what it returns, when to use it
Remove Grep from the agent's tools for every engineer, so that the code-search server is the only choice
Move the server into the committed project file so that it takes priority over the built-in search tools
Rename the tool to Grep so that the agent treats it as though it were the familiar built-in one

questions.question: Which two approaches are sound ways for Priya to continue her webhook-audit work? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The old session is mostly valid but six files changed, so either resume with a note naming those files, or start fresh from a short summary of what still holds. Relying on the old analysis keeps stale results, forking copies the same stale history, and the agent cannot tell which files changed unless it is told.
options: Resume the session and list the six rewritten files so that the agent re-reads them before answering
Start a new session seeded with a short summary of the findings that are still valid
Resume the session and rely on the earlier analysis because it was thorough and carefully checked
Fork the session so that the copy refreshes its own file contents without being told what changed
Ask the agent to decide for itself which of the files might have changed since the analysis

caseStudies.title: Larkspur Freight: Claude Code Across a Monorepo
caseStudies.scenario: Larkspur Freight keeps its route-planning API (TypeScript), customer web app (React) and infrastructure code (Terraform) in one monorepo, and about twenty engineers use Claude Code for features, refactoring, debugging and documentation. Four problems have come up. First, new engineers say Claude ignores the team's naming and error-handling conventions. Investigation shows that those conventions were written into the CLAUDE.md in one senior engineer's home directory, while the repository's own file contains only build commands. Second, the testing conventions (use the shared fixtures, make no network calls) must apply to files ending in .test.ts that sit in dozens of folders, but the 500-line root CLAUDE.md also carries Terraform and React rules, which load for every task. Third, a /release-notes workflow reads fifty merged pull requests and floods the developer's session with intermediate text, while a /deploy workflow must never start unless a person asks for it. Fourth, next sprint the team must replace its in-house job queue with either a hosted queue service or a database-backed queue; each option needs different infrastructure and touches workers, deployment scripts and tests across many modules. A small ticket in the same sprint asks for a fix to an off-by-one error in one pagination helper.

questions.question: Which change gives new engineers the team's conventions while keeping each engineer's personal preferences private?
questions.explanation: The conventions reached only one person because the user-level file lives in a home directory, outside the repository. Committing them in the project-level file gives every clone the same standards, and each engineer's own user-level file stays private. Copying files by hand drifts out of date, auto memory is machine-local notes that Claude writes for one user, and pasting the conventions into every session is the manual routine the instruction file exists to remove.
options: Commit the shared conventions in the project-level file and keep personal preferences in the user-level file
Copy the senior engineer's home-directory file onto every new engineer's machine during onboarding
Let auto memory collect the conventions from developers' corrections, since it keeps shared notes for the whole team
Ask each new engineer to paste the conventions into the opening prompt of every session they start

questions.question: How should the testing conventions be delivered so that they apply to test files in any folder and stay out of the way otherwise?
questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude reads or edits a matching file, and the glob follows the file type wherever it sits. A copy in every test folder would be duplicated dozens of times and miss new folders. An @import organizes content but the imported text still loads at launch, and a heading in the root file still costs its tokens in every session.
options: A rule file in .claude/rules/ whose paths pattern matches every file ending in .test.ts
A copy of the testing conventions in a CLAUDE.md inside each folder that holds tests
An @import line in the root CLAUDE.md that pulls in the testing conventions document
A heading in the root CLAUDE.md saying the testing conventions apply only when editing tests

questions.question: Which two configurations fit the /release-notes and /deploy workflows? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: A skill with context set to fork runs in a separate subagent context, so the long intermediate output stays out of the main session and only the result returns. Setting disable-model-invocation to true on /deploy means the workflow starts only when a person types it. In current Claude Code, allowed-tools pre-approves tools rather than blocking others, so it would make a deploy smoother, not safer. An argument-hint only shows a hint in autocomplete, and procedural steps in the root file cost context in every session.
options: Make /release-notes a skill with context set to fork, so its long intermediate output stays out of the main session
Set disable-model-invocation to true on /deploy, so that the workflow runs only when a person types the command
List the deploy commands in the allowed-tools field of /deploy, so that Claude is blocked from running anything else
Give /deploy an argument-hint, so that Claude cannot start it without a human supplying an argument
Move the release-notes steps into the root CLAUDE.md, so that they are available in every session

questions.question: Which pairing of workflows best fits the queue replacement and the pagination fix?
questions.explanation: The queue decision has architectural and infrastructure consequences across many modules, which is what plan mode is for: explore, compare the options, approve a plan, then execute. The Explore subagent keeps the discovery output out of the main window. The pagination fix is a single-function change with a clear cause, where planning only adds overhead. Applying one mode to both ignores the difference in uncertainty and scope, and the reverse pairing starts the risky change without a design.
options: Plan mode for the queue replacement, using the Explore subagent to map its usage, and direct execution for the pagination fix
Direct execution for both, because the team reviews every pull request before merging and can catch problems then
Plan mode for both, so that every change in the sprint follows the same careful and consistent process
Direct execution for the queue replacement, starting with the hosted service, and plan mode for the pagination fix

caseStudies.title: Northgate Billing: Claude Code in the Pull Request Pipeline
caseStudies.scenario: Northgate Billing runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions to review pull requests and to propose tests for new code. The review job calls claude -p with a prose prompt, splits the answer on blank lines with a script and posts it all as one long comment. Reviewers report four problems. Remarks cannot be attached to lines of the diff, because the script has no reliable way to tell which file and line each one concerns. After every push the job posts the earlier remarks again together with the new ones. The test proposals often repeat cases the suite already covers or exercise trivial getters, and they ignore the team's shared fixtures; the repository's CLAUDE.md contains build commands only. In another workflow, the Claude Code session that writes a feature is then asked to approve its own change, and it approves almost every time. Finally, a nightly changelog job was added as the command claude with the prompt as its only argument; it never finishes, because the process sits waiting for input.

questions.question: How can the review job attach each remark to the correct file and line?
questions.explanation: A schema turns the output into data: each finding carries fields the script maps directly onto an inline comment, and the CLI returns the validated object in the structured_output field. Asking for a layout in the prompt still depends on the model keeping to the wording, stream-json is a format for streaming events rather than a way to enforce a shape, and a markdown table parsed with a pattern breaks as soon as the layout shifts.
options: Use --output-format json with a --json-schema for findings (file, line, severity, message) and post each entry from structured_output
Ask in the prompt for every remark to start with the file name and line number, and keep splitting the text with the script
Switch to --output-format stream-json so that the script receives each remark as a separate event while it is being generated
Ask Claude for a markdown table with one row per remark, and have the script parse each row with a regular expression

questions.question: What is the best way to stop old remarks from being posted again after each push?
questions.explanation: Giving Claude the findings that are already posted, and asking for only new or still-unaddressed issues, fixes the cause: the model knows what has been said and what has been fixed. An exact-match filter in the script misses remarks that are reworded, a cap on remarks hides the repetition without removing it, and skipping later pushes leaves new code unreviewed.
options: Pass the findings already posted into the prompt and ask Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
Have the script drop any remark whose text exactly matches an earlier comment on the same pull request
Cap the job at three remarks per run, so that any repeated remarks matter less to the developers
Review only the first push of each pull request, and skip the review for every push that follows it

questions.question: Which two changes would most improve the test proposals? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Existing test files in the prompt let Claude see which scenarios the suite already covers, and documenting the testing standards, what a worthwhile test looks like and the fixtures in CLAUDE.md steers the output toward valuable tests that use them. Asking for more tests invites the trivial ones, --bare skips CLAUDE.md so it would remove the guidance, and a higher turn limit only lets the job run longer.
options: Include the existing test files in the prompt, so that Claude can see which scenarios the suite already covers
Document the testing standards, what makes a test worth writing and the available fixtures in CLAUDE.md
Ask for as many tests as possible in each run, so that no possible scenario is ever missed
Add --bare to the command, so that project-specific guidance cannot distract the model during generation
Raise the turn limit, so that Claude can keep generating more tests until it runs out of ideas

questions.question: Which two changes address the self-approving reviews and the nightly job that never finishes? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: A session that wrote the change still holds its own reasoning and tends to defend it, so an independent instance given only the diff and the criteria is the better reviewer. The command claude with a prompt opens an interactive session that waits for input; -p makes the run non-interactive, so it prints the result and exits. Asking the writing session to be more critical keeps the bias, a longer timeout with retries only repeats the hang, and bypassing permission checks removes safeguards without touching the cause.
options: Run the review in a separate, fresh Claude Code invocation given only the diff and the review criteria
Add the -p flag to the nightly command, so that Claude Code prints the result and exits
Ask the writing session to review its work again, this time telling it to be as critical as possible
Give the nightly job a much longer timeout and an automatic retry whenever it runs out of time
Run both jobs with all permission checks bypassed, so that nothing can ever wait for a person

caseStudies.title: Ledgerline Supply: An Invoice Reader Finance Cannot Trust
caseStudies.scenario: Ledgerline Supply extracts data from supplier invoices that arrive as PDFs and emails in dozens of layouts. Each invoice's text goes to Claude with an extraction tool whose JSON schema marks invoice_number, po_number and total as required; a validator then checks the result before it feeds the accounting system. Three problems have surfaced. First, about a third of suppliers never use purchase-order numbers, yet their results contain convincing numbers that do not exist. Second, roughly 4% of results pass the schema but have line items that do not add up to the total, and finance finds them only at month end. Third, when the validator finds ship_to_country empty, a loop re-sends the request up to five times with the error. It fixes date and currency formats, but for about 2% of invoices the country stays missing, because it appears only on a customs form attached to the shipment and never sent to the pipeline. Separately, management wants to re-extract a 200,000-invoice archive. Nobody needs the results for two weeks, a few hundred documents are known to exceed the context window, and the prompt has been tried on only a dozen invoices.

questions.question: Which schema change best stops the invented purchase-order numbers without weakening the fields that every invoice has?
questions.explanation: Only the purchase-order number is sometimes absent, so only that field should allow null; invoice_number and total are always present and are worth keeping required so that omissions are caught. Making everything optional invites silent gaps, a prompt sentence cannot overcome the pressure of a required field, and other-plus-detail is a pattern for categories, not for missing values.
options: Make all three fields optional, so that the model is never pushed to produce a value it cannot see in the invoice
Keep all three required and add a prompt sentence telling the model never to invent a purchase-order number
Make po_number nullable and keep invoice_number and total required, since every invoice has those two
Make po_number required but add an "other" value with a detail string for suppliers that skip it

questions.question: Where should the check that the line items add up to the total live?
questions.explanation: A relationship between fields is a semantic rule, and schemas constrain structure and types rather than arithmetic. Validation code can recompute the sum and, on a mismatch, drive a retry that carries the specific error. A prompt reminder is only a hope, and catching the problem after loading means bad data has already reached the accounting system.
options: In the JSON schema, as a rule that the total must equal the sum of all the line items on the invoice
In validation code that recomputes the sum, compares it with the total and sends any mismatch back as a retry error
In a prompt sentence telling the model to double-check its arithmetic before it fills in the total
In the accounting system after the data is loaded, where finance already reconciles the accounts

questions.question: What is the best response to the 2% of invoices whose ship_to_country stays missing after five retries?
questions.explanation: The country is not in the text the model receives, so no retry can find it. Supplying the form that holds it fixes the input, and where the form is missing a person has to follow up. More attempts waste calls, inferring a country from an address invents a fact, and a required field only adds pressure to fabricate.
options: Raise the retry cap from five to ten so that the model has more chances to find the country
Let the model infer the country from the supplier address whenever the field is empty
Mark ship_to_country as required, so that the validator error carries more weight on each retry
Include the customs form in the input where it exists, and route invoices without it to a person

questions.question: Which three steps best fit the archive re-extraction? (Choose three.)
questions.explanation: Nobody waits for the archive results, so the Batches API saves half the cost. A sample run settles prompt and schema problems before they are repeated 200,000 times. custom_id lets you find failures and resubmit only those, with oversized invoices split into chunks. Running everything synchronously forfeits the discount, and results do not arrive in submission order, so position cannot identify an invoice.
options: Submit the archive through the Message Batches API, since nobody needs the results for two weeks
Run a representative sample through the same request shape and refine the prompt before the full submission
Give every request a custom_id, then resubmit only the failures, splitting oversized invoices into chunks
Run all 200,000 invoices on the synchronous API in parallel so that failures appear immediately
Submit everything at once and match results to invoices by their order in the results file

compare.scenario: A team is deciding how its agent loop should decide when to stop calling the model. Which stop condition is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Stop when the response's stop reason is end_turn, with a turn limit kept only as a handled safety net.
compare.optionB: Stop when the response text contains the word "finished", or after ten iterations, whichever comes first.
compare.why: The stop reason is the structured signal that the model has finished. The combined condition looks cautious because it has two triggers, but phrase matching depends on wording the model may never use, and a bare iteration count either truncates legitimate long tasks or lets short ones end on a coincidence.

compare.scenario: A coordinator must have a synthesis subagent write a cited report from search results gathered by an earlier subagent. Which delegation is better?
compare.optionA: Pass the complete findings in the prompt as structured records, each with claim, excerpt, source and date.
compare.optionB: Tell the synthesis agent to combine the results the search agent produced earlier and to cite them.
compare.why: A subagent has an isolated context, so only what is in its prompt exists for it. The short instruction is tempting because the search agent really did produce the results, but the synthesis agent cannot see them, so it will invent or generalize, and prose would lose the attribution anyway.

compare.scenario: A coordinator must research five independent regional markets. Which launch strategy is better?
compare.optionA: Emit five subagent launch calls in one response so the markets are researched concurrently.
compare.optionB: Launch one subagent per turn so that each result can shape the next prompt.
compare.why: The markets do not depend on each other, so running them together cuts the time to roughly the slowest single task. Sequential launching is tempting because earlier results could refine later prompts, but that benefit is imaginary when the tasks are independent and the cost is the sum of all durations.

compare.scenario: An agent must never issue a refund to a customer who has not been verified. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: A gate in code that rejects refund calls until the customer lookup has returned a verified id.
compare.optionB: A system-prompt section that explains the verification rule and gives three worked examples.
compare.why: The rule has financial consequences, so it needs a deterministic guarantee. Worked examples are tempting because they are cheap and do improve compliance, but any prompt-based approach leaves a non-zero chance that a refund goes out unverified.

compare.scenario: A long session mapped a large codebase. Since then sixty commits have changed most of the modules it examined. Which way of continuing is better?
compare.optionA: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of the findings that still hold.
compare.optionB: Resume the old session and ask the agent to be careful about anything that might have changed.
compare.why: Most of the old tool results are now wrong, and a fresh start avoids carrying them forward. Resuming is tempting because it keeps every detail, but the agent cannot re-observe files by being told to be careful, so stale content keeps influencing its answers.

compare.scenario: One process_document tool takes a mode parameter, and its modes return completely different outputs: a list of fields, a prose summary, and a verification verdict. The agent often chooses the wrong mode. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: Split it into extract_fields, summarize_document and verify_claim tools, each with its own contract.
compare.optionB: Keep one tool and describe the output shape of each mode at length in its description.
compare.why: Distinct purposes with distinct output contracts give the model clear choices and callers predictable results. Keeping one tool with longer documentation is tempting because it means fewer tools, but the model must still pick a mode correctly and parse three shapes from the same name.

compare.scenario: A refund tool must report that a request falls outside the 90-day window. Which response is better?
compare.optionA: A result flagged as an error, categorized as a business error, marked not retryable, with a customer-friendly explanation.
compare.optionB: A result flagged as an error with the text "Request failed", so the agent can try again with different arguments.
compare.why: The agent needs to know the failure is final and what to tell the customer. The generic version uses the error flag, which makes it tempting, but a vague message invites retries that can never succeed and gives the agent nothing to say.

compare.scenario: A team wants every developer to have the same Postgres MCP server, with the connection credentials kept out of the repository. Which setup is better?
compare.optionA: A project .mcp.json that references the connection string as ${DATABASE_URL}, supplied from each developer's environment.
compare.optionB: Each developer adds the server to their own user config with the connection string typed in.
compare.why: The shared file gives everyone the same, version-controlled setup while the secret stays local. Per-developer user configs also avoid committing the secret, which makes them tempting, but every developer must configure the server by hand and the setups drift apart.

compare.scenario: A pipeline must run extract_metadata before anything else and then let the model choose follow-up tools from the result. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Force extract_metadata on the first request, then continue on automatic tool choice.
compare.optionB: Instruct the model in the system prompt to call extract_metadata first on every task.
compare.why: Forcing the named tool guarantees the opening step, and automatic choice afterwards leaves the model free to pick enrichment tools. The prompt instruction is simpler and usually works, which makes it tempting, but it cannot guarantee the step happens.

compare.scenario: Kubernetes manifests ending in .k8s.yaml sit in the deploy folder of about thirty services, and every one must follow the same conventions. Developers editing other files should not load these conventions. Which setup is better?
compare.optionA: One rule file in .claude/rules/ whose paths field matches **/deploy/*.k8s.yaml
compare.optionB: A CLAUDE.md in each service's deploy folder that repeats the manifest conventions
compare.why: The glob rule is written once, follows the file type into every folder and loads only when Claude touches a matching manifest. Per-folder files are the tempting runner-up because directory-level files also load on demand, but thirty copies drift apart and a new service is missed until someone remembers to add one.

compare.scenario: A 3,000-line billing module must be split into separate invoice, payment and tax modules. Callers are spread across the repository and the team has not yet decided where the boundaries go. How should the developer open the session?
compare.optionA: Use plan mode: have Claude map the dependencies (using the Explore subagent for the discovery) and propose boundaries, then approve a plan before any edits
compare.optionB: Describe the three modules and let Claude start editing at once, correcting boundary mistakes as they appear in review
compare.why: The boundaries are an unsettled design decision that touches many callers, which is what plan mode exists for: a plan is cheap to change and edits spread across the repository are expensive to unpick. Starting directly feels faster and suits a change you could state in one sentence, but here the speed is borrowed from rework later.

compare.scenario: A pull-request review job reruns on every push, and developers keep seeing remarks they have already read. Which fix is better?
compare.optionA: Pass the findings already posted into the prompt and ask Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
compare.optionB: Have the script compare each new remark with the posted comments and skip those whose text matches exactly
compare.why: Giving Claude the earlier findings lets it recognize the same problem however it would be worded, and also notice which ones have been fixed. The script-side filter is the tempting runner-up because it needs no prompt change, but Claude rarely repeats a remark word for word, so exact matching lets duplicates through and cannot tell resolved issues from open ones.

compare.scenario: A review bot keeps flagging harmless patterns, and developers dismiss most of its comments. The team must choose the prompt change that will cut these false positives. Which is better?
compare.optionA: Tell the model to be conservative and to report only findings it is highly confident about.
compare.optionB: Define which categories to report and which to skip, and add a few example pairs of acceptable and genuinely problematic code with a one-line reason each.
compare.why: Defining categories and adding example pairs gives the model a decision boundary and shows how to apply it to new cases. Confidence wording is tempting because it is cheap and sounds careful, but it changes tone rather than what counts as a problem, and the model's own confidence is not a calibrated measure of precision.

compare.scenario: About a third of supplier invoices carry no purchase-order number, and the extraction schema currently marks that field as required. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: Make po_number nullable and tell the model to return null when the invoice shows no purchase-order number.
compare.optionB: Keep po_number required and add a prompt line saying the model must never invent a purchase-order number.
compare.why: A required field pressures the model to supply something, and a prompt prohibition has to fight that pressure on every call. A nullable field lets the schema itself express honest absence. The prohibition looks safe because it is explicit, but a plausible fake number is worse than a null.

compare.scenario: A coding agent has just finished a change, and you want an automated review that catches subtle defects. Which setup is better?
compare.optionA: Ask the same session to review its own change with extended thinking enabled and a prompt telling it to be highly critical.
compare.optionB: Start a fresh Claude instance that receives only the diff and the review criteria, and have it return findings.
compare.why: The author session still holds the reasoning that produced the change and tends to defend it; more thinking time or a sterner tone does not remove that. Self-review with extended thinking is tempting because it keeps all context and spends more reasoning effort, but independence is what exposes subtle problems.

compare.scenario: A customer writes: "Honestly, get me a real person, I am done with chatbots." The issue is a simple address change that the agent could handle. Which response is better?
compare.optionA: Transfer the customer to a human agent immediately, passing along a summary of what is already known.
compare.optionB: Acknowledge the frustration and offer to complete the address change in one step, since the problem is simple.
compare.why: An explicit request for a human is honored at once, however easy the issue is. The offer is tempting because the fix really is simple, and it is the right pattern when a customer is only frustrated; here it overrides what the customer asked for.

compare.scenario: An agent must map a repository with thousands of files before a refactor, and answer follow-up questions for several hours. Which approach to context is better?
compare.optionA: Let the main agent read everything itself in one session and rely on automatic compaction to make room.
compare.optionB: Send narrow questions to subagents that return short summaries, and keep key findings in a scratchpad file.
compare.why: Delegation keeps bulky reads out of the main window, and the scratchpad keeps findings exact, which counters the drift toward generic answers in long sessions. Relying on compaction alone is tempting because it is automatic, but a summary of hours of raw reading loses the specific classes and paths that later questions need.

compare.scenario: A team wants to cut human review of invoice extractions. Which evidence should they rely on before doing so?
compare.optionA: Accuracy by document type and field on a labeled set, plus ongoing stratified samples of the confident extractions.
compare.optionB: One overall accuracy figure above the target, checked on a random sample drawn from all invoices together.
compare.why: Segment-level results show which document types and fields are safe to automate, and continuing stratified sampling catches new patterns after review is reduced. A single pooled figure is tempting because it is simple and often high, but it is dominated by the largest, easiest segment and hides the weak ones.
